the daily-streak feature keeps more of Parla's users practicing than it drives away from the app
most of Parla's users who practice daily do so only because they do not want to lose their streaks
the central purpose of a language app is to keep as many of its users as possible practicing every day
questions.explanation: Lena holds that a feature that drives learners away is contrary to the app's purpose 'whatever else it does'; Marcus holds that such a feature serves the purpose if it keeps far more learners than it loses, so they disagree over whether driving some learners away settles the matter, as (B) says. (C) is the trap: Marcus asserts it, but Lena never disputes the numbers; her 'whatever else it does' makes them irrelevant to her. (D) stretches Marcus's 'several others' per quitter into a claim about most daily users, and (A) is common ground.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Lena: Drop the streak feature; some users quit after breaking a streak, and a feature that drives learners away is contrary to the app's purpose whatever else it does.; Marcus: Some do quit, but several others practice only to keep their streaks; a feature that keeps far more than it loses serves the app's purpose.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Marcus opens by conceding Lena's fact: some users do quit. So the facts about quitting aren't the issue. Look at the principles. Lena: drives learners away → contrary to the purpose, "whatever else it does." Marcus: keeps far more than it drives away → serves the purpose. Imagine a feature that loses one user and keeps ten. Lena says it's contrary to the purpose; Marcus says it serves it. That's the clash. Now the trap: does Lena deny that the feature keeps more users than it loses? She never addresses it. Her "whatever else it does" means the count doesn't matter to her. An answer about the count has only one speaker on record.

choices.note: Agreement. Lena says it, and Marcus concedes it: "Some users do quit after breaking a streak."

CORRECT. Lena: drives learners away → contrary to the purpose, "whatever else it does." So for her, driving some away is enough (yes). Marcus: a feature that drives some away but keeps far more "serves the app's central purpose." So for him it isn't enough (no). The answer states Lena's principle as a sufficiency claim, which is why it's easy to skip past.

Tempting, and the main trap. Marcus asserts this, so it feels like Lena must deny it. But Lena never disputes the numbers. Her point is that losing learners is disqualifying no matter how many the feature keeps. She could grant the numbers and keep her view. One speaker on record.
Too strong, and Marcus only. He says several users practice for streaks for each one who quits. That doesn't make them most of the daily users. Lena says nothing about it.
Neither speaker defines the app's purpose this way. Marcus's principle is about keeping more learners than you lose, not about maximizing daily practice, and Lena never states the purpose at all.

questions.stimulus:
Okafor: Velarix, a large pterosaur, was a scavenger, not a hunter. Its beak lacked the hooked tip that every living bird of prey uses to tear flesh, and an animal without such a tool could not have subdued live prey of any size.

Strand: Many living storks hunt successfully with straight beaks: they swallow small prey whole. Nothing about Velarix's beak would have kept it from hunting that way. I agree, though, that it could not have taken large prey, which would have been impossible to swallow.
questions.stem: Okafor and Strand disagree over whether
choices: Velarix obtained at least some of its food by eating the remains of animals that were already dead
Velarix lacked the ability to capture and eat live prey of a large size
the shape of Velarix's beak rules out its having caught any live prey
Velarix was a hunter rather than a scavenger of animals that had already died
every living bird of prey uses a hooked beak tip to tear the flesh of the animals it eats
questions.explanation: Okafor says an animal without a hooked tip could not have subdued live prey of any size, so Velarix's beak rules out its catching any live prey; Strand says nothing about the beak would have kept it from swallowing small prey whole, so they disagree over (C). (D) is the trap: Strand says only that Velarix could have hunted that way, not that it was a hunter rather than a scavenger. (B) is explicitly agreed, and (A) is Okafor's view alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Okafor: Velarix was a scavenger; no hooked beak tip, and without one it couldn't subdue live prey of any size.; Strand: Storks hunt small prey with straight beaks, swallowing it whole; nothing about Velarix's beak kept it from doing the same; but it couldn't take large prey.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Okafor's rule: no hooked tip → can't subdue live prey of any size. Velarix had no hooked tip, so for Okafor it couldn't catch even small prey. Strand says nothing about Velarix's beak would have kept it from hunting small prey the stork way. That's a claim about ability: Velarix could do it. That's the clash: ability to take small prey. Now the trap. Is Strand saying Velarix WAS a hunter? No. He says it could have hunted, not that it did. Watch the switch from could to did.

choices.note: Okafor's view: a scavenger eats carrion. Strand never says Velarix didn't scavenge; it could have done both. One speaker only.
Agreement, and stated outright. Okafor says no prey of any size, and Strand says, "I agree, though, that it could not have taken large prey."

CORRECT. Okafor: no hooked tip → couldn't subdue live prey "of any size," so the beak rules out catching any live prey (yes). Strand: "Nothing about Velarix's beak would have kept it from hunting that way" (no). The answer turns Okafor's rule into a claim about what the beak "rules out," so you have to translate before you can match it.

Tempting, and the main trap. Okafor denies it, and Strand seems to be defending Velarix as a hunter. But Strand only says it could have hunted that way. He doesn't conclude that it was a hunter, let alone a hunter rather than a scavenger. Ability isn't a verdict.
Okafor's premise. Strand's storks hunt with straight beaks, but he never calls them birds of prey, so he doesn't contradict Okafor's claim about birds of prey.

questions.stimulus: Solar farm manager: We used to pay a crew to mow the grass that grows beneath our solar panels. This year we stopped mowing and instead leased the land to a farmer whose sheep now graze there. The sheep have kept the grass as short as the mowing did, and the lease earns us money instead of costing us any. So grazing sheep is a better way for us to control the grass than mowing was.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Would sheep raised on land beneath solar panels produce as much wool as sheep raised on open pasture?
Do other solar farms in the region still pay crews to mow the grass that grows beneath their panels?
Does the grass beneath the panels grow more slowly in the shade than grass in open fields does?
Do the sheep grazing beneath the panels cause any damage to the panels or to the wiring that connects them?
Would the farmer be willing to keep leasing the land if the lease payments were raised?
questions.explanation: The manager compares sheep and mowing on two points, grass height and cost, and concludes that sheep are better overall. The argument ignores any new cost the sheep might bring, and (D) asks about exactly that: damage to the panels would weaken the argument, and no damage would strengthen it. (E) is the tempting choice because it is about money, but a yes would only add a bonus and a no would not undo the savings the manager already has. (A) and (B) concern the farmer’s wool and other solar farms, not this farm’s choice.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Grazing sheep is a better way for the solar farm to control the grass than mowing was.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The sheep keep the grass as short as mowing did; the lease earns money, while mowing cost money.

breakdown.analysis: Better in every way that matters? The manager checked two things, grass height and cost, and declared sheep the winner. But sheep are big animals walking around expensive equipment. If they chew wires or crack panels, the savings could vanish. It’s like saying a teenager is a better babysitter than the agency because she’s cheaper and the kids like her, without asking whether she lets them play with matches. We want a question whose answer could go either way and push the argument in opposite directions: “Do the sheep cause damage?”

choices.note: Wool is the farmer’s business, not the solar farm’s. Whether the sheep are good wool producers doesn’t change whether grazing is better for the manager. Irrelevant.
What other farms do doesn’t tell us what’s best for this one. They might not have heard of the idea. Irrelevant.
Slow-growing grass would affect mowing and grazing alike. And the manager already tells us the sheep keep the grass as short as mowing did. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. This is the hidden cost. If the sheep damage panels or wiring, the money from the lease could be wiped out by repairs, and grazing may not be better at all. If they cause no damage, the manager’s comparison holds up. Either answer changes how strong the argument is.

Tempting, because it’s about money. But it’s one-sided. If the farmer would pay more, that’s a bonus; if not, the manager still earns the current lease and still saves the mowing cost. Neither answer touches the gap.

questions.stimulus: Driving instructor: Our school offers an optional course in night driving. Last year, students who took the course had far fewer accidents in their first year of licensed driving than did students who skipped it. So the course makes new drivers safer, and we should require every one of our students to take it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Does the night-driving course cost students more than the school’s other optional courses do?
Were the students who chose to take the course already more cautious drivers than those who skipped it?
Did the course takers who had accidents in their first year have most of those accidents at night?
Did most of the students who took the course rate it highly when they finished it?
Would requiring the course make it harder for the school to schedule its regular driving lessons?
questions.explanation: The students chose whether to take the course, so the difference in accidents might reflect who signed up rather than what the course taught. (B) asks about that: if the course takers were already more cautious, the argument is weakened; if they were not, the course looks responsible. (C) is tempting because it is about night driving, but how the course takers’ few accidents were timed does not show what caused the gap between the groups. (D) confuses liking a course with being helped by it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The night-driving course makes new drivers safer, so all students should be required to take it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Students who took the optional course had far fewer first-year accidents than students who skipped it.

breakdown.analysis: Who signs up for an optional safety course? Probably careful people. If the careful kids chose the course, they’d have fewer accidents anyway, course or no course. It’s like noticing that people who buy bike helmets crash less and concluding that helmets prevent crashes. We need a question that tells us whether the two groups were alike to begin with.

choices.note: The course’s price doesn’t tell us whether it works. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If the course takers were already more cautious, their lower accident rate could be due to who they are, not what they learned, and the argument is weak. If they weren’t, the course is the likely reason, and the argument is strong. Two answers, two directions.

Tempting, because the course is about night driving. But it asks only how the course takers’ few accidents were spread across the day. That doesn’t tell us whether the course, rather than the kind of student who chose it, produced the gap between the two groups.
Liking a course isn’t the same as being made safer by it. Students can rate a course highly and drive no better, or rate it poorly and drive much better. Doesn’t test the causal claim.

This bears on whether requiring the course is convenient, not on whether the course makes drivers safer, which is the claim the requirement rests on. One-sided at best: a yes adds a small cost, and a no tells us nothing.

questions.stimulus: Last spring, heavy snowmelt sent the Tarvin River higher than in any spring on record. Rafting outfitters along the river had predicted a busy season, since high water makes the river’s rapids more exciting. Yet the outfitters booked far fewer rafting trips last spring than they do in an ordinary spring.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Officials closed the river to rafting for much of last spring because the high water made it unsafe.
Rafters who book trips on the Tarvin River generally prefer exciting rapids to calmer stretches of water.
Several of the outfitters raised the prices of their rafting trips slightly before last spring began.
Rafting outfitters on other rivers in the region reported an unusually busy season last spring.
Unusually high water on the Tarvin River seldom lasts more than a few weeks before falling to ordinary levels.
questions.explanation: High water should have drawn more rafters, but if it was so high that officials closed the river for much of the spring, few trips could be booked at all. That is (A). (E) is tempting because it says the exciting water didn’t last, but a return to ordinary levels would give an ordinary season, not far fewer bookings. (C) fails because a slight price rise can’t produce a collapse in bookings, and (B) and (D) make the puzzle worse.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The river was the highest on record, which should have made rafting more exciting and popular, but outfitters booked far fewer trips than usual.

breakdown.analysis: How can the thing that should help the outfitters end up hurting them? Maybe the same high water had a downside. Too much of a good thing is a common answer to paradoxes. It’s like a restaurant expecting a rush during a big snowstorm because people love hot soup, then finding the roads closed. Prephrase: the high water itself kept people off the river.

choices.note: CORRECT. The very thing that made the rapids exciting also made them dangerous enough to close the river. If the river was closed for much of the spring, there were few trips to book. Both facts now fit together.
This explains why the outfitters expected a busy season. It makes the drop in bookings even more surprising. Deepens the puzzle.
Tempting, because price can affect demand. But “slightly” is the problem. A small price bump can’t explain far fewer bookings in a season that should have been unusually popular.
This makes the Tarvin’s slump stranger, not easier to understand. If people were out rafting elsewhere, demand wasn’t the problem. Deepens the puzzle.

Tempting, because it suggests the exciting water didn’t last. But once the river fell back to normal, outfitters should have had an ordinary season. This explains why the spring wasn’t extra busy, not why bookings fell far below an ordinary spring.

questions.stimulus: At Varo Ridge, an inland settlement occupied about 3,000 years ago, archaeologists have found hearths containing large quantities of fish bones. The nearest seacoast is more than 100 kilometers from Varo Ridge. Therefore, the people of Varo Ridge must have obtained their fish through trade with coastal communities.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the people of Varo Ridge preserve some of their fish by drying or salting it?
Did coastal communities of that era eat fish more often than the people of Varo Ridge did?
Were there any rivers or lakes near Varo Ridge 3,000 years ago that held fish?
Did the people of Varo Ridge also trade with other communities for goods other than food?
Was Varo Ridge farther from the seacoast than any other inland settlement of that era that archaeologists have studied?
questions.explanation: The argument treats the sea as the only possible source of fish. (C) tests that: if nearby rivers or lakes held fish, the people could have caught their own and the argument is weakened; if not, trade with the coast becomes the likely explanation. (D) is tempting because it is about trade, but a yes would show only that they traded for something, and a no would not rule out trading for fish. (A) is one-sided for the same reason: fish from a local lake can be dried too.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The people of Varo Ridge got their fish by trading with coastal communities.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Their hearths contain lots of fish bones; the sea is more than 100 kilometers away.

breakdown.analysis: Do fish only live in the sea? Of course not. Rivers and lakes have fish too. The argument treats “far from the sea” as “far from fish.” It’s like finding fresh apples in a city apartment and concluding they must have been shipped from a farm, without checking whether there’s a market downstairs. We need a question that tests whether a local source of fish existed.

choices.note: Tempting, because preserved fish could be carried a long way, which fits the trade story. But it’s one-sided. Fish caught in a nearby lake can be dried too, so a yes doesn’t point to the coast, and a no doesn’t rule trade out.
How much fish the coastal people ate says nothing about how fish got to Varo Ridge. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If nearby rivers or lakes held fish, the people of Varo Ridge could have caught their own, and the argument falls apart. If there were no such waters, trade with the coast is the best explanation left. Either answer moves the argument.

Tempting, because it’s about trade. But it’s one-sided. A yes shows they traded for something, not for fish. A no doesn’t rule out trading for fish. The real question is whether they needed to trade at all.

This borrows the stimulus’s point about distance, but how Varo Ridge ranks among other settlements doesn’t tell us where its fish came from. We already know the sea was over 100 kilometers away. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Council member: Our town’s public pool loses about $60,000 each summer. Last summer roughly 40,000 swimmers paid the pool’s $3 admission fee. If we raise the fee to $5, the extra $2 per swimmer will bring in $80,000, more than enough to cover the losses. So raising the admission fee will end the pool’s losses.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the pool lose more money last summer than it lost in the summer before?
Would far fewer people swim at the pool if the admission fee were raised to $5?
Do the neighboring towns charge more than $3 for admission to their public pools?
Does the town operate any other recreational facilities that also lose money each year?
Do most of the town’s residents want the public pool to remain open in future summers?
questions.explanation: The $80,000 figure assumes that 40,000 swimmers will keep coming at the higher price. (B) asks whether that is so: if attendance would drop sharply, the extra revenue could fall short; if it would not, the plan works. (C) is tempting, but higher fees elsewhere would only suggest that $5 is reasonable, and lower fees elsewhere would not show that swimmers would stay away. The remaining choices do not affect whether the fee increase covers the losses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Raising the pool’s fee from $3 to $5 will end its losses.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The pool loses about $60,000 a summer; 40,000 swimmers paid last summer; an extra $2 each would bring in $80,000.

breakdown.analysis: Will 40,000 people still show up if the price goes up by two-thirds? The math only works if attendance holds. It’s like a café deciding to double coffee prices and counting on selling the same number of cups. We need a question about how swimmers would react to the higher fee.

choices.note: The pool loses “about $60,000 each summer.” Whether last summer was a little worse than the one before doesn’t change whether the new fee covers the loss. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If far fewer people would swim at $5, the extra revenue could easily fall below $60,000, and the plan fails. If attendance would hold, $80,000 covers the losses. That’s the assumption the math rests on.

Tempting, because it hints at whether $5 is a normal price. But it’s indirect and one-sided. Swimmers in this town might still stop coming, and a lower fee elsewhere wouldn’t show that they would. It doesn’t settle the attendance question.
Other facilities losing money is a different problem. Irrelevant.
Residents can want the pool open and still refuse to pay $5 to swim. Doesn’t tell us whether the fee will cover the losses.

questions.stimulus: Lexicographer: The word ‘brackle,’ meaning a sudden summer hailstorm, appears in several letters written in the Tessan Valley in the 1790s. No earlier written use of the word has been found anywhere. So the word most likely originated in the Tessan Valley.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Is the word ‘brackle’ still used by people living in the Tessan Valley today?
Were the letters that use the word written by people with little formal schooling?
Do any modern dictionaries include the word ‘brackle’ among their entries?
Did people in the Tessan Valley in the 1790s have other words for sudden summer storms?
Have many letters and other writings survived from other regions from the 1790s and earlier?
questions.explanation: The argument infers the word’s birthplace from the fact that no earlier use has been found elsewhere. That silence means something only if plenty of writing from elsewhere survives to be searched. (E) asks about exactly that: if little survives, the lack of earlier uses tells us almost nothing; if a great deal survives, the lack is telling. (A) is the tempting choice, but whether people use the word today has no bearing on where it started.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: ‘Brackle’ most likely originated in the Tessan Valley.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: It appears in 1790s letters from the valley; no earlier written use has been found anywhere.

breakdown.analysis: “No earlier use has been found.” Found where? If almost nothing written elsewhere survives, of course no one has found the word there. Not finding something only counts when you had a real chance to find it. It’s like saying a song was first sung at your school because the only old recordings anyone has are from your school’s talent shows. We need a question about how much writing from other places is available to search.

choices.note: Tempting, because it connects the word to the valley. But current use tells us nothing about where the word began. Words travel and settle in new places all the time.
The writers’ schooling doesn’t tell us where the word came from. Irrelevant.
Whether today’s dictionaries list the word says nothing about its origin. Irrelevant.
Other words for storms could exist alongside ‘brackle’ no matter where it began. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If lots of writing from elsewhere survives and none of it uses the word earlier, the valley is a strong candidate. If very little survives, the absence of earlier uses is just a gap in the record. That decides whether the argument’s main evidence means anything.

questions.stimulus: In the year after the city of Corvale opened its bike-share program, the number of cars entering the downtown area each weekday fell by about 8 percent. During that year, riders made an average of 3,000 bike-share trips downtown each weekday. Clearly, the bike-share program is responsible for the drop in downtown car traffic.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did most of the people taking bike-share trips downtown formerly make those same trips by car?
Did the number of bike-share trips taken downtown grow steadily over the course of the year?
Are the people who use the bike-share program younger, on average, than people who drive downtown?
Is the bike-share program operated by the city itself or by a private company under contract?
Would adding bike-share stations in other neighborhoods also reduce car traffic in those neighborhoods?
questions.explanation: Bike-share trips reduce car traffic only if they replace car trips. (A) asks whether they did: if most riders formerly drove, the program plausibly explains the drop; if they formerly walked or took the bus, the 3,000 trips took few cars off the road and something else must explain it. (E) is the tempting choice, but it asks about other neighborhoods in the future, not about what caused this drop downtown.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bike-share program caused the 8 percent drop in downtown car traffic.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Car traffic fell after the program opened; riders made about 3,000 bike-share trips downtown each weekday.

breakdown.analysis: Three thousand bike trips is a lot, but who was taking them? If those riders used to walk or ride the bus, not one car came off the road. A bike trip only cuts car traffic if it replaces a car trip. It’s like a gym crediting its new juice bar for a drop in soda sales across town, when the juice buyers never drank soda. We need a question about what the riders did before.

choices.note: CORRECT. If most riders used to drive, the program took cars off the road and the argument looks good. If most used to walk or ride transit, the program barely touched car traffic, and something else must explain the drop. This is the link the argument needs.
Steady growth versus bursts doesn’t tell us whether the bike trips replaced car trips. Irrelevant.
Riders’ ages don’t affect whether their trips replaced car trips. Irrelevant.
Who runs the program has nothing to do with what caused the traffic drop. Irrelevant.
Tempting, because it’s about the program’s effect on traffic. But it asks about other neighborhoods in the future. The argument is about what caused this drop, downtown, last year.

questions.stimulus: Sweet corn growers in the Ostra region who mounted roost boxes for bats, which feed on the moths whose larvae damage corn, report that larva damage to their crops fell by nearly half over the next two years. So the bats drawn to the roost boxes are responsible for the reduction in damage.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Do the bats that use the roost boxes also feed on insects that do not harm corn?
Are bats more effective at catching moths than are the birds that also feed on moths?
Did damage also fall on the region’s corn farms that had no roost boxes?
Were roost boxes for bats mounted by corn growers in other regions as well as in Ostra?
Did a few of the roost boxes on the growers’ farms remain empty throughout the two years?
questions.explanation: Damage could have fallen for reasons that had nothing to do with bats, such as weather that hurt the moths. (C) supplies the needed comparison: if damage fell just as much on farms without roost boxes, the bats are not the explanation; if it did not, the boxes look responsible. (E) is tempting, but a few empty boxes are fully consistent with bats in the other boxes doing the work. (A) and (B) do not bear on what caused the drop.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Bats drawn to the roost boxes caused the drop in larva damage.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After growers mounted bat boxes, larva damage on their farms fell by nearly half over two years.

breakdown.analysis: Did damage fall everywhere? Moth numbers rise and fall with weather and other things. If farms without boxes saw the same drop, the bats didn’t do it. This is the missing comparison group. It’s like taking vitamin C, getting over your cold in a week, and crediting the vitamin, without asking how long colds last for people who don’t take it. We need a question that checks the farms without boxes.

choices.note: What else the bats eat doesn’t change whether they reduced corn damage. They can eat other insects and moths too. Irrelevant.
Comparing bats to birds doesn’t tell us whether the bats caused this drop. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If farms without boxes saw damage fall just as much, something region-wide caused the drop, and the bats get no credit. If those farms saw no drop, the boxes are the likely reason. That’s the comparison the argument skipped.
Boxes in other regions tell us nothing about what happened in Ostra. Irrelevant.
Tempting, because empty boxes sound like evidence against the bats. But “a few” is too weak to matter. Bats in the other boxes could still be doing all the work.

questions.stimulus: Market manager: Last year the Wexley farmers’ market moved from Wednesday afternoons to Saturday mornings, and its average weekly sales rose by about a quarter. Our Dunmore market serves a town much like Wexley and is also held on Wednesday afternoons. So if we move the Dunmore market to Saturday mornings, its weekly sales should rise by a similar percentage.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Do more shoppers visit the Wexley market in a typical week than visit the Dunmore market?
Did shoppers at the Wexley market spend more per visit after the move than they had before it?
Was the Wexley market founded earlier than the Dunmore market was?
Did the Wexley market add many new vendors at about the same time that it moved to Saturdays?
Do vendors at the Dunmore market charge higher prices than vendors at most other markets in the region?
questions.explanation: The manager credits Wexley’s sales rise to the move to Saturday and expects the same at Dunmore. That works only if the move, not something else, caused Wexley’s rise. (D) checks for another cause: if Wexley added many vendors at the same time, the extra stalls may explain the rise and Dunmore can’t count on it; if it did not, the move looks responsible. (A) is tempting, but the prediction is about a percentage rise, so the markets’ sizes don’t matter. (B) only describes how Wexley’s rise happened, not what caused it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Moving the Dunmore market to Saturday mornings should raise its weekly sales by a similar percentage.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Wexley’s sales rose about a quarter after it moved from Wednesday to Saturday; Dunmore serves a similar town and is also held on Wednesdays.

breakdown.analysis: Did the move cause Wexley’s jump, or did something else change at the same time? The manager has already told us the two towns are alike, so the comparison itself isn’t the weak spot. The weak spot is the cause. It’s like a friend who switched to a new gym and also hired a trainer, then credited the gym for getting fit. We need a question that checks for some other change at Wexley around the time of the move.

choices.note: Tempting, because it compares the two markets. But the prediction is a similar percentage rise. A bigger or smaller market can still grow by a quarter. Size doesn’t matter.
This tells us how Wexley’s sales rose (bigger baskets), not why. Either way, the move could still be the cause, or not. One-sided at best.
Which market is older has nothing to do with whether Saturday hours raise sales. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If Wexley added many vendors when it moved, more stalls could explain the higher sales, and Dunmore can’t expect the same from a schedule change alone. If it added none, the move is the likely cause, and the prediction looks better. Either answer moves the argument.
Dunmore’s prices would be the same on a Wednesday or a Saturday. They don’t tell us whether the move will raise sales. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Tenants’ association president: We slipped a questionnaire under the door of every apartment in our building, and 70 percent of the tenants who returned it said they want the laundry room to stay open overnight. So most of the building’s tenants want the laundry room kept open overnight.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Do other apartment buildings in the neighborhood keep their laundry rooms open overnight?
Were tenants who want overnight laundry hours more likely than other tenants to return the questionnaire?
How many washing machines and dryers are there in the building’s laundry room?
Would keeping the laundry room open overnight raise the building’s electricity costs?
Did any of the tenants who returned the questionnaire say that they never use the laundry room?
questions.explanation: The conclusion is about all the building’s tenants, but the evidence comes only from those who chose to reply. (B) asks whether the replies were skewed: if tenants who wanted overnight hours were more eager to respond, the 70 percent overstates support; if not, the result is likely representative. (D) is tempting because it raises a real drawback, but it bears on whether the room should stay open, not on what most tenants want.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of the building’s tenants want the laundry room open overnight.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of the tenants who returned a questionnaire said they want overnight hours.

breakdown.analysis: Who bothers to fill out a questionnaire? Mostly people who care about the issue. If the tenants who want late-night laundry were the ones eager to reply, 70 percent of replies could be a small share of the building. This is a self-selected sample. It’s like judging a restaurant by its online reviews, which come mostly from people who loved it or hated it. We need a question about whether the people who replied were typical.

choices.note: Other buildings’ hours say nothing about what tenants here want. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If supporters were more likely to reply, the 70 percent overstates support, and the conclusion is weak. If replies came evenly from all kinds of tenants, the sample probably reflects the building. This tests whether the sample is representative.
The number of machines doesn’t tell us what tenants want. Irrelevant.
Tempting, because it’s a real drawback to the idea. But the conclusion isn’t that the room should stay open; it’s that most tenants want it to. Cost is a different question.
Some respondents might not use the laundry room. So? They can still have an opinion, and a few of them wouldn’t change whether the sample represents the building.

questions.stimulus: A year ago the town of Marrow Point banned stores from handing out thin plastic grocery bags, which had made up a noticeable share of the plastic items in the town’s household trash. Yet in the year since the ban took effect, the total weight of plastic in Marrow Point’s household trash has risen.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Since the ban, many residents have bought heavy plastic bags to line their trash cans, a use for which they formerly reused thin grocery bags.
During the past year, the town’s recycling program stopped accepting several kinds of plastic packaging that it had previously collected.
The number of households in Marrow Point grew substantially during the year after the ban took effect.
Over the past year, many residents have switched from tap water to bottled water because of a persistent problem with the taste of the town’s water.
Although thin grocery bags were numerous in the town’s household trash, they made up only a small share of the weight of its plastic.
questions.explanation: Four choices give a reason the weight of plastic trash could rise despite the ban: heavier trash-can liners (A), plastic diverted from recycling into the trash (B), more households (C), and plastic water bottles (D). (E) explains only why the ban would cut the weight of plastic trash by a small amount; it gives no reason for the weight to go up, so it is the exception. (E) is attractive to eliminate early because it echoes the stimulus’s point about the bags, while (B), (C), and (D) look off topic since they don’t mention bags at all, but each adds plastic to the trash.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The town banned thin plastic grocery bags, a noticeable share of its plastic trash, but the total weight of plastic in household trash went up.

breakdown.analysis: In an EXCEPT question, four answers resolve the puzzle and the right answer doesn’t. So we’re hunting for the one that leaves the rise unexplained. A good resolver gives a source of extra plastic in the trash. Watch for the answer that explains only half: why the ban might not help much, without explaining why things got worse. It’s like cutting out dessert and gaining weight. “Desserts weren’t many calories” explains why you didn’t lose much. It doesn’t explain the gain. The traps here are (B), (C) and (D), which don’t mention bags at all, so they look off topic. But each one adds plastic to the trash.

choices.note: This resolves it. People used to reuse thin grocery bags as trash liners. Now they buy heavy liners instead, so more plastic, by weight, goes into the trash.
This resolves it, though it looks off topic. Plastic that used to go to recycling now goes into household trash, which adds weight even if fewer bags are thrown away.
This resolves it. The stimulus gives a total weight, not a per-household amount. More households means more trash overall, which can outweigh the bags that were removed.
This resolves it, though it never mentions bags. Bottled water means plastic bottles, and lots of them, going into household trash. That added weight can outrun what the ban removed.

CORRECT. This explains only why the ban would make a small difference by weight. It doesn’t explain why the weight rose. A small reduction is still a reduction, so the puzzle remains. It’s attractive because it reuses the stimulus’s point about bags, but it explains the wrong thing.

questions.stimulus: Historian: The account books of St. Aubert’s priory show that the quantity of candles the priory purchased fell by more than half between 1347 and 1352. Some scholars attribute this to a rise in the price of wax, but wax prices in the region held steady throughout those years. So the decline most likely reflects a sharp fall in the number of people living at the priory.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the priory also buy smaller quantities of the other supplies it regularly purchased during those years?
Did the number of people living at the priory rise again in the decades that followed 1352?
Did the scholars who blame the price of wax examine the priory’s account books for themselves?
Was wax produced in the region also sold to buyers in other regions during those years?
Did other priories in the region keep account books as detailed as those kept at St. Aubert’s?
questions.explanation: If the priory lost many of its residents, it should have bought less of nearly everything, not just candles. (A) tests this indirectly: a drop in its other regular supplies would support a population decline, while steady purchases of them would point to some cause specific to candles. (B) is the trap because it concerns the priory’s population, but what happened after 1352 cannot show whether the number of residents fell between 1347 and 1352. (C) attacks the scholars, whose view the argument has already rebutted with the price data.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The drop in candle purchases most likely reflects a sharp fall in the number of people living at the priory.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Candle purchases fell by more than half from 1347 to 1352; wax prices held steady, which rules out the scholars’ price explanation.

breakdown.analysis: The historian knocks out one explanation (wax prices) and jumps to another (fewer people). But are those the only two options? Maybe the priory started making its own candles, or cut back on lighting. How could we tell? If people really left, the priory should have bought less of everything. It’s like guessing your roommate moved out because the grocery bill dropped. Check whether the toilet paper and electricity bills dropped too. We need a question that tests whether other purchases fell. The right answer never mentions people at all; it asks about “other supplies,” which is why it’s easy to skip. Most students pick (B) because it’s about the number of residents, which is what the conclusion is about. But it asks about the wrong years. A later recovery tells us nothing about whether the population fell during 1347–1352.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the priory also bought less of its other regular supplies, that’s what we’d expect with far fewer residents, so the argument gets stronger. If those purchases held steady, the drop is specific to candles, and something other than population is likely behind it. Either answer moves the argument.

Tempting, and the main trap. It mentions the priory’s population, which is what the conclusion is about. But the argument is about what happened between 1347 and 1352. Whether numbers recovered later tells us nothing about whether they fell during those years.
This questions the scholars. But the historian has already rejected their view with the wax-price evidence. How they did their research doesn’t affect whether the population explanation is right.
Where the region’s wax was sold doesn’t matter. What matters for the scholars’ view is what wax cost, and the stimulus says the price held steady.
Other priories’ record keeping tells us nothing about why this priory bought fewer candles. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago the city of Kellam installed flashing warning lights at its busiest mid-block crosswalks. Studies show that such lights make drivers much more likely to stop for pedestrians, and Kellam’s own measurements confirm that drivers now stop far more often at those crosswalks. Yet more pedestrians have been struck at those crosswalks since the lights were installed than in the two years before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Drivers who stop at the lighted crosswalks are often struck from behind by other cars, which has raised the number of rear-end collisions there.
Most of the pedestrians struck at the lighted crosswalks were crossing during the evening rush hour, when traffic is heaviest.
The lights were installed at the crosswalks where pedestrians had most often been struck in the years before.
Kellam measured how often drivers stop only in daylight hours, when the flashing lights are easiest for drivers to see.
Many residents who once avoided crossing those streets on foot, finding them too dangerous, now cross there regularly.
questions.explanation: Each crossing can be safer while more people are struck, if far more people now cross there. (E) supplies that, though without saying so outright: residents who used to avoid those streets now cross them, so a lower risk per crossing applies to many more crossings. (C) is the main trap; it seems to explain why those crosswalks see many accidents, but they were the most dangerous spots before the lights too, so it gives no reason for the count to rise. (A) concerns cars hitting cars, not pedestrians, and (D) at most suggests the lights help less at night, not that they make things worse.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The new lights make drivers stop far more often at these crosswalks, but more pedestrians have been struck there since the lights went up than before.

breakdown.analysis: How can a crossing get safer while more people get hit there? Watch the measure. The stimulus gives a count of people struck, not a rate. If many more people now cross at those spots, the count can rise even though each crossing is safer. It’s like a town adding lifeguards at one beach, after which everyone swims there, so more rescues happen at that beach. Prephrase: more pedestrians are using those crosswalks now. The right answer doesn’t say “more pedestrians”; it says people who used to avoid the streets now cross there, and you have to see that this means more crossings. Most students pick (C) because “those were the dangerous spots” sounds like an explanation. It fails because the comparison is the same crosswalks before and after.

choices.note: Tempting, because it finds a real downside to drivers stopping. But it’s about cars hitting cars. The puzzle is about pedestrians struck. A rise in rear-end collisions doesn’t explain it.
Rush-hour timing would have been true before the lights as well. It describes when accidents happen, not why there are more of them now.

Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like selection bias. But the comparison in the stimulus is between the same crosswalks before and after. If they were already the most dangerous spots, that explains high numbers in both periods, not an increase. If anything, the worst spots should improve the most once lights go up.

This attacks the measurement, suggesting the lights may help less after dark. But helping less isn’t hurting. Even weak lights shouldn’t make more people get hit than no lights at all. Doesn’t explain the rise.

CORRECT. People who used to stay off those streets now cross there, so the crosswalks carry many more pedestrians than before. Each crossing can be safer while the total number struck still rises. Both facts fit.

questions.stimulus: In the Teral highlands, sheep farmers who keep guard dogs lose a larger percentage of their flocks to wolves each year, on average, than do farmers who keep no guard dogs. Yet field trials have shown that a guard dog greatly reduces the number of wolf attacks on the flock it protects.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Some breeds of guard dog are considerably more effective than others at driving wolves away from a flock.
Wolves in the Teral highlands attack sheep far more often in the winter months than in the summer months.
Teral farmers who keep guard dogs typically have much larger flocks than do Teral farmers who keep none.
Wolves in the Teral highlands roam mainly in a few districts, which is where nearly all of the region’s guard dogs are kept.
Wolves that have been driven away from a flock by a guard dog often return to the same flock later that night.
questions.explanation: The dog owners may simply be the farmers who face the most wolves. (D) says so indirectly: wolves roam mainly in a few districts, and that is where nearly all the dogs are kept. A dog can cut those farmers’ losses a great deal and still leave them losing more than farmers wolves rarely reach. (C) is the trap: larger flocks would mean more sheep lost in total, but the stimulus compares percentages. (E) explains why the dogs might help less than the trials suggest, not why their owners lose more than farmers with no dogs.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Guard dogs greatly reduce wolf attacks on a flock, but farmers with guard dogs lose a larger percentage of their flocks to wolves than farmers without them.

breakdown.analysis: If the dogs work, why do dog owners lose more? Maybe the dog owners aren’t a random group. Who would buy a guard dog? The farmers with a wolf problem. Their losses could be cut sharply by the dog and still be higher than the losses of farmers with no wolves nearby. It’s like noticing that houses with storm shutters suffer more wind damage than houses without them; the shutters go up on the coast, where the storms hit. Prephrase: the dog owners face far more wolves to begin with. The right answer says this in geography terms (where the wolves are, where the dogs are), so you have to connect the two. Most students pick (C) because bigger flocks mean more sheep lost. But the stimulus says “percentage.” Flock size is already accounted for.

choices.note: Differences among breeds don’t explain why dog owners as a group do worse than farmers with no dogs at all.
Wolves attacking more in winter affects all farmers alike. A fact that applies to both groups can’t explain a difference between them.
Tempting, and the main trap. A bigger flock would lose more sheep in total. But the comparison is by percentage of the flock, so size is already factored out. Watch the switch from a count to a rate.

CORRECT. The wolves roam mainly in a few districts, and that’s where nearly all the dogs are. So the dog owners are the farmers wolves target most. A dog can reduce their losses and still leave them above farmers who rarely see wolves. The dogs work; they just went to the hardest-hit farms.

Tempting, because it shows a limit on what dogs can do. But at most it says the dogs help less than the trials suggest. Less help isn’t more harm: it doesn’t explain why owners lose a larger share than farmers with no dogs at all.

questions.stimulus: Three years ago the Dunlin youth football league banned tackling for players under twelve, allowing only flag football at those ages. Since then, the number of concussions reported among the league’s under-twelve players has fallen by 40 percent. Therefore, tackling must have caused a large share of the concussions suffered by the league’s youngest players before the ban.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Do players over twelve in the league suffer concussions more often than players under twelve do?
Were some of the concussions reported before the ban caused by collisions that did not involve tackling?
Did many families move their children to other leagues that still allow tackling once the Dunlin league switched to flag football?
Do children who play flag football suffer other kinds of injuries, such as sprains, more often than children who play tackle football?
Did most of the league’s coaches support the decision to ban tackling for its younger players?
questions.explanation: The 40 percent drop is a drop in the number of concussions, not in the rate per player. (C) gets at this without saying “enrollment”: if many families moved their children to tackle leagues, the division shrank, and fewer players alone could explain fewer concussions; if few left, the drop points to tackling. (B) is the trap, since it seems to question whether tackling was the cause, but some concussions from other collisions are consistent with tackling causing a large share. (D) concerns other injuries, not concussions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Tackling caused a large share of under-twelve concussions before the ban.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After tackling was banned for players under twelve, the number of reported concussions among them fell by 40 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Fewer concussions out of how many kids? The stimulus gives a count, not a rate. If lots of families pulled their kids out after the switch to flag football, fewer players alone would mean fewer concussions. It’s like a store bragging that shoplifting fell by half after it moved, when the new location gets half the customers. We need a question about whether the number of players changed. The right answer comes at it sideways: families leaving for tackle leagues means fewer kids left in Dunlin’s division. Most students pick (B) because it seems to question the tackling explanation. But the conclusion says tackling caused “a large share,” not all. Some non-tackling concussions fit that perfectly.

choices.note: This compares the wrong groups. The argument is about under-twelve players before and after the ban, not about older players.

Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like an alternative cause. But “some” is too weak to matter. The conclusion only claims a large share came from tackling, which allows some from other collisions. A yes or a no leaves the argument where it was.

CORRECT. If many families left for leagues that still tackle, Dunlin’s under-twelve division got smaller, and the drop in concussions could come from having fewer players. If few left, the drop reflects a real fall in the rate, and tackling looks responsible. This is the count-versus-rate gap, in disguise.
Sprains and other injuries are a different measure. Whether flag football has its own risks says nothing about whether tackling caused concussions. Irrelevant.
Coaches’ support for the ban doesn’t tell us whether tackling caused the concussions. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Plant manager: Six months ago our factory replaced its paper sign-in sheets with electronic time clocks, and since then the number of late arrivals on record has tripled. Admittedly, we hired more workers during that period, but our workforce grew by only 10 percent. So our employees have clearly become less punctual.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the factory hire more new workers during the past six months than it did during the six months before that?
Under the old system, could a worker who arrived late have recorded an earlier arrival time without anyone noticing?
Do late arrivals by the factory’s workers cause delays in its production schedule?
Did installing the electronic time clocks cost the factory more than it had expected?
Are most of the factory’s recorded late arrivals concentrated among workers on its early-morning shift?
questions.explanation: The tripling compares records from two different systems, so it shows a change in punctuality only if both systems caught lateness equally well. (B) gets at this: if workers could quietly write down earlier times on the paper sheets, lateness was probably underreported before and the tripling may be an artifact of honest clocks; if they could not, the comparison is fairer. (A) is the trap because hiring is what the manager concedes, but a 10 percent rise in the workforce is too small to explain a tripling no matter when the hiring happened. (E) concerns which workers are late, not whether lateness increased.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The factory’s employees have become less punctual.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Recorded late arrivals tripled after electronic time clocks replaced paper sign-in sheets; the workforce grew only 10 percent, which can’t explain the rise.

breakdown.analysis: The manager rules out one explanation (more workers) but misses a bigger one: the measuring tool changed. Paper sheets and electronic clocks may not catch lateness the same way. If workers used to write their own times, a lot of “8:00” might really have been 8:10. It’s like switching from a bathroom scale you can nudge with your toe to a doctor’s scale, and concluding you gained weight. We need a question about how lateness was recorded before. Most students pick (A) because it’s about hiring, the factor the manager raised. But the manager already gave us the number: 10 percent. That can’t produce a tripling, whatever the timing of the hires.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It’s about the concession the manager already handled. The workforce grew only 10 percent, and that can’t triple the late arrivals. Comparing this hiring to earlier hiring doesn’t change that.

CORRECT. If workers could write an earlier time on the paper sheet without anyone noticing, lateness was probably underreported before, and the tripling may just reflect an honest clock. If they couldn’t, the old and new numbers are comparable, and the argument holds. This tests whether the comparison is fair, even though it never uses the word “lateness” the way the manager does.
Whether lateness causes production delays is about its consequences, not about whether it increased. Irrelevant.
The clocks’ cost has nothing to do with whether workers became less punctual. Irrelevant.
Which shift has the late arrivals doesn’t tell us whether lateness rose overall. Whatever the shifts, the question is whether the old records can be compared with the new ones.

questions.stimulus: In the year after the state of Calder began requiring all motorcycle riders to wear helmets, the number of motorcyclists treated in Calder hospitals for head injuries rose, even though there were about as many motorcycle accidents in the state as in the year before. Helmets are designed to protect riders against head injuries.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Before the law took effect, many riders who suffered head injuries in serious crashes died before they could receive any hospital treatment.
Some riders in Calder continued to ride without helmets after the law took effect, despite the risk of being fined.
Many riders who began wearing helmets because of the law bought inexpensive models that protect less well than costlier ones.
Helmets prevent most of the head injuries that would otherwise result from motorcycle crashes at low speeds.
In neighboring states, which have no helmet law, motorcyclists were treated for head injuries about as often that year as the year before.
questions.explanation: If many head-injured riders used to die before reaching a hospital, helmets can turn some of those deaths into survivable injuries, and those survivors are now treated in hospitals. That lets hospital treatment for head injuries rise even though helmets protect heads, which is (A). (B) and (C) are the traps: each explains why the helmets helped less than expected, but less help would leave the count flat, not push it up. (D) only shows helmets work, which deepens the puzzle.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Helmets protect against head injuries and accidents held steady, but after helmets became mandatory, more motorcyclists were treated in hospitals for head injuries.

breakdown.analysis: Who gets counted? Only riders treated in a hospital. Before the law, where did the worst head injuries end up? Possibly not in a hospital at all, but in the morgue. If helmets turn some of those fatal crashes into survivable ones, those riders now show up as hospital patients. The helmets worked, and the hospital count went up anyway. It’s like a new ambulance service getting more heart attack patients to the hospital alive: hospital admissions rise because fewer people die on the way. Prephrase: helmets moved riders from the death count into the hospital count. The right answer talks only about the past (before the law), so it’s easy to skip. Most students pick (B) or (C), which explain why helmets helped less than expected. But less help means a smaller drop, not a rise.

choices.note: CORRECT. Before the law, many riders with bad head injuries never reached a hospital because they died first. With helmets, some of them survive and get treated. So hospital treatment for head injuries can rise even though helmets protect heads. Both facts fit.
Tempting, and one of the main traps. Riders who skip helmets explain why the law didn’t help as much as hoped. But those riders were helmetless before the law too. They can’t explain a rise.
Tempting, and the other main trap. Cheap helmets protect less, but they still protect more than no helmet. This explains a smaller benefit, not more head injuries. “Helped less” isn’t “hurt.”
This says helmets work, which is what makes the rise puzzling in the first place. Deepens the puzzle.
Neighboring states with no change in head injuries just confirm that nothing region-wide drove the rise. That makes Calder’s rise harder to explain, not easier.

questions.stimulus: In a ten-year study, adults who ate beans or lentils at least four times a week were 30 percent less likely to develop heart disease than adults who rarely ate them. The two groups did not differ in how much they exercised or in how many of them smoked. So eating beans or lentils frequently reduces a person’s risk of developing heart disease.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Among the adults who ate beans or lentils frequently, did those who exercised regularly develop heart disease less often than those who did not?
Were the adults in the study typical of adults in general in their overall rates of heart disease?
Do beans and lentils contain any nutrients that cannot be obtained from other common foods?
Did the adults who rarely ate beans or lentils eat more of some food known to promote heart disease?
Did some of the adults who ate beans or lentils frequently develop heart disease during the study?
questions.explanation: The study rules out exercise and smoking but not other differences in diet. (D) asks whether the adults who rarely ate beans ate more of some harmful food: if so, that difference rather than the beans could explain the gap in risk; if not, the beans look responsible. (A) is the trap: it brings up exercise, a classic confounder, but the groups were already matched on exercise, so a comparison within the bean-eating group can’t show whether the beans made the difference. (B) and (E) do not bear on whether the beans caused the difference.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eating beans or lentils frequently reduces the risk of heart disease.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Frequent bean and lentil eaters were 30 percent less likely to develop heart disease; the groups didn’t differ in exercise or smoking.

breakdown.analysis: The study ruled out two alternative causes, but did it rule out everything? Someone who eats lentils four times a week is probably eating them instead of something else. If that something else is red meat, the benefit may come from what they skip, not what they eat. It’s like crediting a new phone for your better sleep, when the real change is that you stopped scrolling at midnight on the old one. We need a question about some other way the two groups differed. Notice the right answer looks at the other group, the people who rarely ate beans, and what they ate more of. Most students pick (A) because it targets a group difference, the right kind of gap. But the stimulus already answered it: the groups exercised the same.

choices.note: Tempting because exercise is a classic confounder. But the two groups were already matched on exercise, so comparing exercisers with non-exercisers inside the bean-eating group says nothing about whether beans themselves made the difference. Either answer leaves the argument where it was.

Whether the study group matches the general population in heart disease rates doesn’t affect the comparison between bean eaters and others within the study. A textbook-sounding sampling worry that doesn’t touch this argument.
The argument doesn’t claim beans are the only source of their benefit. Beans could lower risk even if their nutrients exist elsewhere. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If the people who rarely ate beans ate more of something known to cause heart trouble, that food, not the beans, could explain the gap, and the argument weakens. If they didn’t, that alternative is ruled out, and the beans look responsible. The answer pushes in opposite directions.
“Some” bean eaters getting heart disease is consistent with a 30 percent lower risk. Lower risk isn’t zero risk.

questions.stimulus: Building inspector: The fire alarm in the Harlan Building failed to sound during yesterday’s drill. An alarm of this kind fails only if its backup battery is dead or its control wiring is faulty. Minutes before the drill, an electrician tested the alarm’s control wiring and found it to be in perfect order. Therefore, the alarm’s backup battery must have been dead at the time of the drill.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Does a dead backup battery always cause an alarm of this kind to fail to sound?
Did the alarm sound properly during the fire drill held in the Harlan Building last year?
Are there faults in wiring of this kind that the test the electrician used cannot reveal?
Does faulty control wiring ever cause an alarm of this kind to sound when there is no fire?
Are dead batteries a more common cause of failure in alarms of this kind than faulty wiring is?
questions.explanation: Failure requires a dead battery or faulty wiring, so the battery conclusion follows only if the wiring really was sound. The only evidence for that is the electrician’s test, and (C) asks whether the test could miss a fault: if it could, the wiring is back in play and the argument weakens; if it could not, the battery is the only cause left. (A) is the trap because it sounds like the key conditional, but it reverses it: the argument needs “fails only if dead battery or bad wiring,” not “a dead battery always causes failure.” (E) offers a base rate, which doesn’t matter once the wiring has been ruled out.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The backup battery was dead at the time of the drill.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The alarm failed; fail → dead battery OR faulty wiring; an electrician’s test minutes before the drill found the wiring in perfect order.

breakdown.analysis: Lay out the logic. Fail → battery dead OR wiring faulty. The alarm failed, so one of the two was true. The wiring was ruled out by a test. So everything rests on the test. “Found it in perfect order” only means the test found nothing wrong. Can the test miss things? It’s like proving a patient’s fever must come from the flu because the strep test came back negative, when that test misses some strep cases. We need a question about whether the test was good enough to clear the wiring. Most students pick (A) because it sounds like checking the conditional. But it reverses it. The argument uses fail → (battery or wiring). Whether a dead battery always causes failure is the other direction, and the argument never relies on it.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It reverses the conditional. The argument needs “if it fails, the battery or wiring is bad,” which is given. Whether a dead battery is enough to cause failure is the reverse, and it doesn’t matter: the alarm did fail, and we’re working backward from that.
Last year’s drill tells us nothing about what went wrong yesterday. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. If the test can miss some wiring faults, “found in perfect order” doesn’t clear the wiring, and the wiring is back in play as the cause, so the argument weakens. If the test catches every such fault, the battery is the only remaining cause, and the conclusion follows. This tests the one step that removes the alternative.

This reuses “control wiring” but asks about false alarms, the opposite kind of malfunction. Whether bad wiring can make an alarm go off with no fire says nothing about why this one stayed silent. Irrelevant.

Tempting, because it seems to make the battery more likely. But base rates only matter when both causes are still open. The argument says the wiring was ruled out, so the question is whether that ruling holds, not which cause is usually more common.

questions.stimulus: In the Tavel forest, wooden nest boxes with small entrance holes are much less likely to be raided by predators than are boxes with large entrance holes. Nevertheless, the songbirds that nest in the forest’s small-hole boxes fledge fewer young per nest, on average, than do the songbirds that nest in its large-hole boxes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Predators in the Tavel forest raid nests built in natural tree cavities more often than they raid nests built in boxes.
Boxes with large entrance holes let in more rain, which can chill the eggs and newly hatched chicks inside.
Far fewer small-hole boxes than large-hole boxes have been put up by the people who maintain the forest.
Boxes with small entrance holes can be entered only by the forest’s smallest songbird species, whose broods are typically small.
Songbirds in the Tavel forest prefer nest boxes whose entrance holes face away from the prevailing wind.
questions.explanation: The two kinds of box are used by different birds. If only the smallest species can fit through small holes, and those species raise small broods, their nests produce fewer young even though predators rarely reach them, which is (D). (C) is the trap: fewer small-hole boxes would mean fewer young from those boxes in total, but the stimulus compares young per nest, so the number of boxes is irrelevant. (B) makes large-hole boxes look worse, which deepens the puzzle.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Small-hole boxes are much safer from predators, but birds nesting in them fledge fewer young per nest than birds in large-hole boxes.

breakdown.analysis: If small holes keep predators out, why do those nests produce fewer young? Ask who’s inside. A small hole doesn’t just keep out predators; it keeps out bigger birds. So the two kinds of box hold different species. If the small species lay fewer eggs, they’ll fledge fewer young no matter how safe the box is. It’s like noticing that compact cars have fewer passengers per trip than minivans and blaming the car’s safety features. Prephrase: different, less productive birds use the small-hole boxes. Most students pick (C) because fewer boxes means fewer young. But the stimulus says “per nest.” The number of boxes drops out of a per-nest average.

choices.note: Natural cavities aren’t part of the comparison. This tells us nothing about why one kind of box produces fewer young than the other.
This makes the large-hole boxes look worse, so they should produce fewer young, not more. Deepens the puzzle.
Tempting, and the main trap. Fewer boxes would mean fewer young in total. But the comparison is per nest, so the number of boxes doesn’t matter. Count versus rate.

CORRECT. The small holes sort the birds by size. The small species that fit through raise small broods, so their nests fledge fewer young even with less predation. The boxes are safer; the occupants are just less productive.
A preference for boxes facing away from the wind would affect both kinds of box. It doesn’t explain a difference between them.

questions.stimulus: Urban planner: A good test of whether a neighborhood suits young families is whether nearly all of its homes are within a ten-minute walk, at an ordinary adult pace, of a public playground. Marlow passes this test easily. On the city’s official map, nearly every home in Marlow lies within half a kilometer of a playground, and an adult walking at an ordinary pace covers half a kilometer in about six minutes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Does the city’s official map show every public playground in Marlow, including any that were built recently?
Do most young families who live in Marlow actually walk their children to the neighborhood’s playgrounds on a regular basis?
Do many Marlow homes lie across a highway or rail line from their nearest playground?
Are Marlow’s playgrounds as well equipped as the public playgrounds in the city’s other neighborhoods?
Is being near a playground more important to most young families than being near a good school?
questions.explanation: The test is about walking time, but the evidence is distance on a map, which measures a straight line. Those match only if people can walk roughly straight to the playground. (C) asks whether barriers stand in the way: if highways or rail lines force long detours, many homes may be far more than ten minutes away on foot; if not, the map distance is a fair guide. (B) is the trap because it seems to test whether the playgrounds are really walkable, but the test asks whether homes are within a ten-minute walk, not whether families make the walk. (A) is one-sided: playgrounds missing from the map would only add to Marlow’s score.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Marlow easily passes the test of having nearly all homes within a ten-minute walk of a playground.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: On the city map, nearly every home is within half a kilometer of a playground; an adult covers half a kilometer in about six minutes.

breakdown.analysis: How is distance measured on a map? As the crow flies. Nobody walks as the crow flies through a highway. The test is about walking time, and the evidence is map distance. If a rail yard sits between a home and the playground, a half-kilometer gap could be a twenty-minute walk around it. It’s like saying your office is close because you can see it from your window, when the river in between has no bridge for a mile. We need a question that checks whether the straight line matches the real route. Most students pick (B) because it seems to test walkability in real life. But the test is about whether homes are within a ten-minute walk, not whether families walk there. “Can” isn’t “do.”

choices.note: Tempting, because it questions the map, the planner’s source. But it’s one-sided. Playgrounds missing from the map would only put more homes near a playground, so the answer can only help the argument or leave it alone. It doesn’t touch the real gap between map distance and walking distance.

Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like checking the real-world walk. But the test asks whether homes are within a ten-minute walk, not whether families make that walk. Parents might drive out of habit even if the walk is short. “Can” isn’t “do.”

CORRECT. If highways or rail lines block the straight path, the real walk could be much longer than half a kilometer, and many homes might fail the ten-minute test. If no such barriers exist, the map distance is a fair stand-in, and Marlow passes. This targets the gap between the evidence and the test.
How well equipped the playgrounds are isn’t part of the test. Irrelevant.
This questions how much the test matters, but the argument applies the test as given. Ranking playgrounds against schools doesn’t tell us whether Marlow passes it.

questions.stimulus: Six years ago, to protect the trout in Lake Orrin, the province banned commercial net fishing on the lake. The limits on how many trout recreational anglers may take from the lake have not changed since then. Yet surveys show that the lake’s trout population is now substantially smaller than it was before the ban took effect.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Before the ban, trout were the most valuable of the fish that commercial fishers caught in Lake Orrin.
In the years just before the ban, commercial fishers had already been catching far fewer trout in Lake Orrin than in earlier decades.
Some of the commercial fishers who formerly worked on Lake Orrin now fish instead on other lakes in the province.
Most of what the commercial nets removed from Lake Orrin were fish of a species that preys heavily on young trout.
The number of recreational anglers fishing on Lake Orrin has remained about the same since the ban.
questions.explanation: If the nets mostly removed a fish that eats young trout, the ban mainly protected the trout’s predators. More predators would eat more young trout, so the trout population could shrink even though no one nets trout anymore. That is (D). (B) is the trap: if commercial fishers were already catching few trout, the ban would do little to help, but that explains only why the population did not grow, not why it fell. (A) and (E) make the decline harder to explain.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Commercial net fishing was banned to protect the trout, and angling limits didn’t change, but the trout population is now substantially smaller.

breakdown.analysis: How does removing a threat leave the trout worse off? Maybe the nets were doing the trout a favor. What else did the nets catch? If they kept the trout’s predators in check, the ban freed those predators. It’s like getting rid of the barn cats to protect the chickens’ feed and then losing the feed to mice. Prephrase: the nets had been removing something that harms trout. Most students pick (B) because it explains why the ban didn’t help. But “didn’t help” isn’t “made things worse.” It leaves the decline unexplained.

choices.note: If trout were the nets’ most valuable catch, the nets were taking lots of trout, so the ban should have helped them. Deepens the puzzle.

Tempting, and the main trap. If the nets were already catching few trout, the ban wouldn’t do much, so the population might hold steady. But the puzzle is that it fell. This explains a lack of improvement, not a decline.
Where the fishers went doesn’t affect Lake Orrin’s trout. Irrelevant.
CORRECT. The nets were mostly removing a species that eats young trout. Ban the nets and that predator multiplies, so more young trout get eaten. The ban backfired, and the decline makes sense.
Steady angling pressure rules out one alternative explanation. That makes the decline harder to explain, not easier.

questions.stimulus: Analyst: Some credit the high-speed wireless network built in Tamsin County three years ago for the county’s surge in new home-based businesses. Admittedly, such businesses have multiplied in Tamsin since the network was completed. But they have multiplied just as quickly in neighboring Corvel County, where no such network was built. So the network is not responsible for Tamsin’s surge.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Do many new home-based businesses in Corvel rely on service from Tamsin’s network?
Did building the new wireless network create a large number of jobs in Tamsin County?
Has the government of Corvel County considered building a high-speed wireless network of its own?
Were there more home-based businesses in Tamsin than in Corvel before the network was built?
Do the new home-based businesses in Tamsin earn more, on average, than the new ones in Corvel?
questions.explanation: The analyst treats Corvel as a county without the network, so Corvel’s matching surge seems to show that the network made no difference. That comparison works only if Corvel’s businesses really did without the network. (A) asks whether they rely on it: if they do, Corvel’s surge may come from the same network and the argument collapses; if they do not, Corvel is a fair comparison. (D) is the trap because it compares the two counties, but “multiplied just as quickly” is a rate of growth, so the starting numbers do not matter. (B) concerns jobs, not home-based businesses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new network is not responsible for Tamsin’s surge in home-based businesses.

setup.label: Reasoning
