setup.text: Concession: the businesses multiplied after the network was built. But they multiplied just as quickly in Corvel, where no network was built.

breakdown.analysis: The whole argument rests on Corvel as the comparison group: no network, same surge, so the network didn’t matter. But “built in Tamsin” isn’t the same as “used only in Tamsin.” Wireless signals don’t stop at county lines. If Corvel homes get the signal, Corvel had the network too, and its surge supports the network theory instead of undercutting it. It’s like testing whether a new streetlight reduced crime on your block by comparing it with the next block, which is lit by the same light. We need a question about whether Corvel really lacked the network. Most students pick (D) because it compares the counties. But “multiplied just as quickly” is a rate, so the starting numbers don’t matter.

choices.note: CORRECT. A network built in Tamsin isn’t necessarily used only in Tamsin. If many new Corvel businesses rely on it, Corvel isn’t a network-free county at all, and its surge could be the network’s work too. The argument collapses. If they don’t, the comparison is fair, and the argument gets stronger. This tests the comparison group.
Construction jobs are a different effect. Whether the network created jobs doesn’t tell us whether it caused the surge in home-based businesses.
What Corvel’s government has considered doesn’t change whether Corvel had access to the network during the surge. Irrelevant.

Tempting, and the main trap. It compares the two counties, which feels like checking the comparison. But the argument says the businesses “multiplied just as quickly,” a rate of growth. Starting from different numbers doesn’t change whether they grew at the same rate.
How much the businesses earn is a different question from what caused them to start. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Across the Orvald region, the average yield of sugar beets per hectare was higher this year than last year. Yet on nearly every farm in the region that grew sugar beets in both years, the yield per hectare was lower this year than last.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: This year’s growing season in the Orvald region was considerably drier than last year’s growing season.
The farms in the Orvald region that grow sugar beets also grow wheat and barley in rotation with them.
Several of the farms that grew sugar beets in the Orvald region last year grew none at all this year.
Most of the region’s sugar beet farmers planted the same varieties of seed this year as they did last year.
Much of this year’s beet crop came from farms new to growing beets, whose soil suits beets unusually well.
questions.explanation: A regional average depends on which farms are counted. If much of this year’s crop came from farms new to beets with unusually suitable soil, their high yields can lift the regional average even though nearly every farm that grew beets in both years did worse. That is (E). (C) is the near-miss: farms dropping out can change an average, but only if they were the low-yield farms, and we aren’t told that; if the quitters were strong farms, their exit would pull the average down. (A) explains why individual farms’ yields fell, but it would drag the regional average down too.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The region’s average beet yield per hectare rose, but nearly every farm that grew beets in both years had a lower yield.

breakdown.analysis: How can an average go up when almost every member goes down? Change who’s in the group. The second fact covers only farms that grew beets in both years. If new farms with excellent soil joined this year, they count in this year’s average but not in the both-years comparison, and they can pull the average up. It’s like a class average rising after a few very strong students transfer in, even though every returning student scored a little lower. Prephrase: the group changed, with strong newcomers or weak farms leaving. Most students who know this pattern grab (C) because it mentions farms leaving. But leaving helps the average only if the leavers were the weak ones, and (C) doesn’t say that. Others pick (A), which explains the falling farm yields but would drag the average down too.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. A drier season explains why individual farms did worse. But it should pull the regional average down too. It explains one side and leaves the rise in the average even more puzzling.
Crop rotation applies in both years. It doesn’t explain why the regional average and farm yields moved in opposite directions.

Tempting, and the main trap for students who know the pattern. Farms dropping out can raise an average, but only if they were the poor performers. (C) doesn’t say which farms quit. If they were high-yield farms, their exit would pull the average down. Without that detail, it explains nothing.
Using the same seed rules out one possible change. It explains nothing.

CORRECT. Newcomers on better soil count in this year’s regional average but not among farms that grew beets both years. Their high yields can lift the average even though nearly every established farm did worse. Both facts fit.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: The Corran salamander breeds only in pools that form each spring from melting snow. Five years ago, a drainage ditch was dug that keeps such pools from forming in the eastern half of the Corran meadows, though not in the western half. The number of salamander egg masses found in the meadows each spring has not declined since then. So the salamanders must have shifted their breeding to the western half.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Before the ditch was dug, were any salamander egg masses laid in the part of the meadows that the ditch now keeps dry?
Has the number of Corran salamanders breeding outside the Corran meadows also stayed the same?
Do spring pools still form each year in the western half of the Corran meadows?
Do the pools that still form in the western half of the meadows last long enough each spring for the eggs laid in them to hatch?
Do salamanders hatched in the western half survive to adulthood as often as those hatched in the eastern half once did?
questions.explanation: A shift to the western half presupposes that the salamanders used to breed in the eastern half. (A) tests that hidden precondition, describing the east only as the part the ditch keeps dry: if egg masses were laid there before the ditch, the steady count suggests they moved west; if none were, there was nothing to shift and the conclusion fails. (E) is the trap because it compares the two halves, but survival to adulthood is a different question from where the salamanders breed. (D) is about whether western eggs hatch, which also leaves where the eggs are laid untouched, and (C) is already answered by the stimulus.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The salamanders shifted their breeding to the western half of the meadows.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: They breed only in spring pools; the ditch stopped pools forming in the east but not the west; the number of egg masses hasn’t fallen.

breakdown.analysis: “Shifted” means they used to be somewhere else. Did they ever breed in the east? Maybe the eastern pools were too shallow, or too short-lived, and every egg mass was always in the west. Then the ditch changed nothing for the salamanders, and nothing moved. It’s like concluding your neighbor started parking on the street because her driveway was blocked, when she never parked in the driveway. We need a question that checks whether there were eastern breeders before. Most students pick (E) because it compares east and west, which feels on target. But it asks how many young survive, not where the adults breed.

choices.note: CORRECT. “The part the ditch now keeps dry” is the eastern half. If egg masses used to be laid there, they must now be laid somewhere else, and the steady count points west. The argument is strong. If none were ever laid there, the salamanders had nothing to shift away from, and the conclusion fails. This tests what “shifted” assumes.
Breeding outside the meadows is a different population. It doesn’t tell us whether the meadow salamanders moved within the meadows.
The stimulus already answers this. The ditch keeps pools from forming in the east “though not in the western half,” so the western pools still form. A question with a known answer can’t help.

This reuses “pools” and “western half,” so it feels on target. But hatching happens after the eggs are laid. The argument is about where the eggs are laid, and the count of egg masses already tells us breeding continues. Wrong question.

Tempting, and the main trap. It compares the two halves, so it looks relevant. But survival to adulthood is about what happens after the eggs hatch. The argument is about where the eggs are laid. Wrong question.

questions.stimulus: Last spring the Fenwick parks department doubled the number of trash cans in the city’s parks in order to reduce litter. Over the following months, park attendance was about the same as in previous years. Yet park inspectors found considerably more litter on the ground in those months than they had found in the same months of previous years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Park visitors are less likely to drop litter on the ground when a trash can is in sight than when none is.
Many of the new trash cans were placed in areas of the parks that visitors seldom use.
Most of the litter found in Fenwick’s parks consists of items so small that visitors rarely bother carrying them to a trash can.
A neighboring city reduced litter in its parks last year by hiring workers to watch for and fine people who litter.
The department paid for the new trash cans by cutting back on the work crews that service the parks.
questions.explanation: More cans with the same number of visitors should mean less litter. If the department paid for the cans by cutting the crews that service the parks, cans would be emptied less often and litter picked up less often, so overflowing cans and uncollected trash could leave more litter on the ground. That is (E), stated only as a budget decision. (B) and (C) are the traps: each explains why the extra cans might not reduce litter, but neither explains why litter rose. (A) shows the cans should work, deepening the puzzle.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The parks doubled their trash cans and attendance held steady, but inspectors found considerably more litter than before.

breakdown.analysis: More cans, same crowds, more litter? Ask what else changed. Cans don’t empty themselves. Someone has to service them and pick up what misses. If that part got worse, the cans could overflow and litter could pile up. It’s like a restaurant buying twice as many dish racks and laying off half the dishwashers; the kitchen ends up with more dirty dishes, not fewer. Prephrase: the plan’s cost or side effect made cleanup worse. The right answer sounds like dull budget news, so it’s easy to skip. Most students pick (B) or (C) because each explains why the cans didn’t help. But “didn’t help” isn’t “made it worse.”

choices.note: This says the cans should cut litter. That’s the expectation the paradox defies. Deepens the puzzle.
Tempting, and one of the main traps. Badly placed cans explain why the plan didn’t reduce litter. But the old cans were still there, so this gives no reason for litter to rise. No help isn’t harm.
Tempting, and the other main trap. If most litter is too small to carry to a can, more cans won’t help. But that was true before too. It explains no improvement, not an increase.
Another city’s fines tell us nothing about why litter rose in Fenwick. Interesting, but irrelevant.

CORRECT. Fewer crews means cans get emptied less often and litter gets picked up less often. Overflowing cans and uncollected trash leave more litter on the ground, even with twice as many cans. Both facts fit.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Over the past decade, the average price of a new home in Brisa has risen by 40 percent. Over the same period, the average household income in Brisa has also risen by 40 percent. So, for Brisa’s households, new homes are no less affordable today than they were a decade ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the average price of existing homes in Brisa also rise by 40 percent over the past decade?
Did the number of Brisa households with very high incomes grow substantially over the past decade?
Did the number of new homes built in Brisa each year increase over the past decade?
Are new homes in Brisa more affordable than new homes in the cities that border it?
Did average household income in Brisa rise faster in the first half of the decade than in the second half?
questions.explanation: An average income can rise by 40 percent because more households earn very large incomes, while most households gain little. (B) tests this indirectly: if the number of very-high-income households grew a lot, the average was likely pulled up by them and new homes may have become less affordable for most households; if not, typical incomes probably kept pace and the argument holds. (A) is the trap because it looks like a check on housing prices, but the conclusion is about new homes, whose price is given. (E) concerns timing within the decade, which does not change the ten-year comparison.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: New homes are no less affordable for Brisa’s households than they were a decade ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The average new-home price rose 40 percent; average household income also rose 40 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Averages hide a lot. If a few households got very rich, the average income could jump 40 percent while most families’ incomes barely moved. Then most households would find new homes much less affordable. It’s like saying everyone in the room got richer when a billionaire walks in. The average is up; nobody else’s wallet changed. We need a question about whether typical households kept pace with the average. The right answer doesn’t say “typical household” or “median.” It asks whether the very-high-income group grew, and you have to see that this is what would skew the average. Most students pick (A) because it’s about prices, the other half of affordability. But it swaps “existing” for “new,” and the conclusion is only about new homes.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It looks like a check on prices. But the argument is about new homes, and their price is given. What existing homes cost is a different market.

CORRECT. If many more households now have very high incomes, they could pull the average up 40 percent while most households gained far less, and new homes would be less affordable for most of them. If that group didn’t grow, the rise in the average likely reflects broad gains, and the argument stands. That’s the gap between the average and the typical household.
How many homes were built doesn’t change how a home’s price compares with a household’s income. Irrelevant.
A comparison with other cities doesn’t tell us whether affordability in Brisa changed over time.
The argument compares the start and end of the decade. How income rose in between doesn’t change that comparison.

questions.stimulus: Portable fire extinguishers can put out most small household fires. Yet a study based on the Brensk fire department’s records of house fires found that homes with an extinguisher on hand suffered fire damage amounting to a larger percentage of the home’s value, on average, than did homes without one.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Most of the extinguishers sold for household use are designed to put out several different kinds of fire.
Homes in Brensk that have fire extinguishers are, on average, larger and more valuable than homes without them.
The Brensk fire department’s records include an estimate of the damage done by each house fire to which firefighters were called.
Many Brensk residents who own extinguishers keep them where they cannot be reached quickly during a fire.
Most household fires that residents manage to put out on their own are never reported to the fire department.
questions.explanation: The study used only the fire department’s records. If fires that residents put out themselves are rarely reported, the records leave out the cases where an extinguisher worked, so the recorded fires in homes with extinguishers are mostly the ones the extinguisher could not stop. That is (E), though it never mentions extinguishers or the study. (B) is the trap: bigger, more valuable homes would explain more damage in dollars, but the study measured damage as a percentage of the home’s value. (D) explains why an extinguisher might fail to help, but not why homes with one would fare worse.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Extinguishers can put out most small fires, but in the fire department’s records, homes with extinguishers suffered more damage, as a share of home value, than homes without.

breakdown.analysis: Where did the data come from? The fire department’s records. Which fires get into those records? The ones firefighters are called to. If a resident puts out a small fire with an extinguisher, nobody calls, and that success never shows up. The records for extinguisher homes are mostly the fires that got out of hand. It’s like judging a hospital’s skill by its death records alone: the patients it cured never appear. Prephrase: the successes are missing from the data. Most students pick (B) because bigger homes mean bigger damage. But the stimulus measured damage as a percentage of value, which cancels out home size.

choices.note: If extinguishers handle many kinds of fire, they should help more, not less. Deepens the puzzle.

Tempting, and the main trap. Bigger, pricier homes would suffer more damage in dollars. But the study measured damage as a percentage of each home’s value, so home value is already factored out. Count versus rate again.
This just describes what the records contain, which the study already relied on. It’s consistent with both facts and explains neither. True-sounding support for something we already knew.
Tempting in a different way. Hard-to-reach extinguishers would explain why they don’t help. But it doesn’t explain why homes with them fare worse than homes without them. No help isn’t harm.

CORRECT. Fires residents put out themselves rarely get reported, so they never reach the records. The recorded fires in extinguisher homes are mostly the ones that got away, which are bigger fires. The extinguishers can work and the records can still look bad.

questions.stimulus: Cheesemaker: Several recent batches of our aged cheddar have developed a bitter aftertaste. The only change we have made to our cheesemaking process this year is that we now age the wheels in a new limestone cellar rather than on wooden shelves in the barn. Therefore, aging the cheese in the limestone cellar must be what made those batches bitter.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the cheesemaker’s argument depends?
choices: Cheddar aged in limestone cellars by other cheesemakers has sometimes developed a bitter aftertaste.
The milk used for the recent batches did not differ from the milk used earlier in any way that could cause bitterness.
Several customers have complained about the bitter aftertaste in the recent batches of aged cheddar.
The new limestone cellar is more humid than the barn in which the wheels were previously aged on wooden shelves.
Aging cheddar in a limestone cellar shortens the time the wheels need before they are ready to be sold.
questions.explanation: The cheesemaker rules out other causes only within the cheesemaking process, so the argument needs the ingredients, which lie outside that process, not to be the culprit. That is (B): if the milk changed in a way that could cause bitterness, the cellar is no longer the only suspect. (A) would lend the cellar theory some support, but the argument doesn’t need it; this cellar could cause bitterness even if no other has. (D) is tempting because it hints at how the cellar might cause bitterness, but the argument needs no particular mechanism. (C) and (E) do not bear on the cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Aging in the limestone cellar made the recent batches bitter.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Recent batches are bitter; the only change to the cheesemaking process this year is the move to the limestone cellar.

breakdown.analysis: The only change to the process? Fine. But is the process the only thing that could make cheese bitter? What about what goes into it? The argument rules out other causes inside the process and quietly ignores everything outside it, like the milk. It’s like saying “I changed nothing about how I bake, so the new oven ruined the bread,” when the flour supplier also changed. We need an answer that says nothing outside the process, such as the milk, explains the bitterness. Negate each choice and see whether the argument falls apart.

choices.note: Tempting, because it makes the cellar look like a plausible culprit. But it only helps; it isn’t required. Negate it: no other cheesemaker’s cellar-aged cheddar has ever turned bitter. This cellar could still be what did it here, so the argument survives.
choices.negation: No cheddar aged in limestone cellars by other cheesemakers has ever developed a bitter aftertaste.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the milk for the recent batches did differ in a way that could cause bitterness. Now there’s a second suspect outside the process, and the cellar is no longer the only explanation. The argument collapses, so it depends on this.
choices.negation: The milk used for the recent batches differed from the milk used earlier in a way that could cause bitterness.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Complaints tell us how customers reacted, not what caused the bitterness. Negate it and the causal claim is untouched.
choices.negation: No customers have complained about the bitter aftertaste in the recent batches.

choices.note: Tempting, because it hints at a mechanism: maybe the humidity turns the cheese bitter. But the argument doesn’t need any particular mechanism. Negate it (the cellar is no more humid than the barn) and the cellar could still be the cause in some other way.
choices.negation: The new limestone cellar is not more humid than the barn.

choices.note: Interesting fact, but not relevant. How fast the cheese ripens says nothing about what made it bitter. Negate it and nothing changes.
choices.negation: Aging cheddar in a limestone cellar does not shorten the time the wheels need before they are ready to be sold.

questions.stimulus: Under Tolliver’s public art program, the arts commission may approve a mural only if the mural is to be painted on a city-owned building and its design has been presented at a public hearing. The design for the mural proposed for the Garnet Street warehouse was presented at a public hearing last month. Even so, the commission cannot approve that mural.
questions.stem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Some of the warehouses on Garnet Street are owned by private companies rather than by the city of Tolliver.
Several residents objected to the mural’s design at last month’s public hearing.
The commission has not approved any mural this year that was to be painted on a privately owned building in Tolliver’s downtown.
The Garnet Street warehouse is not one of the buildings in Tolliver that the city owns.
The arts commission has rejected other murals proposed for warehouses in Tolliver.
questions.explanation: Approval requires two things: a city-owned building and a public hearing. The hearing requirement is met, so the only way to guarantee the mural cannot be approved is for the other requirement to fail, which is exactly what (D) says. (A) is the tempting near miss: some Garnet Street warehouses are privately owned, but that doesn’t mean this one is. (B), (C) and (E) are facts about objections and past decisions that don’t touch the rule’s requirements.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The commission cannot approve the Garnet Street warehouse mural.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Approve → city-owned building AND design shown at hearing; the warehouse mural’s design was shown at a hearing.

breakdown.analysis: Map it out. Approve → (city-owned AND hearing). Contrapositive: NOT city-owned OR NO hearing → can’t approve. We know the hearing happened, so that escape route is closed. The only way to get “cannot approve” is the other one: the building isn’t city-owned. Prephrase: the warehouse isn’t city property. It’s like a club rule: you can enter only if you have a ticket and you’re on the list. You’re on the list. If you’re still not getting in, it must be because you lack a ticket.

choices.note: Tempting, because it points toward private ownership on the right street. But “some” Garnet Street warehouses isn’t this warehouse. The mural’s building could be one of the city-owned ones, so “cannot approve” doesn’t follow. A sufficient assumption has to pin down the one building that matters.
So? Objections at a hearing aren’t part of the rule. The rule asks only whether the design was presented, and it was. Objections don’t make approval impossible.
This is a pattern from this year, not a fact about the warehouse. We still don’t know who owns the warehouse, so the conclusion doesn’t follow.
CORRECT. Not city-owned → the first requirement fails → the commission cannot approve the mural. Combined with the rule, the conclusion is airtight.
Past rejections don’t prove anything about this mural. Those warehouses might not have been city-owned, or the commission might have simply declined. Nothing here guarantees “cannot approve.”

questions.stimulus: Lightning poses the greatest danger to climbers who are above the tree line. For that reason, a mountain guide should cancel a scheduled summit climb if afternoon thunderstorms are forecast, unless the climbing party is able to reach the summit and get back below the tree line before noon.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Thunderstorms are forecast for this afternoon, and Rafe’s slow-moving party cannot get back below the tree line before noon, so Rafe should cancel today’s climb.
No thunderstorms are forecast, so Ines should go ahead with her slow-moving party’s summit climb.
Thunderstorms are forecast for this afternoon, but Dana’s party can be back below the tree line well before noon, so Dana must lead the climb as planned.
Thunderstorms are forecast for this afternoon, and Kiri’s fast-moving party expects to be back below the tree line by ten in the morning, so Kiri should cancel today’s climb.
Lena’s party could not have returned below the tree line before noon, so she should have canceled yesterday’s climb, even though no storms were forecast.
questions.explanation: The principle says: storms forecast and the party can’t be back below the tree line by noon → cancel. Only (A) supplies both facts and draws the verdict “cancel.” (C) is the tempting trap: the exception means the principle no longer requires canceling, but it never says the guide must go ahead. (D) makes the mirror-image mistake, calling for a cancellation that the exception switches off. (B) and (E) involve no storm forecast, where the principle says nothing.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Afternoon storms forecast AND party can’t be back below the tree line by noon → cancel the climb.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment that meets both conditions and concludes the guide should cancel.

breakdown.analysis: “Unless” sets up an exception. Translate: storms forecast → cancel, unless back by noon. So: storms AND NOT back by noon → cancel. The principle only ever tells you to cancel. It never tells you to climb. So the right answer must: 1. have storms forecast; 2. have a party that can’t be back below the tree line by noon; 3. conclude “cancel.” Any answer that concludes “go ahead” can’t be supported by this rule.

choices.note: CORRECT. Storms forecast: check. Party can’t be back by noon: check. Verdict is cancel: check. Every condition is met and the verdict matches.
No storms are forecast, so the principle doesn’t apply at all. It never says when you should NOT cancel. The verdict here has no support from the rule.

Tempting. Dana fits the exception, so the rule doesn’t require her to cancel. But “not required to cancel” isn’t “must climb.” The principle only produces cancellations. Watch the difference between an exception and a command.

Storms are forecast and the verdict is “cancel,” so it looks right. But Kiri’s party will be back below the tree line well before noon, so the exception kicks in. Under the exception the principle no longer calls for canceling. It doesn’t forbid canceling either, but it can’t justify it.
No storms were forecast, so the first condition fails. Being slow alone never triggers a cancellation under this principle.

questions.stimulus: To transmit through the Hollis Radio Club’s mountaintop repeater, a club member must hold an advanced operator’s license. Every club member who holds an advanced license has also passed the club’s emergency-procedures exam. Therefore, Kofi Mensah, a member of the club, has passed the emergency-procedures exam.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
choices: Kofi Mensah has transmitted through the club’s mountaintop repeater at least once.
Every club member who transmits through the repeater holds an advanced operator’s license.
Some members of the Hollis Radio Club who hold advanced licenses transmit through the repeater regularly.
Kofi Mensah has been studying for the club’s emergency-procedures exam.
Most of the members of the Hollis Radio Club have transmitted through the mountaintop repeater.
questions.explanation: The chain is: transmits through the repeater → advanced license → passed the exam. Nothing yet connects Kofi to the start of the chain, and (A) does: if he has transmitted, he must hold the license and so must have passed the exam. (B) only restates the first premise, and (D) is tempting but studying for the exam isn’t passing it. (C) and (E) are about other members, never Kofi.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Kofi has passed the emergency-procedures exam.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Transmit through repeater → advanced license; advanced license → passed exam; Kofi is a member.

breakdown.analysis: Build the chain: Transmit → License → Exam. The conclusion is about Kofi reaching “Exam.” But we know nothing about Kofi except that he’s a member. We need to put him somewhere on the chain. Getting him to “Transmit” or “License” does the job. Prephrase: Kofi has transmitted through the repeater, or Kofi holds an advanced license.

choices.note: CORRECT. Kofi transmitted → he holds an advanced license → he passed the exam. The chain runs all the way to the conclusion.
Tempting, because it sounds like part of the chain. It is: it just restates the first premise. Repeating Transmit → License still says nothing about Kofi, so nothing follows about him.
Says nothing about Kofi. Facts about some other members can’t prove anything about him.
Tempting, because it mentions the very exam in the conclusion. But studying for an exam isn’t passing it, and this doesn’t place Kofi anywhere on the chain.
“Most” members isn’t Kofi. He could be in the minority who never transmitted. Too weak to guarantee the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Communications director: A study of printed newsletters found that readers remembered more of an article when it was set in a serif typeface than when it was set in a sans serif typeface. Our city’s website currently displays all public notices in a sans serif typeface. So switching the website to a serif typeface would help residents remember more of the notices they read there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the communications director’s argument?
choices: Most residents who read public notices on the city’s website would prefer that those notices be set in a serif typeface rather than a sans serif one.
Many residents read the city’s public notices on their phones rather than on larger screens.
The advantage in recall that serif type gives to readers of printed text does not disappear when text is read on a screen.
Residents read the city’s public notices on its website more often than they read the notices in printed form.
The study of printed newsletters included readers from a wide range of ages and educational backgrounds.
questions.explanation: The evidence is about print; the conclusion is about a website. The argument needs the print result to carry over to screens, and (C) is the minimal version of that: the recall advantage doesn’t vanish on a screen. (B) mentions screens but says nothing about recall, so negating it leaves the argument untouched. (E) would make the study more convincing but isn’t required, and (A) and (D) are about preference and frequency, not memory.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Switching the website to a serif typeface would help residents remember more of the notices.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A study of printed newsletters found better recall for serif type; the website now uses sans serif.

breakdown.analysis: Print isn’t a screen. Why should a paper study tell us anything about a website? The argument jumps from one medium to another and assumes the effect comes along. It’s like testing a running shoe on a track and assuming it grips just as well on ice. We need an answer that says the recall advantage still holds on a screen. Use the negation test: if negating the answer kills the argument, it’s required.

choices.note: Preference isn’t memory. Negate it (most residents wouldn’t prefer serif) and they could still remember more with serif type. The argument is untouched.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most residents who read public notices on the website would prefer them in a serif typeface.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s about screens, the very thing the argument skips over. But it doesn’t say whether serif type helps recall on any screen. Negate it (few residents read on phones) and the argument is exactly where it was.
choices.negation: Few residents read the city’s public notices on their phones rather than on larger screens.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the recall advantage disappears on a screen. Then switching the website’s typeface does nothing for memory, and the conclusion collapses. That’s the gap between print and screen, filled minimally.
choices.negation: The advantage in recall that serif type gives to readers of printed text disappears when text is read on a screen.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The claim is about notices read on the website. How often people read print versions doesn’t matter. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: Residents do not read the public notices on the website more often than they read them in printed form.

choices.note: This would make the study more trustworthy, but it isn’t required. Negate it: the study had a narrow group of readers. That weakens the evidence a bit, but the argument doesn’t depend on it. A narrow sample could still show a real effect. Helpful isn’t the same as necessary.
choices.negation: The study of printed newsletters did not include readers from a wide range of ages and educational backgrounds.

questions.stimulus: Sports commentator: The league’s video review officials were right to let stand the goal awarded in last night’s match. The replay footage came from a camera angle that did not clearly show whether the ball had fully crossed the goal line, and the referee on the field had an unobstructed view of the play.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the sports commentator’s reasoning?
choices: If replay footage clearly shows that the ball fully crossed the goal line, the officials should let the goal stand.
A league should install enough cameras for every goal-line call to be clearly reviewable.
Video review should be used only for goals that are scored during the final ten minutes of a match.
Video review officials should consult the on-field referee before making any decision about a disputed goal, especially when the replay footage is unclear.
An on-field ruling should be overturned on video review only if the footage clearly shows it to be wrong.
questions.explanation: The commentator concludes the goal should stand because the footage wasn’t clear. (E) makes clear footage a requirement for overturning, so unclear footage means the ruling stays. (A) is tempting because it reaches the same verdict, but only when the footage clearly shows the ball crossing, which it didn’t. (B) is about future equipment, (C) introduces timing we aren’t told about, and (D) is about procedure rather than the verdict.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Officials were right to let the goal stand.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The footage didn’t clearly show whether the ball crossed the line; the referee had a clear view.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. The conclusion is “leave the call alone,” and the key fact is “the footage wasn’t clear.” So we want a rule like: don’t overturn unless the footage clearly shows a mistake. In arrows: overturn → footage clearly shows error. Contrapositive: footage not clear → don’t overturn. That’s exactly the commentator’s move.

choices.note: Tempting, because it ends with the commentator’s verdict: let the goal stand. But its trigger is clear footage, and here the footage wasn’t clear. With the condition unmet, the rule is silent about this goal.
This is advice about the future. It doesn’t say what officials should do with unclear footage now.
We don’t know when the goal was scored, and the commentator never mentions timing. This rule can’t connect to the conclusion.

Tempting, because the commentator mentions the referee’s clear view. But this is about how officials should go about deciding (consult first), not what they should decide. It doesn’t justify letting the goal stand.
CORRECT. Overturn only if the footage clearly shows error. The footage didn’t, so the ruling shouldn’t be overturned, which is just what the commentator concludes.

questions.stimulus: Each oyster filters large volumes of water as it feeds, removing algae as it does so. Every summer, algae blooms in Merrick Bay starve the water of oxygen and kill large numbers of fish. The state should therefore allow more oyster farms in the bay as a way of reducing the summer fish kills.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Oysters on new farms would remove enough algae to prevent the bay’s summer blooms entirely.
Algae blooms are the only cause of the fish deaths that occur in Merrick Bay each summer.
Oysters on new farms would take up algae fast enough to make the bay’s summer blooms at least slightly smaller.
Most people who fish commercially in Merrick Bay would support allowing more oyster farms there.
Oyster farming in Merrick Bay is more profitable than commercial fishing there.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from “oysters remove algae” to “more farms will reduce the fish kills,” which needs the added oysters actually to make the blooms smaller. (C) says that, in the minimal form a required assumption takes: at least slightly smaller. (B) is the tempting too-strong answer; the blooms need only be one cause of the kills. (A) asks for far more than the plan needs (no blooms at all), and (D) and (E) are about public support and profit.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The state should allow more oyster farms in Merrick Bay to reduce the summer fish kills.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Oysters remove algae as they feed; summer algae blooms starve the water of oxygen and kill fish.

breakdown.analysis: Oysters eat algae, and algae blooms kill fish. So more oysters, fewer dead fish? Not so fast. Removing some algae isn’t the same as shrinking a bloom. A bay-sized bloom could swamp whatever the new oysters filter. It’s like saying sponges soak up water, so a few more sponges will stop a flood. The plan works only if the extra oysters make a dent in the blooms. Prephrase: the new oysters would shrink the blooms at least a little.

choices.note: Sufficient, not necessary. If the new oysters wiped out the blooms, the plan would clearly work, but it doesn’t need that much. Negate it (the blooms would still occur) and smaller blooms could still mean fewer dead fish.
choices.negation: Oysters on new farms would not remove enough algae to prevent the bay’s summer blooms entirely.

choices.note: Tempting, but too strong. The plan needs the blooms to be a cause of the fish kills, not the only cause. Negate it: something else also kills some fish. Shrinking the blooms could still reduce the kills.
choices.negation: Algae blooms are not the only cause of the summer fish deaths in Merrick Bay.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the new oysters wouldn’t make the blooms any smaller. Then the plan’s whole mechanism fails, and there’s no reason to expect fewer fish kills. The argument depends on this.
choices.negation: Oysters on new farms would not take up algae fast enough to make the summer blooms any smaller.

choices.note: Public support isn’t part of the reasoning. Whether the plan would reduce fish kills doesn’t depend on who likes it.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most people who fish commercially in Merrick Bay would support allowing more oyster farms there.

choices.note: Wrong dimension: profit, not fish kills. Negate it and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: Oyster farming in Merrick Bay is not more profitable than commercial fishing there.

questions.stimulus: An online seller should give a buyer a full refund for a returned item if the item was misdescribed in the seller’s listing, or if the buyer sends the item back undamaged within thirty days of its delivery. A seller that follows this policy treats buyers fairly without exposing itself to abuse.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Corinne sent back an undamaged lamp forty days after delivery, and its listing was accurate, so the seller should give her a full refund.
Abdul returned his accurately listed coat torn a week after it arrived, so he should get a full refund.
Petra’s teapot was misdescribed in its listing, so the seller should refund her in full even if she keeps it.
Yusuf returned his chair seven weeks after delivery, but its listing had misstated the chair’s dimensions, so he should get a full refund.
Hana sent back an undamaged rug two weeks after it arrived, so the seller should refund her in full only if the rug was misdescribed.
questions.explanation: A returned item earns a full refund if either it was misdescribed or it came back undamaged within thirty days. Yusuf’s chair was returned and misdescribed, so the late return doesn’t matter, as (D) says. (C) is the tempting trap: the misdescription is there, but the principle covers returned items, and Petra may keep hers. (A) and (B) meet neither condition, and (E) adds a requirement the principle doesn’t impose on an undamaged return made within thirty days.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Item returned AND (misdescribed OR undamaged within 30 days) → full refund.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment where a returned item meets at least one of the two conditions and the verdict is a full refund.

breakdown.analysis: This is an “or” rule: either condition is enough. But both conditions sit inside a bigger frame: the item is returned. So the right answer needs: 1. the item comes back; 2. it was misdescribed, OR it came back undamaged within 30 days; 3. the verdict is a full refund. Watch for answers that meet one condition but break the frame, and for answers that pile on extra conditions.

choices.note: Accurate listing, so not misdescribed. Forty days is past thirty. Neither condition is met, so the principle doesn’t support a refund.
Accurate listing, and the coat came back torn. Within a week, yes, but not undamaged. Neither condition is met.
Tempting, since misdescription alone is enough. But the principle is about refunds for returned items. Petra might keep the teapot, and then the rule doesn’t apply. Half-right isn’t right.
CORRECT. The chair was returned and misdescribed. That’s one full condition, so the timing doesn’t matter. Full refund.
Hana returned it undamaged within thirty days, so she already qualifies. This judgment adds a misdescription requirement the principle doesn’t impose. It contradicts the rule instead of following it.

questions.stimulus: A hot-air balloon flight should not be launched if surface winds at its landing site are expected to exceed fifteen kilometers per hour. Whenever a cold front passes through the Arlen Valley, surface winds throughout the valley exceed that speed. So this afternoon’s scheduled flight should not be launched.
questions.stem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: This afternoon’s flight will land in the Arlen Valley, through which a cold front is expected to pass this afternoon.
If no cold front passes through the Arlen Valley this afternoon, surface winds in the valley will stay below fifteen kilometers per hour.
Most balloon flights launched when a cold front is expected end in rough landings that damage the balloon’s basket or envelope.
Several local pilots have launched balloon flights this year despite strong winds.
Cold fronts pass through the Arlen Valley more often in the afternoon than at any other time of day.
questions.explanation: Strong winds expected at the landing site → don’t launch, and a cold front in the valley → strong winds there. To reach “don’t launch” for this flight, we need its landing site in the valley and a front expected there, which (A) supplies. (B) is the tempting distractor; it says what happens without a front, but it neither forecasts a front nor places the flight in the valley. (C) and (D) are about outcomes and other pilots, and (E) is a general tendency, not a forecast for today.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: This afternoon’s flight should not be launched.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Winds expected over 15 km/h at landing site → don’t launch; cold front in the valley → winds over 15 km/h in the valley.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Cold front in valley → strong winds in valley → (if you land there) strong winds at landing site → don’t launch. The premises are general. Nothing ties them to this afternoon’s flight. We need two facts about this flight: it lands in the valley, and a front is expected there this afternoon. Then the chain runs straight to “don’t launch.”

choices.note: CORRECT. Landing in the valley + front expected → strong winds expected at the landing site → don’t launch. Every link is in place.

Tempting, because it’s about fronts and winds in the valley. But it only tells us what happens when there’s NO front. It doesn’t say a front is coming, and it doesn’t say where this flight lands. Nothing about this flight follows.
This adds a new consequence (damaged balloons) instead of placing today’s flight in the chain. We still don’t know whether a front is expected or where the flight lands.
What other pilots did has nothing to do with whether this flight should launch.
“More often in the afternoon” isn’t a forecast for this afternoon. And we still don’t know where the flight lands.

questions.stimulus: Restaurant owner: Our servers should share a portion of their tips with the kitchen staff. Diners decide how much to tip largely on the basis of how good the food was, and it is the cooks, not the servers, who are chiefly responsible for the quality of the food.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the restaurant owner’s argument?
choices: Servers should be paid a wage high enough that their income does not depend on the tips they receive from diners.
Diners ought to base their tips on the quality of the service rather than of the food.
Anyone whose work largely determines what a customer is paying a gratuity for ought to receive part of that gratuity.
Cooks should earn more than servers when their work takes longer to learn.
A restaurant should not require its servers to share tips with others unless a majority of its servers agree to it.
questions.explanation: The owner’s facts are that tips reward the food and the cooks are responsible for the food; the conclusion is that cooks should get part of the tips. (C) generalizes that link: whoever’s work largely determines what a gratuity pays for deserves part of it. (B) is tempting because it is about what tips should reward, but it pushes against the owner’s reasoning instead of supporting it. (A) and (D) are about wages, and (E) adds a voting condition that would, if anything, block the owner’s proposal.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Servers should share some of their tips with the kitchen staff.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Diners tip mostly based on the food; the cooks are chiefly responsible for the food.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. The conclusion is “cooks get a share of the tips,” and the reason is “the tip is really paying for the cooks’ work.” So the principle is: if your work is what the tip rewards, you should get part of it. It’s like a group project where the teacher praises the slides. The person who made the slides should get the credit.

choices.note: This is about servers’ wages, not about who should get tips. It doesn’t lead to sharing with the kitchen.
Tempting, because it’s about what tips should reward. But it says diners should tip for service, which points toward servers keeping their tips. It works against the owner.

CORRECT. The food is what diners are paying the tip for, and the cooks’ work largely determines the food. So the cooks ought to get part of the tip. That’s the owner’s conclusion, stated in more general words.
Wrong dimension: wages and training time, not tips. It doesn’t justify sharing tips.
This adds a condition (servers must agree) that the owner never addresses, and it would restrict the policy rather than justify it.

questions.stimulus: Any compost pile whose center stays at 55 degrees Celsius or higher for three days in a row kills the weed seeds it contains. Every compost pile that is turned once a week throughout the summer gets enough air to keep its microbes fully active. Ruth turned her compost pile once a week throughout the summer. Therefore, the weed seeds in Ruth’s compost pile have been killed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
choices: Ruth’s compost pile reached a temperature of 55 degrees Celsius at its center at least once during the summer.
Most compost piles whose microbes are kept fully active reach 55 degrees Celsius at their centers.
Weed seeds that survive composting can sprout wherever the compost is later spread.
Any compost pile whose microbes are kept fully active has a center that stays at 55 degrees Celsius or higher for three straight days.
Ruth’s compost pile contained fewer weed seeds at the end of the summer than it contained at the beginning of it.
questions.explanation: Ruth’s weekly turning gets her pile to “microbes fully active,” and the rule kills seeds once the center stays at 55 degrees for three days, so the missing link is microbes active → hot for three days, which (D) supplies. (A) is the near miss: reaching 55 degrees once isn’t staying there three days in a row. (B) is too weak twice over (“most,” and reaching 55 degrees isn’t staying there), (C) is about what happens afterward, and (E) allows some seeds to survive.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The weed seeds in Ruth’s pile have been killed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Center at 55°C+ for three days in a row → seeds killed; turned weekly all summer → microbes fully active; Ruth turned her pile weekly all summer.

breakdown.analysis: Two steps. First, chain what we have: Ruth turned weekly → microbes fully active. Then the rule: hot for 3 days → seeds killed. The chain stops at “microbes active”; the rule starts at “hot for 3 days.” Bridge them: every pile with fully active microbes stays hot for three days. Then Turned weekly → Active → Hot → Seeds killed. Watch for an answer that skips the middle link or settles for less than three straight days.

choices.note: Tempting, because it puts Ruth’s pile at the magic number. But reaching 55°C once isn’t staying there for three days in a row. The rule needs the longer run, so the seeds might have survived.
Too weak. “Most” piles with active microbes leaves room for Ruth’s to be an exception. And reaching 55°C isn’t the same as staying there for three days in a row.
Irrelevant. This is about what surviving seeds might do later, not about whether Ruth’s seeds were killed.
CORRECT. Ruth turned weekly → microbes fully active → center stays hot three days → seeds killed. The bridge connects the middle link to the rule, and the conclusion follows.
Fewer seeds isn’t zero seeds. Some could still be alive, so this doesn’t prove they’ve been killed.

questions.stimulus: A person should be listed as an author of a scientific paper only if that person helped to design the research the paper reports or helped to write the paper itself. People who contributed to the research in other ways, however valuable their contributions, should instead be thanked in the paper’s acknowledgments.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Because Ana helped to write the paper on soil bacteria, she should be listed as one of that paper’s authors.
Because Dev designed the experiment but did not help to write the report, he should be thanked in the acknowledgments rather than listed as an author.
Because Mira supplied the funding for the study, she should be listed as an author, since without her the research could not have been done.
Because Lars both helped to design the study and helped to write the paper, he should be listed as the paper’s first author.
Because Rui only collected data, without helping to design the study or to write the paper, he should not be listed as an author.
questions.explanation: “Only if” makes designing or writing a requirement for authorship: author → designed or wrote. Rui did neither, so he shouldn’t be listed, as (E) says. (A) is the tempting reversal; meeting a necessary condition doesn’t guarantee authorship. (B) contradicts the principle, since designing qualifies Dev’s work as more than an “other” contribution, (C) lists someone who did neither, and (D) ranks authors, which the principle never addresses.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Listed as author → helped design OR helped write. Contrapositive: did neither → not listed.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment that follows: someone who neither designed nor wrote should not be listed.

breakdown.analysis: “Only if” introduces a necessary condition. Author → (design OR write). So the rule can tell you who should NOT be an author (anyone who did neither), but it never tells you who SHOULD be. It’s like “you can vote only if you’re registered.” Being registered doesn’t mean you voted. The right answer must 1. describe someone who neither designed nor wrote, and 2. conclude they shouldn’t be listed.

choices.note: Tempting, since Ana meets the condition. But meeting a necessary condition isn’t enough. “Only if” doesn’t work in reverse. The principle never says who must be listed.
This contradicts the principle. Designing the research is one of the two qualifying contributions, so Dev’s design work isn’t one of the “other ways” that belong in the acknowledgments.
Mira neither designed nor wrote, so the principle says she should NOT be listed. This judgment goes the opposite way.
The principle says nothing about author order. “First author” goes beyond the rule.
CORRECT. Rui did neither, so by the contrapositive he shouldn’t be listed. This is exactly the verdict the principle produces.

questions.stimulus: The rusty skimmer, a dragonfly, lays its eggs only in ponds that contain no fish. Every pond in the Orrel Heath preserve is fed by Callow Creek, which was stocked with trout ten years ago. So the rusty skimmer does not currently lay its eggs anywhere in the Orrel Heath preserve.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
choices: Trout eat the larvae of rusty skimmers wherever the two are found together.
Every pond that is fed by Callow Creek now contains fish.
Most of the ponds fed by Callow Creek still contain trout.
Rusty skimmers laid their eggs in many of the preserve’s ponds before Callow Creek was stocked.
Every pond in which rusty skimmers lay their eggs is a pond that contains no fish of any kind.
questions.explanation: Skimmers lay eggs only in fish-free ponds, so they lay none in the preserve if no pond there is now fish-free. The premises put every preserve pond on Callow Creek but say only that the creek was stocked ten years ago. (B) links the creek to fish now: preserve pond → fed by the creek → contains fish → no eggs. (C) is the tempting but too-weak version, since the remaining creek-fed ponds could be fish-free, and (E) merely restates the first premise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rusty skimmers don’t currently lay eggs anywhere in the preserve.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Skimmer lays eggs → pond has no fish; every preserve pond is fed by Callow Creek; the creek was stocked with trout ten years ago.

breakdown.analysis: Lays eggs here → fish-free pond. Contrapositive: pond has fish → no eggs. So we need every preserve pond to have fish now. What we have: preserve pond → fed by Callow Creek. And the creek was stocked a decade ago, which isn’t the same as fish now. It’s like saying “the building’s water comes from a reservoir that was treated in 2015, so every tap is safe today.” Bridge it: every creek-fed pond has fish now. Then: preserve pond → creek-fed → fish → no eggs.

choices.note: This explains why skimmers avoid fish, but it doesn’t tell us any pond still has fish. If some creek-fed pond has no trout today, skimmers could breed there.
CORRECT. Preserve pond → fed by Callow Creek → contains fish → (contrapositive of the first premise) no skimmer eggs. Two links, and the conclusion follows.
Tempting, because it updates the ten-year-old fact. But “most” leaves some creek-fed ponds possibly fish-free, and skimmers could lay eggs in those. Too weak for a sufficient assumption.
History. What skimmers did before the stocking says nothing about whether the ponds have fish today.
This just restates the first premise. It adds nothing about whether the preserve’s ponds have fish now.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: A company that advertises a product as ‘handmade’ deceives its customers if machines perform any step in making the product that those customers believe is done by hand. Velloway Candles advertises its candles as handmade, but it uses a machine to pour the melted wax into molds, and its customers believe that every step that gives a candle its shape is done by hand. Therefore, Velloway deceives its customers.
questions.stem: The ethicist’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Pouring the melted wax into molds is one of the steps that give a candle its shape.
Velloway’s customers believe that the wicks of its candles are trimmed by hand.
Velloway’s customers would be less willing to buy its candles if they knew that a machine pours the wax.
Pouring wax is a step that machines do more consistently than people.
Most companies that advertise candles as handmade use machines for at least one step.
questions.explanation: Deception requires a machine step that the customers believe is done by hand. A machine pours the wax, and customers believe every shaping step is done by hand, so we need pouring to be a shaping step, which is (A): then customers believe the pouring is done by hand. (B) is the tempting near miss: a belief about the wicks is about a different step, one we aren’t told a machine performs. (C) concerns motive, not deception, and (D) and (E) are irrelevant comparisons.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Velloway deceives its customers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Advertised as handmade AND a machine does a step customers believe is done by hand → deceives; Velloway advertises “handmade” and a machine pours the wax; customers believe every shaping step is done by hand.

breakdown.analysis: The rule needs three things: 1. “handmade” advertising (yes); 2. a step done by machine (yes, pouring); 3. customers believe that same step is done by hand. Number 3 takes two links: customers believe shaping steps are done by hand, but nobody has said pouring is a shaping step. Prephrase: pouring the wax is a step that shapes the candle. Then Pouring → shaping step → believed handmade, and all three conditions are met.

choices.note: CORRECT. Pouring is a shaping step → customers believe it’s done by hand → a machine does it → all three conditions are met, so by the rule Velloway deceives its customers.
Tempting, because it’s about a belief that a step is done by hand. But it’s the wrong step. We’re told a machine pours the wax, not that one trims the wicks. The belief has to match the machine step.
This is about what customers would do if they knew, not about what they believe. The rule turns on belief, so this doesn’t trigger it.
Irrelevant comparison. Whether machines pour more consistently has nothing to do with deception.
What other companies do doesn’t tell us what Velloway’s customers believe or which steps shape a candle.

questions.stimulus: The bronze coin unearthed last month at the Avel site bears the seal of the mint at Tirra. Historical records show that the Tirra mint closed permanently in the year 410 and never reopened. So the coin must have been made no later than 410.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The Avel site was inhabited while the Tirra mint was still operating.
Few coins bearing the Tirra seal have been found at sites as far from Tirra as the Avel site is.
No coin bearing the seal of the Tirra mint was made anywhere other than at that mint.
Most coins bearing the Tirra seal that experts have examined proved to be genuine.
Some coins bearing the Tirra seal were made at the Tirra mint before it closed.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from “bears the Tirra seal” to “made at the Tirra mint,” and that move fails if someone else, such as a later forger, could have stamped the seal. (C) closes the gap: seal → made at the mint, and the mint stopped working in 410. (E) is too weak: some sealed coins being genuine doesn’t make this one genuine. (D) is too weak for the same reason, since “most” leaves room for this coin to be a copy, and (A) only shows the coin could be early.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The coin was made no later than 410.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The coin bears the Tirra mint’s seal; the mint closed for good in 410.

breakdown.analysis: So it has the seal. Does that mean the Tirra mint made it? Someone could have copied the seal later. A designer logo on a handbag doesn’t prove the designer made the bag. The argument needs: seal → made at the Tirra mint. Then, since the mint stopped in 410, the coin is from 410 or earlier.

choices.note: Being inhabited back then makes an early date possible, but it doesn’t rule out a later date.
Rarity at distant sites doesn’t tell us when this coin was made.
CORRECT. Seal → made at the Tirra mint → made while it was open → no later than 410.
Too weak. “Most” examined coins were genuine leaves room for this one to be a later copy. A sufficient assumption has to guarantee the conclusion.
Tempting, because it ties the mint and the seal together. But “some” genuine coins doesn’t make this coin genuine. Other coins with the seal could have been made elsewhere, later.

questions.stimulus: At the Ardley Culinary Institute, only apprentices whose dishes are served at the annual Founders’ Dinner receive the Gold Ladle award. Every apprentice whose dish is served at the Founders’ Dinner has trained under one of the institute’s head chefs. It follows that every apprentice who receives the Gold Ladle this year has worked at least one shift in the institute’s banquet kitchen.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every apprentice who works a shift in the banquet kitchen goes on to train under a head chef.
No apprentice trains under any of the institute’s head chefs without first working at least one shift in the banquet kitchen.
Some apprentices whose dishes are served at the Founders’ Dinner have worked in the banquet kitchen.
Most apprentices who have worked a banquet-kitchen shift have had dishes served at the Founders’ Dinner.
No apprentice who has not trained under one of the institute’s head chefs has ever received the Gold Ladle.
questions.explanation: Gold Ladle winners must have had a dish served at the dinner, and those apprentices have trained under a head chef, so the missing link is trained → banquet shift. (B) supplies it in disguised form: no one trains under a head chef without first working a banquet shift. (A) is the tempting reversal (banquet shift → trained). (E) restates a link the premises already give, and (C) and (D) are too weak.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Every apprentice who receives the Gold Ladle this year has worked at least one banquet-kitchen shift.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Gold Ladle → dish served at the Founders’ Dinner; dish served → trained under a head chef.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Gold Ladle → dish served → trained under a head chef → ??? → worked a banquet shift. “Banquet shift” shows up only in the conclusion, so the bridge has to run from “trained” to “banquet shift.” Prephrase: everyone who trained under a head chef has worked a banquet shift. Watch the form: the right answer may come dressed as “no one does X without first doing Y,” which just means X → Y.

choices.note: Tempting, because it links the same two ideas. But it runs Banquet shift → Trained. We need Trained → Banquet shift. Every banquet worker going on to train doesn’t mean every trainee was a banquet worker.

CORRECT. “No one trains under a head chef without first working a banquet shift” means Trained → Banquet shift. Add it to the chain: Gold Ladle → served → trained → banquet shift. The conclusion follows.
Too weak. “Some” of the dinner apprentices leaves room for this year’s winner to be one who never worked a banquet shift.
Wrong direction and too weak. It runs from banquet shift to dinner, and only for “most.” It can’t guarantee anything about Gold Ladle winners.
Sounds useful, but the premises already give us this: Gold Ladle → served → trained. Repeating a link we have doesn’t add the one we’re missing (trained → banquet shift).

questions.stimulus: Maple producers in Ardane County made far less syrup this spring than they do in a typical year. Sap flows most freely when freezing nights alternate with thawing days, and this March brought far fewer freezing nights than usual. So the scarcity of freezing nights must be what reduced the county’s syrup production this year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Freezing nights in March matter more to sap flow than freezing nights in April do.
Maple producers in neighboring counties also made less syrup this spring than they do in a typical year.
Next spring is likely to bring more freezing nights to Ardane County than this spring did.
Syrup made from sap collected in a spring with few freezing nights is darker than syrup made in other years.
Ardane County’s producers did not tap substantially fewer maple trees this spring than they do in a typical year.
questions.explanation: The argument blames the weather for a drop in total syrup, so it must assume there wasn’t some other reason the total fell, such as fewer trees being tapped. (E) rules that out. (A) compares March with April, which the argument never needs to do. (B) would help a little but isn’t required, and (C) and (D) are irrelevant to the cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Fewer freezing nights reduced the county’s syrup production this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Production was far lower than usual; sap flows best with freeze-thaw cycles; March had far fewer freezing nights.

breakdown.analysis: The weather explanation is plausible, but is it the only one? Total syrup depends on how much sap each tree gives AND how many trees get tapped. If producers tapped half as many trees, production would drop no matter the weather. It’s like blaming a slow sales month on rain when the store was also closed for a week. We need an answer that rules out another cause of the drop. Negate each choice and see if the argument breaks.

choices.note: Wrong scope. The argument is about this March’s freezing nights; it never compares March with April. Negate it (April’s freezes matter just as much) and March’s missing freezes could still explain the drop.
choices.negation: Freezing nights in March do not matter more to sap flow than freezing nights in April do.

choices.note: This might corroborate the weather story, but it isn’t required. Negate it: neighbors made normal amounts. Their weather may have been different, so the argument still stands.
choices.negation: Maple producers in neighboring counties did not make less syrup this spring than usual.

choices.note: A prediction about next year has nothing to do with what caused this year’s drop.
choices.negation: Next spring is not likely to bring more freezing nights than this spring did.

choices.note: Syrup color is irrelevant to the amount produced. Negate it and nothing happens.
choices.negation: Syrup made in a spring with few freezing nights is not darker than syrup made in other years.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: producers tapped substantially fewer trees. Now there’s another explanation for the low total, and the weather might not be the cause at all. The argument falls apart.
choices.negation: Ardane County’s producers tapped substantially fewer maple trees this spring than they do in a typical year.

questions.stimulus: Luthier: In blind listening tests, professional violinists consistently preferred violins whose tops were carved from spruce cut in winter to violins whose tops were carved from spruce cut in summer. Apart from the wood of their tops, the violins in the tests were identical. So the season in which spruce is cut affects how a violin made from it sounds.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the luthier’s argument depends?
choices: Violins whose tops are carved from winter-cut spruce sell for higher prices than violins made from summer-cut spruce.
The winter-cut and summer-cut spruce in the tests did not come from forests that differ in ways that affect sound.
Professional violinists hear small differences in sound better than amateurs do.
Cutting spruce in winter improves the sound of cellos as well as of violins.
Most violin makers who know about the results of the tests now carve violin tops only from spruce cut in winter.
questions.explanation: The tests held everything constant except the wood, but “the wood” differs in more than its cutting season. If the winter wood and summer wood came from forests that produce different-sounding spruce, the forest, not the season, could explain the preference. (B) rules that out. (D) is about cellos, which the argument doesn’t need. (A), (C) and (E) concern price, amateurs and other makers’ choices.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The season spruce is cut in affects how a violin made from it sounds.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Blind tests: players preferred violins with winter-cut spruce tops; the violins differed only in the wood of their tops.

breakdown.analysis: “Differed only in the wood” sounds airtight. But the wood can differ in more ways than its cutting season. What if all the winter spruce came from one forest and all the summer spruce from another? Then the forest could explain the difference. It’s like comparing summer and winter apples when the winter apples all came from a better orchard. We need an answer that rules out another difference between the two batches of wood.

choices.note: Price isn’t sound. Negate it (winter-spruce violins don’t sell for more) and the test results still point to the season.
choices.negation: Violins with winter-cut spruce tops do not sell for higher prices than violins with summer-cut spruce tops.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the two batches came from forests that differ in ways that affect sound. Now the forest could explain the preference, and the season might do nothing. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: The winter-cut and summer-cut spruce used in the tests came from forests that differ in ways that affect sound.

choices.note: The argument doesn’t mention amateurs. Negate it (professionals aren’t better than amateurs at this) and the professionals’ preferences still show a difference in sound.
choices.negation: Professional violinists are not better able than amateur players to hear small differences in sound.

choices.note: Wrong scope, and helpful at most. The luthier’s claim is about violins. Negate it (the season makes no difference for cellos) and the violin results still stand.
choices.negation: Cutting spruce in winter does not improve the sound of cellos as well as of violins.

choices.note: What other makers do afterward has no bearing on whether the season affects the sound.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most violin makers who know the results now use only winter-cut spruce.

questions.stimulus: Every mushroom species that grows on fallen birch trunks in the Larrow Woods is safe to eat. All of the mushrooms Odette gathered this morning belong to the white-gilled species that she found growing beside the stream. So all of the mushrooms Odette gathered this morning are safe to eat.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Some of the mushrooms Odette gathered this morning were growing on fallen birch trunks lying beside the stream.
Every white-gilled mushroom species that grows anywhere in the Larrow Woods is safe to eat.
The stream beside which Odette found the white-gilled species runs through the middle of the Larrow Woods.
Odette has never yet gathered a mushroom that turned out to be unsafe.
The white-gilled species Odette found beside the stream is one that grows on fallen birch trunks in the Larrow Woods.
questions.explanation: The rule is about species: grows on fallen birch in the Larrow Woods → safe. Odette’s mushrooms are all one species, so we need that species to be one that grows on fallen birch in the Larrow Woods, which is (E). (B) is the near miss: it would cover her species only if the stream were in the Larrow Woods, which we aren’t told, and (C) supplies that location without the safety link; each does half the job. (A) says only that some of her mushrooms grew on birch, somewhere.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: All the mushrooms Odette gathered are safe to eat.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Species grows on fallen birch in Larrow Woods → safe; all of Odette’s mushrooms are the white-gilled species from the stream.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Odette’s mushrooms → white-gilled species → ??? → grows on fallen birch in Larrow Woods → safe. The missing link is between “the white-gilled species” and “grows on fallen birch in the Larrow Woods.” Notice the rule is about species, not individual mushrooms, and it’s about the Larrow Woods specifically. Prephrase: the white-gilled species is one that grows on fallen birch in the Larrow Woods. Beware answers that each supply half of what’s needed.

choices.note: Tempting, because it mentions fallen birch. But we don’t know the stream is in the Larrow Woods, and the rule is about species anyway. Saying some of her mushrooms grew on birch somewhere doesn’t place the species in the rule.

Tempting, because it seems to cover Odette’s white-gilled species. But we’re never told the stream is in the Larrow Woods. If the species she found grows somewhere else, this rule doesn’t reach it. You’d need (C) as well, and a sufficient assumption has to do the job alone.

Location alone isn’t enough. Even with the stream in the Larrow Woods, the premise makes safe only species that grow on fallen birch, and we don’t know this one does. (Paired with (B) it would work, but it can’t work alone.)
Her track record isn’t proof. Past luck can’t guarantee that this morning’s mushrooms are safe.
CORRECT. The white-gilled species grows on fallen birch in the Larrow Woods → it’s safe → all of Odette’s mushrooms, which belong to it, are safe.

questions.stimulus: Heritage fund officer: Our fund will pay to restore a historic pipe organ only if the restoration keeps the organ’s original pipes. Old organ pipes sound properly only at the wind pressure for which they were originally made, and the restoration proposed for the organ at St. Aldric’s would raise its wind pressure well above that level. So our fund will not pay for that restoration.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the heritage fund officer’s argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The fund has refused before to pay for restorations that raise wind pressure.
The proposed restoration of the organ at St. Aldric’s would leave its original pipes unable to sound properly.
The fund prefers restorations that leave an organ’s original pipes able to sound properly.
A restoration that leaves an organ’s original pipes unable to sound properly does not count as keeping them.
The only change the proposed restoration would make to the St. Aldric’s organ is a rise in wind pressure.
questions.explanation: The premises show the restoration would leave the old pipes unable to sound properly, but the fund’s rule is about keeping the original pipes. (D) bridges the two: pipes that can’t sound properly don’t count as kept, so the fund won’t pay. (B) is the tempting choice, but it only restates what the premises already establish and leaves the bridge missing. (C) states a mere preference, not a rule, and (A) and (E) don’t touch the requirement.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The fund will not pay for the St. Aldric’s restoration.
