setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Fund pays → restoration keeps the original pipes; old pipes sound properly only at their original wind pressure; this restoration would raise the pressure well above that.

breakdown.analysis: Look at what the premises deliver: the restoration leaves the old pipes unable to sound properly. Now look at the rule: the fund pays only if the restoration keeps the original pipes. Those aren’t the same thing! The pipes are still physically there. The officer treats “pipes that won’t sound right” as “pipes not kept.” Chain: raised pressure → pipes won’t sound properly → ??? → pipes not kept → fund won’t pay. It’s like a landlord who returns deposits only if the tenant “keeps the original furniture,” then refuses because the couch is ruined. That works only if a ruined couch counts as not kept. Prephrase: pipes that can’t sound properly haven’t been kept.

choices.note: Past refusals aren’t a rule. The fund could have had other reasons then, and nothing here guarantees what it does now.

Tempting, because it’s the fact everything hinges on. But the premises already give us this: old pipes sound right only at their original pressure, and the pressure would go well above it. Restating it doesn’t connect “won’t sound properly” to “not kept,” which is what’s missing.

Relevant but not enough. A preference isn’t the fund’s rule, and it still doesn’t say pipes that can’t sound properly fail to count as kept. The fund could dislike this restoration and still pay for it.
CORRECT. Pipes unable to sound properly → not kept → the fund won’t pay. With the premises, the conclusion follows.
Knowing the restoration changes nothing else doesn’t tell us whether pipes that won’t sound right count as kept. The gap stays open.

questions.stimulus: Biologist: Gray rock lizards on Selwin Island spend far less time basking in the sun than gray rock lizards on the nearby mainland. Some researchers attribute this to the island’s many hawks, which prey on basking lizards. But on the island’s northern cliffs, where no hawks nest or hunt, the lizards bask just as little as they do elsewhere on the island. So the hawks are not the reason island lizards bask less.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the biologist’s argument depends?
choices: The cliff lizards’ habit of basking little is not mainly a trait inherited from ancestors that hawks preyed upon.
Island lizards bask less than mainland lizards do mainly because air temperatures on Selwin Island are higher than on the mainland throughout the year.
Hawks on Selwin Island catch more gray rock lizards each year than do all of the island’s other predators combined.
On the mainland, gray rock lizards bask less in areas where hawks nest than they do in areas where hawks are absent.
The northern cliffs are home to more gray rock lizards than is any other part of Selwin Island.
questions.explanation: The biologist treats the hawk-free cliffs as a control: lizards there bask little without hawks, so hawks aren’t the reason. But if the cliff lizards’ caution is inherited from ancestors shaped by hawk predation, hawks are still the reason, just not the hawks living there now. (A) denies this. Most students pick (B) because it gives a tidy alternative explanation that supports the biologist; but negating it changes nothing, so it is helpful, not required. (C) and (E) are irrelevant, and (D) would, if anything, support the researchers.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Hawks are not the reason island lizards bask less than mainland lizards.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Researchers blame hawks; on the northern cliffs, with no hawks, lizards bask just as little as elsewhere on the island.

breakdown.analysis: The cliffs look like a perfect control group: no hawks, same low basking, so hawks don’t matter. But does a hawk-free cliff today mean the lizards there are free of hawk influence? Their behavior could be built in, inherited from ancestors that lived with hawks. It’s like a family that still locks every door though they moved from a high-crime city to a safe village. Crime is still why they lock up. The obvious gap (hawks hunting there anyway) is already closed by “no hawks nest or hunt.” So the hidden gap is history. We need: the cliff lizards’ low basking isn’t a hawk-shaped inheritance.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the cliff lizards bask little mainly because of a trait inherited from hawk-hunted ancestors. Then hawk predation IS the reason, and the cliffs prove nothing. The argument collapses. Note the defender form: it just rules out one way the cliffs could mislead.
choices.negation: The cliff lizards’ habit of basking little is mainly a trait inherited from ancestors that hawks preyed upon.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it. It gives a neat alternative cause, so it would strengthen the biologist a lot. But it isn’t required. Negate it: warmer air isn’t the reason. The argument never relied on any particular alternative; it only claims hawks aren’t the cause. Helpful isn’t necessary.
choices.negation: Island lizards do not bask less than mainland lizards because of higher air temperatures on the island.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How many lizards hawks catch compared with other predators doesn’t tell us whether hawks explain the basking difference.
choices.negation: Hawks on the island do not catch more lizards than all the island’s other predators combined.

choices.note: This would support the researchers’ hawk theory, so it isn’t something the biologist assumes. Negating it only helps the biologist.
choices.negation: On the mainland, lizards do not bask less where hawks nest than where hawks are absent.

choices.note: Population size on the cliffs doesn’t matter. The comparison works whether the cliffs hold many lizards or few.
choices.negation: The northern cliffs are not home to more lizards than every other part of the island.

questions.stimulus: Journal editor: Admittedly, the reviewers we consulted found no errors in Dr. Okoye’s paper, and her earlier work has always held up. Nonetheless, we should not publish the paper. Its central result depends on a data set that Dr. Okoye has declined to share, so our reviewers had to rely on her own summaries of the data, and no researcher outside her laboratory has any way to check that result.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the journal editor’s reasoning?
choices: A journal should publish any paper its reviewers find free of errors, except when the paper’s central result cannot be checked by researchers outside the author’s laboratory.
A paper should not be published if its reviewers could not examine for themselves the data on which its central result rests.
Researchers ought to share the data underlying a submitted paper with the journal’s reviewers whenever the reviewers ask to see it.
A journal should give more weight to the findings of its reviewers than to the reputation of a paper’s author.
A paper whose central result conflicts with earlier findings should not be published until that result has been independently replicated.
questions.explanation: The editor concedes the paper looks sound but rejects it because the data behind its central result were never independently examined: the reviewers saw only Dr. Okoye’s summaries. (B) turns that into a verdict: a paper whose reviewers couldn’t examine its data should not be published. (A) is the trap: it reuses the editor’s point about outside researchers, but an exception to a rule for publishing only switches that rule off; it never says the paper should be rejected. (C) is about what researchers owe, not what journals should do, and (D) and (E) don’t fit the facts.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The journal should not publish Dr. Okoye’s paper.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Concession: the reviewers found no errors and her past work holds up; the central result rests on data she won’t share, so the reviewers relied on her summaries and no outsider can check the result.

breakdown.analysis: The editor grants the good news (no errors found, a solid track record) and still says no. Why? Nobody independent has actually looked at the data. A principle-justify answer has to deliver the verdict, here “don’t publish,” from facts the stimulus gives. Watch for rules that only take away a reason to publish. “Publish X, except when Y” tells you nothing about what to do when Y holds; it just turns the rule off. Prephrase: don’t publish a paper whose reviewers couldn’t check the data behind its main result.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it: it names the editor’s last premise almost word for word. But read the logic. Publish error-free papers, except when outsiders can’t check them. The exception only switches the publishing rule off; it never says “don’t publish.” Compare: “take the express train, except when it’s running late” doesn’t tell you to avoid the late express. It just stops recommending it.

CORRECT. Reviewers who had only Dr. Okoye’s summaries couldn’t examine the data for themselves. That triggers the rule, and the rule’s verdict is “should not be published.” Notice it works through the less obvious premise (what the reviewers saw), not the one about outside researchers.
Wrong target. This says what researchers ought to do, not what journals should publish. Dr. Okoye may be at fault for refusing, but nothing here says the paper should be rejected.
This favors the reviewers’ findings over reputation. The reviewers found no errors, so if anything it points toward publishing.
Nothing says the result conflicts with earlier findings. The trigger isn’t met, so the rule doesn’t apply.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A graduate student who has completed at least one year of study should receive a travel stipend to attend a conference if the student will present a paper there or serves on the conference’s organizing committee, but in either case only if the student has not received a stipend within the past two years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?
choices: Noor, a third-year graduate student who last received a stipend eighteen months ago, will present a paper at a conference this spring, so she should receive a stipend to attend it.
Felix, who began graduate study four months ago, will present a paper at a conference and has never received a stipend, so he should receive one.
Ines finished her first year of graduate study last spring and has never received a stipend; since she serves on the Calder conference’s organizing committee, she should receive one to attend it.
Bram, a fourth-year student who has received no stipend in three years, will neither present a paper at nor help organize the conference he plans to attend, so he should not receive a stipend.
Tova, a second-year student who has never received a stipend, served on the organizing committee for last year’s Calder conference, so she should receive a stipend to attend this year’s.
questions.explanation: The principle has three requirements (a completed year of study; presenting at or organizing that conference; no stipend in the past two years) and only ever concludes that a stipend should be given. (C) meets all three. (A) fails narrowly, since eighteen months ago is within two years, and (E) fails because Tova organized last year’s conference, not this one. (D) is the classic trap: missing both triggers doesn’t mean the principle says no stipend. (B) fails the year-of-study condition.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Completed 1+ year AND (presenting OR on the organizing committee) AND no stipend in the past 2 years → should receive a stipend to attend.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment that meets every condition and concludes the student should receive a stipend.

breakdown.analysis: Untangle it. The “if … or …” gives two ways in: presenting or organizing. “But in either case only if” adds a gate that applies to both: no stipend in the last two years. And the whole thing covers only students past their first year. So the right answer needs: 1. at least one year completed; 2. presenting at, or organizing, that conference; 3. no stipend in the past two years; 4. the verdict “should receive.” The principle only ever says who should get a stipend. It never says who shouldn’t.

choices.note: Close. Third year: check. Presenting: check. But eighteen months ago is within the past two years, so the gate shuts. Read the numbers.
Four months of study isn’t a completed year. Felix fails the first condition.
CORRECT. Finished her first year: check. On this conference’s organizing committee: check. Never had a stipend: check. Verdict “should receive”: check.

Tempting, because Bram really does meet neither trigger. But the principle only tells you when a student should get a stipend. It never says a student who misses both triggers should not get one. Treating a sufficient condition as a necessary one is the classic error.
Watch the conference. Tova organized last year’s Calder conference, not this year’s, and she isn’t presenting. Neither trigger is met for the conference she wants to attend.

questions.stimulus: Crowdfunding platform spokesperson: The backers of the Lumen desk lamp project are not entitled to refunds, even though the lamps reached them more than a year late. The project’s creators told backers about each delay as soon as they learned of it, and the lamps that were finally delivered matched the original description in every respect.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the spokesperson’s reasoning?
choices: A delay in delivering a crowdfunded product does not entitle backers to refunds if the delay resulted from circumstances that the project’s creators could not have controlled.
The creators of a crowdfunded project should tell backers about any delay as soon as they learn of it.
Backers of a crowdfunded project are entitled to refunds if its creators concealed problems from them or delivered something other than what was described.
People who back a crowdfunded project should recognize that they are taking a risk.
Backers have a claim to a refund only if a project’s creators kept them in the dark or delivered something other than what was promised.
questions.explanation: The spokesperson’s facts are that backers were kept informed and got what was described; the verdict is no refund. (E) makes one of those two failures necessary for any refund claim, so their absence means no claim. (C) is the converse: it says when backers are entitled and is silent here. (A) has the right verdict but a condition, a delay beyond the creators’ control, that the stimulus never establishes. (B) and (D) don’t address entitlement.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Lumen backers aren’t entitled to refunds, despite the year-long delay.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The creators reported every delay promptly; the lamps matched the original description.

breakdown.analysis: The spokesperson concludes “no refund” from two facts: the backers were told everything, and they got what was described. To justify a “no” verdict, the principle has to make those failures the only routes to a refund: refund → (kept uninformed OR wrong product). Contrapositive: informed AND right product → no refund. Beware the converse, “if they hid things or delivered the wrong product, refund.” That tells you when backers DO get money and is silent here. And beware rules whose verdict is right but whose condition we can’t confirm.

choices.note: Tempting: right verdict, and it’s about delays. But we’re never told the delay was beyond the creators’ control. The trigger isn’t met, so the rule doesn’t apply.
This is a duty the creators met, not a rule about refunds. It doesn’t say what backers are owed.
The converse. It tells us when backers ARE entitled. Here neither condition holds, so the rule is silent. It can’t produce “not entitled.”
Advice about attitude, not entitlement. Expecting a risk doesn’t settle whether you’re owed a refund.
CORRECT. Refund → kept in the dark OR wrong product. The Lumen creators did neither, so the backers have no claim, just as the spokesperson says.

questions.stimulus: Policy analyst: The government’s new subsidy for rural broadband service will not slow the movement of people from rural towns to cities. Surveys show that people who have left rural towns overwhelmingly cite a lack of jobs, not poor internet service, as their reason for leaving. Better internet service would no doubt make rural life more convenient, but convenience is not what those who leave are seeking.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the policy analyst’s argument?
choices: Most people who have left rural towns for cities would have stayed if suitable jobs had been available near their homes.
The broadband subsidy will cost more per rural household than any other program designed to slow rural migration.
Poor internet service is the reason that rural residents give least often when asked why they are moving to cities.
Better internet service would not enable any rural residents who would otherwise leave for lack of work to find work without moving.
A lack of jobs is the only reason for which the residents of rural towns ever decide to leave their towns and move to cities.
questions.explanation: The analyst assumes that because people leave for jobs rather than for internet service, better service can’t keep them. But better service could bring the jobs, through remote work or new local businesses, and then it would slow migration. (D) denies that. It sounds strong, but the conclusion is absolute (“will not slow”), so even a few people kept home would sink it. Most students pick (E) or (A), which echo “jobs”; but (E) is far too strong, and negating either does no harm. (B) and (C) are irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The broadband subsidy will not slow migration from rural towns to cities.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Leavers cite lack of jobs, not poor internet, as their reason; better internet would only make rural life more convenient.

breakdown.analysis: People leave because of jobs, not internet. Fine. But can internet affect jobs? Remote work, online businesses, new employers who need fast connections. If broadband creates work, it attacks the very reason people leave. It’s like saying “people quit the gym because of the hours, not the parking, so a new parking lot won’t help” when the new lot lets the gym stay open later. The analyst assumes internet and jobs are separate. We need: better service won’t let would-be leavers find work at home. Note: the conclusion is absolute, so the assumption can be strong too.

choices.note: Tempting, because it backs up the survey’s focus on jobs. But it isn’t required. Negate it: most leavers wouldn’t have stayed even with jobs. That doesn’t make the subsidy any more likely to slow migration. Not needed.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most people who have left would have stayed if suitable jobs had been available.

choices.note: Cost compared with other programs has nothing to do with whether this one slows migration.
choices.negation: The subsidy will not cost more per household than every other program designed to slow migration.

choices.note: Too specific. Internet service needn’t be the least-cited reason; the argument only needs it not to be the main one. Negate it and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: Poor internet service is not the reason rural residents give least often.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: better internet service would let some would-be leavers find work without moving. Then the subsidy slows migration, and the conclusion is false. Strong wording is fine here because the conclusion (“will not slow”) is absolute.
choices.negation: Better internet service would enable at least some rural residents who would otherwise leave for lack of work to find work without moving.

choices.note: Tempting, since it echoes “jobs,” but way too strong. Negate it: some people move for other reasons too, like family or schools. The argument survives. And even if it were true, the analyst would still need internet service not to create jobs.
choices.negation: A lack of jobs is not the only reason that rural residents ever move to cities.

questions.stimulus: It is wrong for anyone to accept a gift from a person whose application he or she will soon be deciding on, unless every other applicant seeking the same decision has been told about the gift beforehand. Without such disclosure, the other applicants have no way to raise concerns about the fairness of the decision.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle stated above?
choices: Before choosing among the applicants for a studio lease, Renata accepted a gift from one of them, but she had first told every other applicant about the gift, so accepting it was not wrong.
Tomas, who next week will decide among three applicants for a city contract, accepted wine from one of them after telling only one of the other two about it, so he acted wrongly.
Ilse accepted a gift from an applicant whose application she had already rejected, without telling any other applicant, so accepting it was wrong.
Because Omar told no one that a contractor whose bid he would soon review had given him a gift, Omar should now withdraw from reviewing the contractors’ bids.
Priya accepted a gift from an applicant whose application a colleague would soon decide on, and she told no other applicant, so accepting the gift was wrong.
questions.explanation: The principle condemns accepting a gift from someone whose application you will soon decide unless every other applicant was told beforehand. Tomas told only one of the two other applicants, so (B) meets every condition and reaches the verdict. (A) is the trap: Renata satisfies the exception, but an exception only keeps the principle from condemning her; it never says her acceptance was not wrong. (C) and (E) fail the deciding condition, and (D) draws a different verdict.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Accept a gift from someone whose application you’ll soon decide AND not every other applicant was told beforehand → wrong.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment that meets both conditions and concludes the acceptance was wrong.

breakdown.analysis: “Unless” marks the exception: telling every other applicant beforehand. So: gift from someone whose application you’ll soon decide + NOT everyone else told → wrong. The principle only ever condemns. It never certifies an acceptance as fine. The right answer needs: 1. the person accepting will soon decide on the giver’s application; 2. at least one other applicant wasn’t told beforehand; 3. the verdict “wrong.” Note that “every” makes the exception hard to meet: telling some isn’t enough.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it, because Renata fits the exception perfectly. But meeting the exception only means the principle doesn’t condemn her. It never says an acceptance is “not wrong.” Unless-clauses switch a rule off; they don’t flip its verdict.

CORRECT. Tomas will soon decide on the giver’s application, he accepted the wine, and one of the other two applicants wasn’t told. The exception requires telling every other applicant, so it fails, and the verdict is “wrong.”
Ilse had already rejected the application, so she wasn’t about to decide on it. The principle’s first condition fails.
Wrong verdict. The principle says accepting is wrong; it says nothing about withdrawing from the review.
A colleague, not Priya, will decide the application. The principle covers people deciding on the giver’s application, so it doesn’t reach her.

questions.stimulus: Public works director: Last winter, for the first time, we treated the city’s residential streets with a brine spray instead of rock salt, and accidents on those streets fell by a third compared with the winter before. Some attribute the decline to light snowfall last winter, but last winter’s snowfall was in fact about average for the city. So the brine spray deserves the credit.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the public works director’s argument?
choices: Accidents on the city’s main roads, which were treated with rock salt both winters, became more frequent last winter.
The winter before last did not bring the city less snowfall than last winter did.
Most residents who drive on the city’s residential streets noticed that those streets were less icy last winter than the winter before.
Brine spray prevents ice from forming on streets more effectively than rock salt does at every temperature.
The drop in accidents on residential streets was not concentrated on days when those streets were free of snow and ice.
questions.explanation: The director rules out light snowfall and concludes the brine caused the drop. But brine only matters on days with snow or ice, so the argument needs the drop not to be mostly in accidents on clear days, which (E) says. (B) is the trap: it borrows the snowfall comparison but points the wrong way; a lighter winter before would only help the director. (A) and (D) are too strong, and (C) isn’t needed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The brine spray deserves the credit for the one-third drop in accidents on residential streets.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brine replaced rock salt on residential streets last winter; accidents there fell by a third; the light-snow explanation fails because snowfall was about average.

breakdown.analysis: The director knocks out one rival (light snow) and declares brine the winner. But brine can only matter when there’s snow or ice on the road. What if the accidents that disappeared were mostly dry-day accidents, fender-benders on clear pavement? Then the spray, which does nothing on a dry street, couldn’t be what cut them. It’s like crediting a new umbrella for a better commute when most of the improvement came on sunny days. Prephrase: the decline wasn’t mainly in accidents that brine couldn’t have affected. Notice how far this is from the snowfall point the stimulus pushes you toward. That’s what makes it hard.

choices.note: Tempting, because a rise on the salt-treated roads would make a nice contrast. But it’s too strong. Negate it: main-road accidents didn’t rise (say they held steady). The brine could still deserve the credit. Not required.
choices.negation: Accidents on the city’s main roads did not become more frequent last winter.

choices.note: Tempting, and it reuses the snowfall language, but it points the wrong way. Negate it: the winter before had less snow than last winter. Then accidents fell despite more snow, which helps the director. An answer whose negation strengthens the argument isn’t required. (The real worry would be a snowier winter before, not a lighter one.)
choices.negation: The winter before last brought the city less snowfall than last winter did.

choices.note: Not required. Drivers needn’t notice anything for the brine to work. Negate it and the streets could still have been safer.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most residents who drive on the residential streets noticed they were less icy.

choices.note: Too strong. Brine needn’t beat salt at every temperature, just often enough last winter. Negate it (salt does better in extreme cold) and the argument survives.
choices.negation: Brine spray does not prevent ice more effectively than rock salt at every temperature.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the drop was concentrated on days when the streets were clear of snow and ice. Brine does nothing on a dry street, so it couldn’t account for most of the decline, and the claim that it deserves the credit falls apart.
choices.negation: The drop in accidents on residential streets was concentrated on days when those streets were free of snow and ice.

questions.stimulus: Five years ago, 40 percent of the tea harvested in the Darjan hills was sold abroad. Last year, 60 percent of the Darjan harvest was sold abroad, even though several new tea-growing regions now compete for foreign buyers. So the amount of Darjan tea sold abroad has grown over the past five years.
questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: The total amount of tea harvested in the Darjan hills did not decline at all over the past five years.
Foreign buyers generally prefer Darjan tea to tea from the newer tea-growing regions.
The Darjan harvest declined by less than 20 percent from five years ago to last year.
The Darjan harvest did not shrink by a third or more between five years ago and last year.
The price that foreign buyers pay for Darjan tea has risen over the past five years.
questions.explanation: A larger percentage of a smaller harvest can be a smaller amount. Exports grew only if 60 percent of last year’s harvest beat 40 percent of the earlier one, which requires last year’s harvest to be more than two-thirds of the earlier one; that is, the harvest can’t have shrunk by a third or more, as (D) says. (C) is the trap: it hedges in the right direction but picks the wrong cutoff, since a 25 percent drop would still leave exports higher. (A) is too strong, and (B) and (E) don’t bear on the amount.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The amount of Darjan tea sold abroad has grown over the past five years.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Five years ago 40% of the harvest was sold abroad; last year 60% was.

breakdown.analysis: A bigger slice doesn’t mean more pie if the pie shrank. 40% of 100 tons is 40 tons; 60% of 60 tons is only 36. So the argument needs the harvest not to have shrunk too much. How much is too much? Set them equal: 0.6 × new = 0.4 × old, so new = two-thirds of old. Exports grew only if last year’s harvest was more than two-thirds of the earlier one, i.e., it shrank by less than a third. Prephrase: the harvest didn’t fall by a third or more. The bit about competing regions is a distraction.

choices.note: Too strong. The harvest could have shrunk a little and exports would still have grown. Say it fell 10%: 60% of 90 is 54, more than 40. Negate it (the harvest declined somewhat) and the argument survives.
choices.negation: The total Darjan harvest declined at least somewhat over the past five years.

choices.note: Not required. The percentages already tell us foreign buyers took a larger share; why they did doesn’t matter. Negate it and the math is unchanged.
choices.negation: Foreign buyers do not generally prefer Darjan tea to tea from the newer regions.

choices.note: Tempting: it does the right kind of math and sounds properly hedged. But 20% is the wrong cutoff. A 25% drop still works: 60% of 75 is 45, more than 40. The harvest could fall by more than 20% and the conclusion could still be true, so this is too strong.
choices.negation: The Darjan harvest declined by 20 percent or more from five years ago to last year.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the harvest shrank by a third or more. Then 60% of two-thirds (or less) of the old harvest is 40% (or less) of it, so exports did not grow. The argument fails. This is the exact cutoff, stated indirectly.
choices.negation: The Darjan harvest shrank by a third or more between five years ago and last year.

choices.note: Price isn’t amount. The conclusion is about how much tea was sold, not what it earned.
choices.negation: The price foreign buyers pay for Darjan tea has not risen over the past five years.

questions.stimulus: Under the rules of the Fenmoor Herding Association, no dog may compete in the open class at its sheepdog trials unless the dog has placed in a novice trial. Every dog that has placed in a novice trial within the past two years is eligible for the association’s breeding registry. Brack is not eligible for the registry. So Brack may not compete in this year’s open class.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any dog that placed in a novice trial over two years ago has also placed in one in the past two years.
Brack has not placed in any novice trial that was held during the past two years.
No dog that placed in a novice trial more than two years ago is eligible for the association’s breeding registry.
Most of the dogs that compete in the association’s open class have placed in a novice trial within the past two years.
Dogs that placed in a novice trial more than two years ago rarely go on to compete in the open class.
questions.explanation: From the premises we get only that Brack hasn’t placed in a novice trial in the past two years, but the open class requires a placing at any time. The gap is an older placing. (A) closes it with a general link: any older placing comes with a recent one, so Brack, lacking a recent one, has never placed. (B) is the trap: it is already implied by the premises and leaves the older window open. (C) links old placings to the registry rather than the open class, and (D) and (E) are too weak.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Brack may not compete in this year’s open class.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Open class → has placed in a novice trial (at any time); placed within the past 2 years → eligible for the registry; Brack isn’t eligible.

breakdown.analysis: Run the contrapositive: Brack isn’t eligible → he hasn’t placed in the past two years. But the open-class rule asks whether he has EVER placed. What if he placed three years ago? Then he’s not eligible for the registry and can still enter the open class. So we need to shut the older window. Prephrase: Brack never placed more than two years ago, or a general rule that an older placing always comes with a recent one. Chain with the key: placed over 2 years ago → placed within 2 years → eligible. Brack isn’t eligible, so he placed in neither window, so he has never placed, so no open class.

choices.note: CORRECT. Any old placing brings a recent one with it. Brack has no recent placing (he isn’t eligible), so he has no old one either. He has never placed, so he can’t enter the open class. Abstract, but airtight.
Tempting, and true, but it’s already implied: not eligible → no placing in the past two years. Restating it doesn’t touch the real gap, a placing more than two years ago.

This connects old placings to the registry, the wrong pair. It just explains why an old placing wouldn’t make Brack eligible, which is perfectly consistent with his having one. He could still qualify for the open class.
Too weak, and about other dogs. “Most” open-class dogs placing recently says nothing about whether Brack ever placed.
“Rarely” isn’t “never,” and it’s about what dogs tend to do, not what the rules allow. Brack could still be allowed into the open class.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Strengthen, Weaken, Inference & Parallel

questions.stimulus: Manager of Pinecrest Lanes: Last winter we replaced the old wooden surfaces of our bowling lanes with synthetic ones. Since then, the average score bowled at Pinecrest has risen by about twelve pins per game. The synthetic surfaces, which hold the lane oil more evenly than wood does, are clearly what has improved our customers' scores.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the manager's argument?
choices: Many longtime bowlers at Pinecrest say that they prefer the feel of the old wooden lanes to that of the new synthetic ones.
Synthetic lane surfaces cost more to install than wooden surfaces do, but they are less expensive to maintain over the years.
At other alleys that switched to synthetic lanes, average scores rose by similar amounts, while scores at alleys that kept wood did not.
According to the company that installed them, synthetic surfaces hold a coat of lane oil more evenly than wooden surfaces do.
The number of games bowled at Pinecrest each week has grown steadily since the synthetic lanes were installed last winter.
questions.explanation: The manager infers that the new surfaces caused the higher scores from a before-and-after change at one alley. (C) supplies the missing comparison: alleys that made the same switch saw the same rise, and alleys that did not switch saw none, which makes some other local cause much less likely. (D) is the trap: it confirms the premise about oil, which the manager already asserts, but says nothing about whether the surfaces are what raised the scores. (A) is about preference, not scores.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The synthetic lane surfaces caused the rise in Pinecrest's average scores.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Scores rose about twelve pins per game after the switch; synthetic surfaces hold oil more evenly.

breakdown.analysis: Scores went up after the lanes changed. So what? Lots of things could have changed at the same time. This is a classic before-and-after causal argument, and the easiest way to strengthen it is to show the same cause producing the same effect somewhere else, or to rule out a rival cause. It's like saying a new fertilizer grew your tomatoes: you'd believe it more if neighbors who used it got the same result and neighbors who didn't got nothing. We need an answer that ties higher scores to the synthetic surface itself.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What bowlers like isn't what makes them score higher. The argument is about scores, not taste.
Wrong dimension. Cost and upkeep have nothing to do with whether the surfaces raised scores.
CORRECT. Same switch elsewhere, same jump in scores; no switch, no jump. That pattern points to the surface as the cause rather than something peculiar to Pinecrest.

Tempting, because it backs up the manager's explanation of how the surfaces work. But the manager already states that as a fact. Confirming a premise doesn't show that the surfaces, rather than something else, raised the scores.
So? More games bowled says nothing about why each game scores higher. If anything, more practice is another possible cause.

questions.stimulus: The cones of the Kerrin pine open and release their seeds only after they have been exposed to the intense heat of a fire. In the Dunlin Hills, every fire for the past eighty years has been put out before it could spread, and during that time almost no young Kerrin pines have appeared there, although mature Kerrin pines remain common.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: The suppression of fires in the Dunlin Hills has probably reduced the number of new Kerrin pines that have taken root there.
If fires were allowed to burn freely in the Dunlin Hills, the Kerrin pine would soon become the most common tree in the region.
Fire suppression has also reduced the number of young trees of other species in the Dunlin Hills over the past eighty years.
Kerrin pines are more common in regions where fires burn freely than in any other kind of region where the tree grows.
Mature Kerrin pines in the Dunlin Hills are more likely than young ones to be killed when a fire does break out there.
questions.explanation: Seeds are released only after intense fire heat, fires have been stopped for eighty years, and almost no young pines have appeared; together these strongly support the modest causal claim in (A). (B) is the tempting overreach: the facts say nothing about how fast the pine would spread or how it would compare with other trees. (C), (D) and (E) bring in other species, other regions or mortality rates the facts never mention.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Kerrin pine cones release seeds only after intense fire heat; 2. In the Dunlin Hills, fires have been put out before spreading for eighty years; 3. In that time almost no young Kerrin pines have appeared; 4. Mature Kerrin pines are still common.

breakdown.analysis: Put the facts side by side: no fire heat means no seeds released, no big fires for eighty years, and hardly any young pines. The obvious, modest conclusion is that stopping fires has cut down on new pines. That's the kind of answer most-strongly-supported questions reward: it connects two facts and doesn't claim more than they show. Watch for answers that predict the future or rank the pine against other trees.

choices.note: CORRECT. No intense heat means the cones stay shut, and the fires have been stopped for eighty years, so the lack of young pines is very likely the result. "Probably" keeps the claim at the right strength.

Tempting, because it runs the same logic forward. But "soon" and "most common tree in the region" go far beyond the facts. We know nothing about other trees or how fast pines would spread. Too strong.
We don't know this. The facts are only about Kerrin pines. Other species may not need fire at all.
Unsupported comparison. The facts describe one place. Nothing ranks fire-prone regions against every other kind.
No information about which trees die in a fire. This brings in something new.

questions.stimulus: Salon owner: In January we began playing soft classical music in our salon, and since then the average tip our stylists receive has risen by about 15 percent. Nothing about the way our stylists do their work has changed in that time. Evidently, then, the music puts our customers in a more generous mood.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the salon owner's argument?
choices: Several regular customers have said that they would rather hear popular music than classical music while they are in the salon.
Stylists at salons in the area that play no music at all also receive tips from most of the customers they serve.
The stylists say that the music has made their long workdays at the salon noticeably more pleasant than they used to be.
In January the salon also raised its prices, and most of its customers tip a set percentage of their bill.
Customers who book longer appointments at the salon tend to leave larger tips than customers who book shorter ones do.
questions.explanation: The owner concludes that the music caused tips to rise, having ruled out only changes in how the stylists work. (D) offers an alternative cause: prices rose in January and most customers tip a percentage of the bill, so tips would rise with or without the music. (C) is tempting but still credits the music, and (A) is about preference, not tipping.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The classical music makes customers more generous.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Average tips rose about 15 percent after the music started; the stylists' work hasn't changed.

breakdown.analysis: Tips went up after the music started. But is the music the only thing that changed? The owner rules out one rival (how the stylists work), but not others. A weakener here will give another reason tips rose. Think of it like this: your paycheck went up the month you started wearing a lucky tie. Maybe it was the raise everyone got that month. We want the salon's version of that raise.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Some customers preferring other music doesn't tell us whether the music changed how much people tip.
So? Customers elsewhere tip too. That doesn't explain why tips at this salon rose.

Tempting, because it suggests a mechanism (happier stylists, better service). But that path still runs through the music, so it doesn't weaken the claim that the music raised tips. It might even help it.
CORRECT. Prices went up at the same time, and most customers tip a percentage of the bill. Higher bills mean higher tips, no generous mood required.
Interesting fact, but we don't know appointment lengths changed. Without that, it doesn't explain the rise.

questions.stimulus: The Ellwood Glassworks makes only two products: drinking glasses and vases. This year the glassworks produced 15 percent more vases than it produced last year. Even so, the total number of items it produced this year was smaller than the total number it produced last year.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: This year the Ellwood Glassworks produced more vases than it produced drinking glasses.
The Ellwood Glassworks produced fewer drinking glasses this year than it produced last year.
Demand for the glassworks' drinking glasses fell this year, while demand for its vases rose.
The glassworks earned less money from the sale of its products this year than it earned last year.
Next year the Ellwood Glassworks will produce fewer drinking glasses than it produced this year.
questions.explanation: Only two products exist, vase output went up, and total output went down; the only way the total can fall while one part rises is for the other part to fall, so (B) must be true. (A) could be false, since glasses may still outnumber vases. (C) supplies an unproven cause, and (D) and (E) concern money and next year, which the facts never address.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. The glassworks makes only glasses and vases; 2. Vase output rose 15 percent this year; 3. Total output this year was lower than last year.

breakdown.analysis: Total = glasses + vases. Vases went up, but the total went down. What had to happen? Glasses had to go down, and by more than vases went up. Quick example: last year 100 glasses + 100 vases = 200. This year 115 vases; total under 200, so glasses must be under 85. That's the must-be-true. Everything else is a guess about causes, money or the future.

choices.note: We don't know this. In the example above, 115 vases and 80 glasses works, but so does 30 vases rising to about 35 alongside 200 glasses falling to 150. The count comparison could go either way.
CORRECT. Two products, one went up, the total went down, so the other must have gone down. That's arithmetic.
Tempting, because it's a natural story. But the facts are about how many were made, not why. Maybe a furnace broke. An unsupported causal claim.
Money is never mentioned. Fewer items could still bring in more revenue if prices rose.
A prediction. The facts cover only this year and last year.

questions.stimulus: County commissioner: A survey of people attending this year's Ludlow County Fair found that 78 percent of them favor spending county funds on a new livestock arena at the fairgrounds. The survey questioned more than 600 people, so its results are reliable. Clearly, most residents of Ludlow County favor building the new arena.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the commissioner's argument?
choices: The new livestock arena would cost the county more than any other building project it has undertaken in the past decade.
Some of the people questioned at the fair said that they had not yet decided whether they favored building the arena.
The more than 600 people questioned at the fair made up less than 2 percent of Ludlow County's adult residents.
Several county commissioners have stated publicly that they intend to vote against spending county funds on the arena.
The survey was conducted at the fair's livestock barns, where most of the people questioned were exhibitors who would use the arena.
questions.explanation: The commissioner generalizes from fair attendees to all county residents and defends the survey only on size. (E) shows the sample is unrepresentative: most respondents were exhibitors who stand to benefit from the arena. (C) is the trap: it notes that the sample was a small share of the county, but a small share can still be representative; the issue is who was asked. (A) and (D) concern cost and votes, not residents' opinions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most Ludlow County residents favor building the arena.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 78 percent of 600-plus fair attendees surveyed favor it; the sample is large.

breakdown.analysis: Who answered this survey? People at a county fair, which already leans toward people who care about fairs. A big sample doesn't help if it's the wrong people. It's like polling a golf club about whether to build a golf course and calling the result "public opinion." We need an answer that shows the people questioned weren't like county residents in general on this issue.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The cost might make it a bad idea, but the question is whether most residents favor it.
So? A few undecided respondents don't change the fact that 78 percent were in favor.

Tempting, because it seems to attack the sample. But a well-chosen sample can be a tiny share of the population and still be reliable; national polls question a few thousand people out of millions. Size isn't the problem here. Who was asked is.
Irrelevant. How commissioners vote doesn't tell us what residents think.
CORRECT. The people surveyed were mostly exhibitors who would use the arena. Of course they want it. That's a biased sample, so it tells us little about residents as a whole.

questions.stimulus: If Marta finishes the draft of her thesis by March, her advisor will be able to review it in April. And if her advisor reviews the draft in April, Marta will be able to defend her thesis in June. Marta is certain to finish the draft by March. So Marta will be able to defend her thesis in June.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: If Elm Road is repaved this summer, the Route 4 bus will be detoured. The county will approve the road budget this spring, and if it does, Elm Road will be repaved this summer. So the bus will be detoured.

If the bakery's new oven arrives this week, the bakery will start selling bagels. If it starts selling bagels, it will need another baker. The bakery has just hired another baker, so its new oven must have arrived this week.

Most graduate students who finish their thesis drafts early go on to defend their theses on schedule. Lena finished her draft two months early. So Lena will very likely defend her thesis on schedule, as she had planned.

If it rains on Saturday, the club's picnic will be moved indoors. If the picnic is moved indoors, there will be no room for games. It will not rain on Saturday, so there will be room for games at the picnic.

If the library extends its evening hours, it will need to hire more staff. Hiring more staff would strain the library's budget. So the library should not extend its evening hours, at least not during this year.
questions.explanation: The argument is a valid chain: if A then B, if B then C, A is true, so C. (A) follows that chain with the road budget, the repaving and the detour, though it states the second link first. (B) runs the chain backward from the last result, (D) denies the first condition, (C) shares the thesis topic but reasons from a 'most' generalization, and (E) ends in a recommendation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Marta will be able to defend her thesis in June.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Draft by March → review in April; review in April → defense in June; she will finish by March.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A → B; B → C; A; so C.

breakdown.analysis: Strip out the topic and you get a plain chain: A → B → C, and A happens, so C happens. That's valid. Look for an answer with two linked if-thens, the first condition stated as true, and the last result as a certain conclusion. Ignore anything about theses or students; topic doesn't matter in parallel questions.

choices.note: CORRECT. The premises are shuffled, but the chain is the same: budget → repaving; repaving → detour; the budget will be approved; so the detour happens. A → B → C, A, so C. Same certainty, same shape.
This runs backward: it starts from the last result (hired a baker) and concludes the first condition (oven arrived). That's affirming the consequent, and it's invalid. Our argument goes forward.
Tempting, because it's about a thesis. But it reasons from "most students" to "very likely," a probability argument with no if-then chain. Same topic, different structure.
Looks like a chain, but it denies the first condition (no rain) and concludes the last result won't happen. That's a different (and invalid) move. Our argument affirms the first condition.
Ends with a recommendation ("should not") and has no stated fact triggering the chain. Different conclusion type.

questions.stimulus: Parks director: On weekday evenings our public tennis courts are so crowded that players often wait an hour for a court, yet the courts sit mostly empty before noon. So we plan to cut the court fee in half for morning play. This should reduce the evening crowding, since some players who now play in the evening will switch to the cheaper morning hours.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the parks director's argument?
choices: The lights that make evening play possible on the public courts are expensive for the parks department to operate.
Many current evening players have free mornings and say the fee is what keeps them off the courts before noon.
Players who already use the courts in the morning say that they would play more often if the court fee were reduced.
Several private tennis clubs in the area charge their members much more for court time than the public courts charge.
Morning players and evening players currently pay the same fee for each hour they use the public tennis courts.
questions.explanation: The plan works only if evening players are able and willing to move to the cheaper mornings. (B) supports both halves: they are free in the morning, and the fee is what keeps them away. (C) is the trap: it shows the discount would draw more morning play from people already playing in the morning, which does nothing to empty the evening courts. (E) restates what the plan already implies, and (A) and (D) are about costs and other clubs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Halving the morning fee will reduce evening crowding.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Evening courts are packed while morning courts are empty; some evening players will switch to cheaper mornings.

breakdown.analysis: The whole plan rests on one claim: evening players will actually move. Can they? Plenty of people work in the morning, and no discount helps someone who has to be at a desk at 9. We need an answer that shows evening players can and will switch for a lower price.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. This could be a reason to want less evening play, but it doesn't show the discount will move anyone.
CORRECT. Evening players are free in the morning and name the fee as the obstacle. Cut the fee and they have a reason to move, which is exactly the link the plan needs.
Tempting, because it shows the discount changes behavior. But it's the wrong group: people already playing in the morning. More morning play from them does nothing to free up evening courts.
Irrelevant comparison. Private clubs' prices don't tell us whether public evening players will shift to mornings.
Already implied: the plan creates a price difference that doesn't exist now. Saying so doesn't show anyone will respond to it.

questions.stimulus: Angler: On Tamber Lake, fishing lures painted bright chartreuse catch about twice as many bass as lures that are identical except that they are painted blue. Since the only difference between the lures is their color, it is clear that the lake's bass are more strongly attracted to chartreuse than to blue.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the angler's argument?
choices: Bass in Tamber Lake feed most actively in the early morning and during the hour or so just before sunset each day.
Chartreuse lures cost slightly more than blue lures at the bait shop nearest to Tamber Lake.
Many of the fish that live in Tamber Lake are able to distinguish colors that are invisible to the human eye.
Most chartreuse lures were used by guides fishing the coves where bass gather; most blue ones were cast from the pier.
Some anglers on Tamber Lake catch more bass with lures of other colors than they catch with either chartreuse or blue lures.
questions.explanation: The angler says color is the only difference between the lures, but that ignores who uses them and where. (D) shows the chartreuse lures were mostly used by skilled guides in the best spots, which could explain the extra catches without any color preference. (C) is the trap: it sounds scientific, but it neither shows nor rules out a preference for chartreuse. (E) concerns other colors and some anglers only.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Tamber Lake bass are more attracted to chartreuse than to blue.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Chartreuse lures catch about twice as many bass as otherwise identical blue lures.

breakdown.analysis: The lures differ only in color. Fine, but do the people and places using them differ? The angler ignores that. It's like saying a brand of running shoe makes people faster because its wearers win more races, when it turns out mostly pros wear it. We need an answer showing that something other than color separates the chartreuse catches from the blue ones.

choices.note: Irrelevant. When bass feed doesn't explain why one color catches more.
Price has nothing to do with what bass are attracted to.
Tempting, because it's about fish and color vision. But seeing extra colors doesn't tell us whether they prefer chartreuse to blue. It neither helps nor hurts.
CORRECT. Experts fishing where the bass are used the chartreuse lures; casual anglers on the pier used the blue ones. That could explain the difference in catches with no color preference at all.
So? Other colors doing even better for some people says nothing about chartreuse versus blue.

questions.stimulus: Every ride at the Marrick Point amusement park that turns riders upside down has a height requirement. No ride at the park that has a height requirement is open to children under the age of six. The Comet is a ride at Marrick Point that is open to children under the age of six.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Every ride at Marrick Point that is open to children under six moves more slowly than the park's other rides.
Every ride at Marrick Point that does not turn riders upside down is open to children under the age of six.
The Comet is not one of the rides at the Marrick Point amusement park that turn their riders upside down.
Some rides at Marrick Point that have a height requirement do not turn their riders upside down.
Most of the rides at the Marrick Point amusement park are closed to children under the age of six.
questions.explanation: The rules chain: upside down → height requirement → not open to children under six. The Comet is open to children under six, so by the contrapositive it has no height requirement and does not turn riders upside down, which is (C). (B) is the trap: it negates the first condition and its result, which the rules don't support. (D) and (E) could be true but aren't required, and (A) brings in speed.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Upside down → height requirement; 2. Height requirement → not open to under-sixes; 3. The Comet is open to under-sixes.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: upside down → height requirement → not open to under-sixes. Contrapositive: open to under-sixes → no height requirement → not upside down. The Comet is open to under-sixes, so it doesn't go upside down. That's the answer to look for. Watch for answers that flip or negate the chain.

choices.note: Speed is never mentioned. New information.
Tempting, because it uses the rule's terms. But it negates both sides: "not upside down → open to under-sixes." The rules never say that. A gentle ride could still have a height requirement.
CORRECT. Open to under-sixes → no height requirement → not upside down. Straight contrapositive of the chain.
Could be true, but nothing forces it. Maybe every height-requirement ride goes upside down.
We don't know how many rides there are or how many have height requirements. Could be false.

questions.stimulus: Inspector: This morning I selected thirty jars at random from the Fenley plant's production run of strawberry jam, and every one of them was properly sealed. Because the jars were chosen at random, it is likely that nearly all of the jars produced in this morning's run are properly sealed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: A grocer picked a dozen apples at random from the top layer of a crate, and every one was ripe. So the apples in the crate's lower layers are very probably ripe as well.
Most of the magazine's readers probably dislike its new layout and would prefer the old one back, since every reader who wrote to the magazine about the redesign said that he or she disliked it.

Nearly all of the bottles of cider produced at the Ardmoor orchard last month were properly labeled. So the bottle of cider that Gareth bought from the orchard last month was very probably labeled properly.
Every jar on this shelf must be properly sealed. Any jar that is not properly sealed will leak when it is turned upside down, and none of these jars leaked when they were turned over.
A gardener examined forty seedlings, picked at random, from the nursery's greenhouse and found no sign of blight on any. So very probably almost none of the seedlings in the greenhouse have blight.
questions.explanation: The inspector generalizes from a random sample in which every item had a property to the probable conclusion that nearly all of the group the sample came from has it. (E) does the same with randomly chosen seedlings. (A) is the near miss: same rhythm, but it draws from the top layer and concludes about the lower layers. (B) generalizes from self-selected letter writers, (C) reasons from the group to one member, and (D) uses a certain conditional rule.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Nearly all of this morning's jars are probably properly sealed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Thirty randomly selected jars were all properly sealed.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Every member of a random sample of group G has property P; so probably nearly all of G has P.

breakdown.analysis: This is a generalization from a random sample: test a random handful, find they all pass, conclude the whole batch probably passes. The key features are (1) a random sample, (2) drawn from the same group the conclusion is about, (3) all of it has the property, and (4) a probable conclusion about nearly all of that group. Don't match on word order: several choices put their conclusions first, and order proves nothing. And watch for an answer that copies the rhythm but samples one group and concludes about another.

choices.note: Tempting, because it copies the surface: a random pick, all pass, "very probably." But the sample comes from the top layer and the conclusion is about the lower layers, a group the sample wasn't drawn from. The inspector's sample comes from the very run she draws a conclusion about.
Tempting, because it also goes from a group of respondents to "most." But letter writers pick themselves; they aren't a random sample. The original's key feature is the random selection.
This runs the other direction: from the whole group (nearly all bottles) to one member (Gareth's bottle). The original goes from a sample to the group.
A certain deduction from a conditional rule (not sealed → leaks; nothing leaked; so all sealed). No sampling and no "probably."

CORRECT. Same skeleton: a random sample from the greenhouse, every one free of blight, so very probably almost all of the greenhouse is free of it. Random sample, all pass, probable conclusion about nearly all of the same group.

questions.stimulus: Public works director: Most of the litter on our downtown sidewalks consists of paper coffee cups. People tend to litter when no trash can is close at hand, so doubling the number of trash cans on downtown sidewalks will substantially reduce the amount of litter there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the public works director's argument?
choices: Emptying the additional trash cans will require the city to hire at least two more sanitation workers for the downtown area.
Most of the coffee cups found on downtown sidewalks were dropped within a few steps of an existing trash can.
Several downtown cafés plan to begin offering a discount to customers who bring their own reusable mugs.
Some of the paper litter on downtown sidewalks is blown there from the open bins of a recycling center a few blocks away.
Some downtown shop owners have complained that trash cans placed in front of their stores make their entrances look cluttered.
questions.explanation: The plan assumes downtown litter happens because trash cans are too far away. (B) undercuts that: most cups were dropped right next to an existing can, so adding more cans is unlikely to change behavior. (D) is the trap: some litter blows in from elsewhere, but the plan targets the cups, which make up most of the litter, and (D) says nothing about them. (C) is a separate remedy, and (A) and (E) raise costs and complaints, not whether litter will fall.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Doubling downtown trash cans will substantially reduce litter.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most downtown litter is coffee cups; people litter when no trash can is close at hand.

breakdown.analysis: More cans means less litter, but only if a missing can is why people are littering downtown. What if the cans are already right there and people toss their cups anyway? Then more cans won't help. We need an answer that shows the downtown litter isn't caused by cans being too far away.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Hiring costs might make the plan expensive, but they don't show it won't reduce litter.
CORRECT. The cups are being dropped a few steps from a can that's already there. Distance to a can isn't the problem, so doubling the cans probably won't fix it.
This might reduce cup litter on its own, but it doesn't show the director's plan won't work. Both could help.

Tempting, because litter that blows in from elsewhere won't be stopped by more cans. But it's only "some" of the paper litter, and the premise says most litter is coffee cups. The director's plan targets the cups, and nothing here shows the cups won't be reduced.
Complaints about clutter are a cost, not evidence that litter won't fall.

questions.stimulus: Agronomist: The wheat variety Tolva yields well only in soil with a pH above 6. Nearly all of the farmland in the Brannock district has soil with a pH below 6. Even so, many Brannock farms that planted Tolva last year harvested excellent yields of it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the agronomist's statements?
choices: Some Brannock land where Tolva grew last year had soil with a higher pH than the soil on most of the district's farmland.
Most of the Brannock farmland on which Tolva was planted last year had soil with a pH above 6.
Farmers in the Brannock district who harvested excellent Tolva yields last year must have treated their soil to raise its pH.
In soil with a pH below 6, Tolva yields better than the other wheat varieties that are commonly grown in the Brannock district.
Any farm in the Brannock district that plants Tolva on soil with a pH above 6 will harvest an excellent yield of it.
questions.explanation: Tolva yields well only above pH 6, so every farm that got an excellent Tolva yield had soil above pH 6. Since nearly all Brannock farmland is below pH 6, those farms were on unusual land. (A) says exactly that: some of the Tolva land had higher-pH soil than most district farmland. (B) is the trap: it raises 'many farms' to 'most of the land planted with Tolva,' and (C) picks one possible explanation (treating the soil) when the farms might simply sit on the district's rare high-pH land. (E) treats the necessary condition as sufficient, and (D) adds a comparison the agronomist never makes.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Tolva yields well → soil pH above 6; 2. nearly all Brannock farmland is below pH 6; 3. many Brannock farms got excellent Tolva yields last year.

breakdown.analysis: Put facts 1 and 3 together. Excellent yield → pH above 6, so every one of those farms had soil above pH 6. Fact 2 says that kind of soil is rare in Brannock. So those farms were on land unlike nearly all of the district's farmland. We don't know how: maybe the soil was limed, maybe the farms sit on the district's few high-pH patches. An answer that picks one of those stories goes too far. Watch also for "many" quietly turning into "most," and for the "only" rule run backward.

choices.note: CORRECT. The farms with excellent Tolva yields had soil above pH 6, and nearly all district farmland is below pH 6. So at least some of last year's Tolva land had higher-pH soil than most of the district's farmland. The answer doesn't say why, which is why it's safe.

Tempting, because it's the right idea. But the agronomist says "many" farms got excellent yields, not most. Plenty of Tolva could have been planted on ordinary low-pH land and yielded badly. Too strong.
Possible, but not required. The high-yield farms might sit on the district's rare naturally high-pH soil. "Must have treated" picks one explanation out of several.
We don't know this. The agronomist compares Tolva with no other variety, and low-pH soil is exactly where Tolva does poorly.
This reverses the rule. High pH is necessary for a good Tolva yield, not enough to guarantee one. Drought or pests could still ruin a high-pH field.

questions.stimulus: Archivist: The water stains on the maps donated to our library were made either while the maps were being shipped or after they arrived here. But the shipping crate's seal was unbroken when it reached us, and its moisture indicator showed no exposure to water. So the stains must have been made after the maps arrived.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Lionel will spend his vacation either hiking in the mountains or visiting his sister in Calder. He has already bought new hiking boots for the trip. So he will not be visiting his sister in Calder during his vacation.

Maps stored in the library's basement have far more water stains than those stored upstairs, and the basement floods now and then. So flooding in the basement is probably what caused most of the stains on the library's maps.

Most packages that arrive at our warehouse damaged were damaged by the delivery company rather than by the sender. This package arrived damaged. So it was most likely damaged by the delivery company, not the sender.
Ilse searched her car thoroughly this morning without finding her spare key. Since she always keeps that key either in her car or in her desk at work, it must be in the desk.

The concert will go ahead only if the stage is repaired and the permit is approved. The permit has now been approved. So, as long as the stage is repaired, the concert will certainly go ahead as scheduled.
questions.explanation: The archivist argues by elimination: either X or Y; evidence rules out X; so Y. (D) does the same with the key: desk or car, not the car, so the desk. (A) is the near miss: it starts with an either/or but concludes that one option is false because the other is true, which doesn't follow, since he could do both. (B) shares the map topic but reasons causally, and (C) reasons from a 'most' generalization.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The stains were made after the maps arrived.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The stains were made either during shipping or after arrival; the sealed, dry crate rules out shipping.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Either X or Y; not X; so Y.

breakdown.analysis: Process of elimination: two possibilities, one ruled out, so the other. Look for an answer that names two options, gives evidence that eliminates one, and concludes with certainty that the other is true. Be careful with answers that use "either/or" but then do something else with it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it opens with "either/or." But then it affirms one option (hiking) and denies the other. That doesn't follow: he could hike and also visit his sister. Our argument eliminates an option; this one uses one option to eliminate the other.
Same topic (stained maps), different reasoning: a correlation (basement maps are more stained) used to infer a probable cause. No either/or elimination.
Applies a "most" generalization to one case to reach a "most likely" conclusion. No elimination of an option.
CORRECT. Reordered (the evidence comes before the either/or), but it's the same move: desk or car; not the car; so the desk. Either X or Y, not X, so Y.
This is about necessary conditions ("only if") and wrongly treats them as enough. No either/or elimination.

questions.stimulus: Engineer: We poured two test slabs from the same batch of concrete on the same day in the same yard. One slab was kept covered with wet burlap while it cured; the other was left uncovered. A month later, the covered slab was markedly stronger. Since the slabs differed only in whether they were covered, covering the concrete while it cured must have made it stronger.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Using flashcards must improve students' scores on the history final, since students who use flashcards when studying for that exam tend to score noticeably higher on it than do students who study for it without them.

After the Corlow bakery switched to a new brand of flour last month, its bread sales rose sharply. So the new flour must have made the bakery's bread taste better to its customers than the old flour did.

The practice quizzes must be what raised scores in one section of a chemistry course, which outscored the other section on the final. The sections shared an instructor, a textbook, and a schedule; only the quizzes set them apart.

Seedlings that are watered daily generally grow taller than seedlings that are watered once a week. Ines has watered her seedlings daily. So her seedlings are probably taller than most of the seedlings in the community garden.

The growers' association should require all of its members to prune their trees in winter. Two orchards were treated identically except that one was pruned in winter and the other in spring, and the winter-pruned orchard produced more fruit.
questions.explanation: The engineer compares two cases that are alike except for one factor and concludes that the factor caused the difference in outcome. (C) does the same with two course sections that differ only in the quizzes. (E) is the near miss: it has the same controlled comparison but ends in a recommendation for everyone rather than a causal conclusion. (A) uses a bare correlation, (B) a before-and-after change, and (D) applies a generalization to one case.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Covering the concrete while it cured made it stronger.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Two slabs alike in every way except covering; the covered one ended up stronger.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Two cases alike except for factor F; the case with F had outcome O; so F caused O.

breakdown.analysis: This is a controlled comparison, the logic of an experiment: hold everything constant, change one thing, see a different result, and credit the one thing. Find the answer with (1) two cases, (2) explicitly alike except for one factor, (3) a different outcome, and (4) a causal conclusion about that factor.

choices.note: A plain correlation with no claim that the groups are otherwise alike. Maybe stronger students use flashcards. Not a controlled comparison.
One bakery before and after, with no claim that nothing else changed, and the conclusion jumps to taste. Not two matched cases.

CORRECT. The skeleton matches: two sections alike in instructor, textbook and schedule; only one had quizzes; that one scored higher; so the quizzes raised scores. Its conclusion comes first, but order doesn't matter in parallel questions.
Different structure: a general rule applied to one case to reach a probable conclusion. No comparison of two matched cases.

Tempting, because the first half is a perfect controlled comparison. But the conclusion is a recommendation for every grower, not a claim about what caused the difference. Changing the conclusion type breaks the match.

questions.stimulus: Groundskeeper: Whenever the sky over the Bexley golf course stays clear all night in October, frost covers the greens by dawn. This morning, an October morning, there was no frost on the greens at all. So the sky over the course must not have stayed clear all last night.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: The Halloway choir must have been singing at the spring festival last night, since Nadia performed a solo at last night's concert and she performs one whenever the choir sings at the festival.
The Brenner Street bakery will not close early today. It closes early whenever it runs out of rye bread, and today it has not run out.
Frost usually forms on the greens after a clear October night. Last night was clear and cold, so there was probably frost on the greens this morning, though no one has gone out yet to check.
The greens at the golf course were damaged last winter after several nights of hard frost. So the groundskeepers should cover the greens on any night this year when hard frost is expected.
The basement circuit breaker in Dr. Okafor's lab trips every time the lab's large centrifuge runs, and yesterday the breaker held all day. So the lab cannot have run that centrifuge yesterday.
questions.explanation: The groundskeeper reasons: whenever X, Y; not Y; so not X, the valid contrapositive. (E) does the same with the centrifuge and the breaker. (A) affirms the result to conclude the condition, and (B) denies the condition to conclude the result is absent; both are invalid. (C) and (D) share the frost and golf-course topic but use a probability claim and a recommendation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The sky did not stay clear all last night.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Clear October night → frost on the greens; there was no frost this morning.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X → Y; not Y; so not X.

breakdown.analysis: Clear night → frost. No frost → so not a clear night. That's the contrapositive, and it's valid. The answer must have the same move: a "whenever" rule, the result fails to happen, so the condition didn't happen either. Two classic decoys: affirming the result (Y, so X) and denying the condition (not X, so not Y).

choices.note: Affirms the result (Nadia sang a solo) to conclude the condition (it was the spring festival). Invalid; she might solo at other concerts too. Our argument denies the result.
Denies the condition (didn't run out of rye) to conclude the result won't happen. Invalid; it could close early for other reasons. Different move.
Tempting, because it's frost on the greens again. But it's a "usually" probability argument that runs forward from the condition. Topic match, structure miss.
Same golf-course topic, but it ends in a recommendation drawn from one bad winter. No if-then rule.
CORRECT. The wording changes ("held" for "did not trip"), but the logic is the same: centrifuge → breaker trips; breaker didn't trip; so no centrifuge. X → Y, not Y, so not X.
