questions.stimulus: Pantry coordinator: Most of the people who volunteer at the Delling food pantry are retired teachers. Moreover, every retired teacher who volunteers at the pantry works the Saturday morning shift. It follows that most of the people who volunteer at the pantry work the Saturday morning shift.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: No pear tree in the Harlow orchard was planted in 1990 or later, and pears account for most of the orchard's trees. So more than half of its trees date from before 1990.
Most of the members of the Ridley hiking club live in the city, and most of the city's residents own a car. It follows that most of the members of the Ridley hiking club own a car.

Every painting in the Varga collection was framed by the Lisle workshop, and most of the works framed by the Lisle workshop are oil paintings. It follows that most of the paintings in the Varga collection are oil paintings.

Most of the students in Ms. Dorn's class play an instrument, and every student in her class who plays an instrument is in the school band. It follows that every student in Ms. Dorn's class is in the school band.

Most of the volunteers at the city animal shelter are college students, and most college students in the city have flexible schedules. So Priya, who volunteers at the shelter, probably has a flexible schedule.
questions.explanation: The coordinator's argument is a valid quantifier chain: most A are B, all B (in A) are C, so most A are C. (A) matches it with trees, pear trees and planting dates, though it gives the 'every' premise first. (B) chains two 'most' statements, which is invalid, and (C) puts the 'all' and 'most' in the wrong places. (D) is the near miss: same premises, but it concludes 'every' instead of 'most'. (E) concludes about one person.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most pantry volunteers work the Saturday morning shift.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most volunteers are retired teachers; every retired-teacher volunteer works that shift.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; every B among the A is C; so most A are C.

breakdown.analysis: Check the quantifiers, not the topic. Most volunteers are retired teachers, and all of those work Saturday. So the Saturday group includes at least that majority, and most volunteers work Saturday. Valid. The match needs "most," then "every," then "most" in the conclusion. Watch for "most + most" (invalid), "all + most" in reverse order, and a conclusion that jumps to "every."

choices.note: CORRECT. Premises swapped and reworded, but the quantifiers match: most trees are pear trees; every pear tree predates 1990; so most trees predate 1990. Most + all → most.
Most + most. Invalid: the car-owning majority of city residents could exclude the hikers entirely. The original's second premise is "every," not "most."
The quantifiers are in the wrong slots: all A are B, most B are C. The Varga paintings could be among the framed works that aren't oils. Different (and invalid) structure.
Tempting, because the premises match perfectly (most, then every). But the conclusion says "every student," when the premises only support "most." One word breaks the parallel.
Uses two "most" premises and concludes about one person with "probably." Different quantifiers, different conclusion type, even though it shares the volunteer theme.

questions.stimulus: Harbor commission: We want the Port Sennet shipping channel to remain usable by the new, deeper cargo ships. The channel fills with silt every winter, and dredging it each spring is the only way to keep it deep enough for those ships. So we should arrange to have the channel dredged every spring.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: The town wants to reduce traffic on Mill Street, and adding a traffic light at the corner of Mill and Fifth is one of several ways it could do so. So the town should add a traffic light at that corner as soon as it can.

Most runners who finish a marathon in under three hours follow a coach's training plan. Malik wants to finish this year's city marathon in under three hours. So Malik should follow a coach's training plan.

Rosa wants to be able to read her grandmother's letters, which are written in Portuguese. Taking a year of Portuguese classes is the only way she could learn to read them. So she should enroll in a year of Portuguese classes.

The library wants to keep its rare-book room open on weekends. The only way to do that is to hire another archivist, and the budget cannot cover another salary. So the library should give up on opening the room on weekends.

Every winter, silt fills the Port Sennet channel, and in years when the channel is not dredged, fewer cargo ships call at the port. So the silt is probably the main reason fewer ships call at Port Sennet in those years.
questions.explanation: The commission reasons: we want goal G; action M is the only way to achieve G; so we should do M. (C) matches: Rosa wants to read the letters, classes are the only way, so she should take them. (A) is the near miss: the light is merely one of several ways, which is a weaker premise. (D) starts the same way but concludes the goal should be abandoned, (B) relies on what most people do, and (E) shares the harbor topic but draws a causal conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The commission should have the channel dredged every spring.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The goal is a channel usable by deeper ships; annual spring dredging is the only way to achieve it.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: We want G; M is the only way to get G; so we should do M.

breakdown.analysis: Goal plus only means equals do the means. The "only way" is what makes this argument tick: if the action were just one option among many, the conclusion wouldn't follow. Find an answer with a goal, a single necessary means, and a recommendation to take that means. Watch for "one of several ways" and for answers that flip the conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's goal → action → "should." But the light is "one of several ways," not the only way. That's a weaker premise, so it's a different (and weaker) argument.
Reasons from what most successful runners did, not from an only means. Following a plan isn't shown to be required. A statistical recommendation.
CORRECT. Goal (read the letters); only means (a year of classes); so she should take them. Same skeleton.
Starts the same way, with a goal and an only means, but then adds a cost and concludes the goal should be dropped. Opposite kind of conclusion.
Same harbor and silt, but it's a causal inference (silt explains fewer ships), not a recommendation based on an only means.

questions.stimulus: Shipbuilder: The new trawler Gannet was built at the same yard, to the same design, and from the same timber as the trawler Petrel, which has needed no major hull repairs in its twenty-five years at sea. So the Gannet will probably also go many years without needing major hull repairs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every boat built at the Kessing yard has a hull strong enough to last for decades without major repairs. The Merlin was built at the Kessing yard. So the Merlin will last for decades without needing major hull repairs.

This year's trainee nurses at Corran Hospital had the same instructor, methods, and simulators as last year's, nearly all of whom passed the licensing exam. So most of this year's will probably pass it too.

The Heron was built at the same yard as the Osprey, which has needed few repairs. But the Heron was built from a different timber than the Osprey was. So the Heron will probably need more repairs than the Osprey has needed.

Of the twenty bridges built by the Ardley firm that engineers inspected this year, none showed any structural flaw. So probably few of the bridges that the Ardley firm has built have structural flaws.
Ruth's apple trees have never had scab, while her neighbors' trees of the same variety often have. So the soil in Ruth's orchard must be what protects her trees from scab.
questions.explanation: The shipbuilder argues by analogy: a new case shares several relevant features with an older case that had a good outcome, so the new case will probably have the same outcome. (B) does this with two classes of trainee nurses taught the same way. (A) is the trap: it reaches a similar conclusion but deduces it from a rule covering every boat, not from a comparison with one case. (C) draws a contrast from a difference, (D) generalizes from a sample, and (E) makes a causal claim.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Gannet will probably go many years without major hull repairs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The Gannet matches the Petrel in yard, design and timber; the Petrel has needed no major hull repairs in twenty-five years.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: New case N shares features a, b, c with old case O; O had result R; so N will probably have R.

breakdown.analysis: This is an argument by analogy: same yard, same design, same wood as a boat that held up, so this one probably will too. The match needs a new case, an older case with several shared features, the old case's good result, and a "probably" prediction for the new one. A rule about every member of a group is a different argument, even if the conclusion sounds alike.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about boats from one yard lasting without repairs. But it deduces the result from a universal rule ("every boat built at the Kessing yard") with certainty. The original compares one boat to another and says "probably."
CORRECT. Same instructor, methods and simulators as last year's trainees, nearly all of whom passed; so this year's will probably pass. Shared features → same likely result. Same pattern.
Uses a difference between the cases to predict a different result. The original relies on similarities to predict the same result.
A generalization from an inspected sample to all of the firm's bridges. No single comparison case.
A causal claim about why one case differs from others. The original never explains anything; it just predicts that the new case will match the old one.

questions.stimulus: The robotics team at Wellsby High will compete in the national finals only if it wins the regional tournament, and it will win the regional tournament only if its robot is rebuilt before March. The team's coach has just learned that the robot cannot be rebuilt before March. So the team will not compete in the national finals.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Danica will be named head chef only if she completes the advanced pastry course, and she will complete that course only if the restaurant pays her tuition. The restaurant has agreed to pay her tuition. So Danica will be named head chef.

The orchestra must not have found a corporate sponsor this year, despite all of the director's efforts to secure one. It will tour Europe only if it finds such a sponsor, and it did not tour Europe this year.

The museum will open its new wing only if it raises the needed funds, and it will raise those funds only if the city provides a grant. So the museum should apply for the city's grant as soon as it possibly can.

The Brandt farm cannot get enough compost, so it will not earn the organic label. No farm earns that label without giving up synthetic fertilizer, and the Brandt farm will give that up only if it gets enough compost.
Odile will probably be hired as a bus driver, since she is about to complete the city's driver-training course and most applicants who complete that course are hired as bus drivers.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two necessary conditions and then denies the last one: A only if B, B only if C, not C, so not A. (D) has the same chain, though it states one link as 'no farm earns that label without.' (A) is the trap: it has the same 'only if' chain but affirms the last condition and concludes the first, treating necessary conditions as sufficient. (B) uses one link and reasons backward, (C) ends in a recommendation, and (E) reasons from 'most.'

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The team will not compete in the national finals.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Finals → regional win → robot rebuilt before March; the robot can't be rebuilt in time.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A only if B; B only if C; not C; so not A.

breakdown.analysis: Translate "only if": finals → win regional → rebuilt by March. The robot won't be rebuilt, so no regional win, so no finals. Valid contrapositive chain. The match must have two necessary-condition links and must deny the last condition to deny the first. It may not say "only if" twice; "no X without Y" means the same thing. The classic decoy uses the same chain but affirms the last condition, which proves nothing.

choices.note: Tempting, because the "only if" chain looks identical. But it affirms the last condition (tuition paid) and concludes the first (head chef). Necessary isn't sufficient: paying tuition doesn't guarantee she finishes or gets the job.
Only one link, and it reasons from "didn't tour" to "no sponsor," which is backward: a sponsor is necessary for touring, not enough for it.
Same two-link chain, but no fact triggers it, and it ends with a recommendation. Different conclusion type.

CORRECT. Rearranged and reworded ("no farm earns that label without" is another way to say "only if"), but the chain is the same: label → give up synthetic fertilizer → enough compost; not enough compost; so no label. A only if B, B only if C, not C, so not A.
It reasons from "most" to "probably." No necessary conditions at all, and no chain.

questions.stimulus: Some residents blame vibration from the new highway for the cracks that have appeared in Varlow's old town hall. But if traffic vibration were the cause, the walls facing the highway would be the most badly cracked, and in fact the cracks are spread evenly over all four walls. So vibration from the highway is probably not what is causing the cracks.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Some people say runoff from the new farm is killing the river's fish. If runoff were the cause, the fish nearest the farm would be dying first, and that is exactly what has happened. So runoff from the farm is surely the cause.
The new highway is probably not the cause of the noise in the neighborhood, whatever some residents claim. The engineers who designed it insist that it is quieter than the old road it replaced.
The cracks in the town hall must have been caused by vibration. They were caused either by vibration or by settling of the foundation, and inspectors found that the foundation has not settled at all.

Some blame the rising price of coffee for the café's falling sales. But even if the café lowered its prices, it would still face stiff competition from the new shop across the street. So the café should not lower its prices.

The bakery's new recipe is probably not why its bread sales dropped, whatever some claim. Were the recipe to blame, loaves made with it would show the steepest decline; instead, all its breads slipped about equally.
questions.explanation: The argument tests a proposed cause by its prediction: if H were true, we would see a certain pattern; we don't; so H is probably false. (E) does the same with the recipe and the pattern of bread sales. (A) is the near miss: same setup, but the prediction comes true and the hypothesis is called certain. (B) relies on what experts say, (C) shares the town-hall topic but argues by elimination, and (D) ends in a recommendation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Highway vibration is probably not causing the cracks.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: If vibration were the cause, the walls facing the highway would be the most cracked; instead the cracks are spread evenly.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Some blame H for E; if H, we'd expect pattern P; P is absent; so H probably isn't the cause.

breakdown.analysis: This is how you test a suspect: if vibration did it, the damage would be worst on the highway side. It isn't, so vibration probably didn't do it. Find the answer that names a suspected cause, says what pattern that cause would produce, shows the pattern is missing, and rejects the cause with "probably." The match may come in a different order, so check the steps, not the sentence shapes. Expect a decoy where the predicted pattern does show up.

choices.note: Tempting, because it has the same "if H, we'd see P" setup. But here P shows up and the argument concludes the cause is certain. That runs the reasoning the other way and overstates it.
Same highway topic, but the rebuttal rests on what the designers say, not on a missing pattern. An appeal to authority.
Same town hall and cracks, but it's elimination (vibration or settling; not settling; so vibration), and it ends up blaming vibration.
Rejects lowering prices because of competition. No prediction tested against evidence, and it ends in a recommendation.

CORRECT. "Were the recipe to blame" stands in for "if the recipe were the cause," but the steps match: a suspected cause, the pattern it would produce (steepest drop in new-recipe loaves), the pattern is missing (all breads slipped equally), so probably not the cause.

questions.stimulus: Biologist: In the Tarsk Range, pikas whose winter dens lie beneath boulders thickly covered with moss are far more likely to survive the winter than pikas whose dens lie beneath bare boulders. A thick mat of moss traps a layer of air against the rock, so it probably insulates the dens beneath it from extreme cold, and this insulation is what improves those pikas' chances of surviving the winter.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the biologist's argument?
choices: In the Tarsk Range, moss on a boulder hides the entrance of the den beneath it from weasels, which hunt pikas all winter.
Thick moss keeps the boulders beneath it cooler during the summer, which matters to pikas because they overheat easily.
Most of the pikas in the Tarsk Range that die over the winter are young animals in their first year of life.
Moss grows on the range's boulders only where the rock stays damp for much of the short alpine summer.
In the range's lowest valleys, where winters are mild, pikas under mossy boulders survive no more often than those under bare ones.
questions.explanation: The biologist claims a specific mechanism: moss helps because it insulates against extreme cold. (E) supports that mechanism indirectly: where the cold is not extreme, the survival advantage disappears, which is what insulation predicts and what other advantages of mossy boulders would not predict. (C) is the main trap: it sounds like a survival fact, but it matters only if the two groups differ in age. (A) offers a rival advantage of moss (hiding dens from predators), which weakens, (B) is about summer, not winter, and (D) describes where moss grows.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The moss's insulation against extreme cold is what improves the pikas' winter survival.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pikas under mossy boulders survive winter far more often than those under bare boulders; moss traps air and so probably insulates.

breakdown.analysis: The correlation (moss, more survivors) is given. The argument's real claim is the mechanism: insulation against extreme cold. So what else could make mossy dens better? Steadier rock, better hiding, food. A strong strengthener ties the advantage to the cold itself. Think of a winter coat: if it's really the coat keeping you alive, the coat stops mattering on a mild day. Watch for answers that hand moss some other benefit; those point away from insulation, not toward it.

choices.note: Opposite direction. This hands mossy dens a different advantage: protection from weasels. That's a rival explanation for the survival gap, so it weakens the claim that insulation is what helps.
Wrong season. It even uses the insulation idea, but the argument is about surviving winter cold. A summer benefit, if anything, is another possible reason mossy-den pikas do better.

Tempting, because it's about who dies over the winter. But young pikas could die most often everywhere. This matters only if mossy and bare dens hold different shares of young pikas, and we aren't told that.
Interesting fact about where moss grows, but it says nothing about why pikas under moss survive the winter.

CORRECT. Where winters aren't severe, the moss advantage vanishes. That's what insulation against extreme cold predicts. If moss helped some other way, the advantage should show up in the mild valleys too.

questions.stimulus: Park ranger: Of the hikers who had to be rescued on Mount Tavel last year, 75 percent were carrying a GPS device at the time. Clearly, then, carrying a GPS device does little to keep hikers on the mountain from getting into the kind of trouble that requires a rescue.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the park ranger's argument?
choices: Hikers rescued on Mount Tavel who carried a GPS device were, on average, located by rescuers much more quickly than those who did not.
Nearly all of the GPS devices carried by hikers rescued on Mount Tavel last year were still working when the hikers were found.
Hikers without a GPS device made up a larger share of last year's rescues on Mount Tavel than of its hikers.
The batteries in many GPS devices drain quickly in cold weather, which can leave hikers without a working device.
Most of last year's rescues on Mount Tavel took place on the three most heavily used trails on the mountain.
questions.explanation: The ranger treats 75 percent of rescues as a high number without asking what share of all hikers carry GPS. (C) supplies that base rate: hikers without GPS made up 25 percent of the rescued but less than 25 percent of hikers, so they needed rescue out of proportion to their numbers, which suggests GPS does help. (A) is the dominant trap: it shows a real benefit of GPS, but after the trouble starts (being found faster), not in avoiding trouble. (B) and (D) tend to support the ranger, and (E) is irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Carrying a GPS device does little to keep hikers out of rescue-level trouble.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 75 percent of rescued hikers were carrying GPS.

breakdown.analysis: Is 75 percent a lot? That depends on how many hikers carry GPS in the first place. If 90 percent of hikers carry one, then GPS carriers are underrepresented among the rescued, and the 10 percent without GPS account for a quarter of rescues. That's a big risk difference. It's like saying most drivers in accidents were wearing seatbelts, so seatbelts don't help; almost everyone wears one. (C) states the base rate abstractly: hikers without GPS are 25 percent of the rescued but a smaller share of all hikers. Most students pick (A) because it shows GPS helps. It fails because it helps with a different thing: getting found faster. The ranger's claim is about getting into trouble, not about the rescue.

choices.note: Tempting. It's pro-GPS and about rescues. But it shows GPS helps rescuers find people faster, after they're already in trouble. The ranger's claim is that GPS doesn't keep hikers out of trouble. Wrong part of the argument.
Working devices and still rescued? If anything, that fits the ranger: the devices worked and the hikers got into trouble anyway.

CORRECT. Hikers without GPS were 25 percent of the rescued but less than 25 percent of all hikers. So they got into rescue-level trouble out of proportion to their numbers, and GPS carriers less often than their numbers would predict. That suggests GPS does help.
Dead batteries would make GPS less useful, which fits the ranger's conclusion rather than weakening it.
Irrelevant. Where rescues happen says nothing about whether carrying GPS lowers a hiker's chance of needing one.

questions.stimulus: Cheesemaker: Cheeses aged in our dairy's old limestone caves develop a richer flavor than identical cheeses aged in our modern aging rooms, even though the rooms are kept at the same temperature and humidity as the caves. The difference must come from the molds that live naturally in the caves and settle on the cheeses' rinds as they age.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the cheesemaker's argument?
choices: In blind tastings, a panel of experienced judges consistently rated the cave-aged cheeses as having a richer flavor than the room-aged cheeses.
Several of the mold species that live naturally in the caves are also found growing on the rinds of cheeses aged in the modern rooms.
The caves' limestone walls absorb and release moisture, which keeps the humidity in the caves steady without any of the machinery the rooms need.
Cheeses aged in the limestone caves sell for a higher price than cheeses aged in the dairy's modern aging rooms.
Room-aged cheeses set on shelves first left in the caves until cave molds colonized them gained the richer flavor; those on new shelves did not.
questions.explanation: The cheesemaker credits the caves' molds rather than anything else about the caves. (E) moves the molds without the caves: shelves colonized by cave molds in the caves were moved to the modern rooms, and cheeses aged on them there took on the richer flavor while cheeses on new shelves did not, so the flavor follows the molds rather than the rock or the air. (A) is the dominant trap: it confirms that cave cheeses taste richer, which the argument already takes as given. (B) sounds like support for the molds but, if anything, narrows the difference between caves and rooms, (C) explains how the caves keep humidity steady, a point already granted, and (D) is about price.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The caves' natural molds cause the richer flavor.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Cave-aged cheeses taste richer than identical room-aged cheeses; temperature and humidity are the same in both.

breakdown.analysis: The cheesemaker rules out temperature and humidity. But caves differ from rooms in lots of other ways: rock, airflow, who tends the cheese. We need evidence that points to the molds in particular. The neat way is to move the suspected cause and see if the effect moves with it, with a control that lacks it. Shelves colonized by cave molds carry the molds but not the rock or the air. Most students pick (A) because it's strong evidence about flavor. It fails because the flavor difference is the premise. Proving the premise again doesn't explain the cause.

choices.note: Tempting. It's careful, expert evidence. But it only confirms that the cave cheeses taste richer, which the argument already assumes. It says nothing about whether molds are why.

Tempting, because it's about the cave molds. But read it closely: some of the same molds already grow on the room-aged cheeses. That makes the caves and rooms more alike in molds, which if anything weakens the mold explanation.
Explains how the caves keep their humidity, but the cheesemaker already says humidity is the same in caves and rooms. It supports a point that's granted, not the mold explanation.
Price tells us nothing about what causes the flavor.

CORRECT. The shelves picked up the molds in the caves, then went to the modern rooms. Cheeses on those shelves got the richer flavor; identical cheeses on new shelves didn't. The rock and air stayed behind, and the flavor followed the molds.

questions.stimulus: Last year, deliveries made by Pelling Couriers' bicycle couriers took 20 percent less time, on average, than they had the year before, while deliveries made by its van drivers took 5 percent more time, on average. Each group made about the same number of deliveries in both years. Yet the average time taken by all of the company's deliveries was greater last year than it had been the year before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: In each of the two years, Pelling Couriers' van drivers made more deliveries than its bicycle couriers did.
In the year before last, total time spent on van deliveries was more than four times total time spent on bicycle deliveries.
Most of the deliveries that the company's van drivers made last year took longer than such deliveries had taken the year before.
In the year before last, the average van delivery took more than four times as long as the average bicycle delivery.
Pelling Couriers could reduce its average delivery time by assigning a larger share of its deliveries to bicycle couriers.
questions.explanation: Each group made the same number of deliveries both years, so the overall average rose only if total delivery time rose. Bicycle time fell by 20 percent of the bicycle total and van time rose by 5 percent of the van total; the net is an increase only if 5 percent of the van total exceeds 20 percent of the bicycle total, that is, only if the van total was more than four times the bicycle total. (B) states exactly that. (D) is the dominant trap: it has the same 'four times' but compares average times per delivery, which isn't required, since the van group could have made many more deliveries. (A) is the other near miss, but a few very long van deliveries could also do it. (C) confuses an average with 'most,' and (E) adds a plan.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Bicycle deliveries got 20 percent faster on average; 2. van deliveries got 5 percent slower on average; 3. each group made about the same number of deliveries both years; 4. the company's overall average delivery time rose.

breakdown.analysis: How can the average rise when one group improved by 20 percent and the other slipped by only 5? Since the delivery counts didn't change, the overall average rises only if total time rises. Call the earlier year's totals V (van) and B (bicycle). Last year's total is 1.05V + 0.80B. For that to beat V + B, you need 0.05V > 0.20B, so V > 4B. Example: if bikes logged 100 hours, vans logged more than 400. Most students who do the math pick (D) because it has the magic "four times." It fails because it's about the average delivery, not the total. Totals are average × count, and the counts can differ: 100 van trips averaging 1 hour (100 hours) and 10 bike trips averaging 2 hours (20 hours) fit the facts, yet the average van trip is shorter.

choices.note: Tempting, because more van trips is one way to get a big van total. But it's not the only way. Ten van trips averaging 50 hours each outweigh 100 bike trips averaging 1 hour. Not required.
CORRECT. With the counts fixed, the overall average rises only if 5 percent of the van total beats 20 percent of the bike total. That means the van total was more than four times the bike total.
An average can rise because a few deliveries got much slower while most got a bit faster. "Average" isn't "most."

Tempting. Same "four times," and it's about the right year. But it compares per-delivery averages, not totals. If vans made far more trips than bikes, the van total can be four times the bike total even when the average van trip is shorter. Rate vs. total.
A plan the facts don't support. We don't know that bikes could handle van deliveries, or how fast they would be.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Critics claim that the congestion charge Ostley imposed on drivers entering its downtown has hurt downtown retailers, whose sales fell 8 percent in the year after the charge took effect. Admittedly, fewer shoppers now drive downtown. But retail sales fell by a similar percentage throughout the region, including at suburban malls the charge does not affect. So the charge is not what hurt downtown retailers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the economist's argument?
choices: For years before the charge, downtown retail sales had kept rising even in years when sales elsewhere in the region fell.
Since the charge took effect, the number of cars entering downtown Ostley during business hours has fallen by about a third.
Revenue from the congestion charge has been used to expand bus service between Ostley's suburbs and its downtown shopping district.
Retailers at the region's suburban malls attribute most of their recent drop in sales to the growth of online shopping.
Most suburban malls in the region provide free parking, whereas parking in downtown Ostley has long been expensive.
questions.explanation: The economist uses the region as a comparison group: since sales fell just as much where there is no charge, the charge can't be the cause. (A) undermines that comparison: downtown sales used to keep rising even when regional sales fell, so falling in step with the region is a break from the usual pattern, and a downtown-specific cause such as the charge becomes likely. (B) is the dominant trap: it shows fewer drivers, but the economist already concedes that, and fewer drivers alone doesn't show lost sales. (D) offers a region-wide cause, which fits the economist's view, (C) tends to help the economist, and (E) describes a long-standing difference.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The congestion charge is not what hurt downtown retailers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Downtown sales fell 8 percent, but sales fell by a similar percentage across the region, including where there is no charge (concession: fewer shoppers drive downtown).

breakdown.analysis: The whole rebuttal rests on one comparison: downtown fell about as much as everywhere else, so nothing special to downtown was at work. But is the region the right baseline? If downtown normally holds up when the region slumps, then "falling the same" is actually doing much worse than expected. It's like a straight-A student who has always aced tests the rest of the class struggled with getting a C along with everyone else this time: matching the class is a slump for her. Most students pick (B) because it shows the charge kept cars out. It fails because the economist already admits fewer shoppers drive downtown; the question is whether that cost retailers sales, and (B) says nothing about sales.

choices.note: CORRECT. Downtown used to keep growing even when the region shrank. This time it fell along with the region. That's a break from its usual pattern, and it points to something downtown-specific, like the charge. The regional comparison no longer clears the charge.

Tempting. It makes the charge's effect vivid. But the economist already concedes that fewer shoppers drive downtown. Fewer cars doesn't show fewer sales: those shoppers may come by bus. It supports a point the argument already granted.
If anything, this helps the economist: better buses could bring back shoppers who stopped driving, softening any harm from the charge.

Tempting, because it seems to give the suburbs a different cause. But online shopping hits downtown stores too, so it's a region-wide cause that, if anything, backs the economist's point that something other than the charge did the damage.
This was true before the charge and stays true. It doesn't explain why the charge would or wouldn't change sales, and it doesn't touch the comparison.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologist: Since 2015, the forestry service has felled most of the old trees in Fenwold Wood, and over the same period the wood's population of marsh tits, which nest only in cavities in old trees, has fallen by half. Admittedly, the past several winters have been unusually harsh, and harsh winters can kill many small birds. Still, the loss of nesting sites, not the weather, is the main cause of the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ornithologist's argument?
choices: Marsh tits in Fenwold Wood have never been observed nesting anywhere other than in cavities in the wood's old trees.
Since 2015, populations of other cavity-nesting birds in Fenwold Wood, such as nuthatches, have also fallen by about half.
At least some of the old trees that were felled in Fenwold Wood contained cavities that marsh tits could have used for nesting.
Banding records show that the proportion of Fenwold Wood's marsh tits surviving each winter has not declined since 2015.
The forestry service has announced that it will stop felling old trees in Fenwold Wood once its current contracts expire.
questions.explanation: The ornithologist concedes a rival cause (harsh winters) and must show that nest-site loss, not weather, drove the decline. (D) does that indirectly: if the share of birds surviving each winter hasn't changed, the harsh winters aren't killing more of them, so the decline must come from elsewhere, such as fewer nesting sites. (B) is the dominant trap: it looks like a cavity-nester pattern, but other small birds are just as exposed to harsh winters, so a parallel decline doesn't separate the two causes. (A) and (C) confirm what the premises already establish, and (E) is about the future.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The loss of nesting sites, not the harsh winters, is the main cause of the marsh tit decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most old trees were felled and marsh tits nest only in old-tree cavities; the population fell by half (concession: recent winters were harsh, and harsh winters kill small birds).

breakdown.analysis: Two suspects, one decline. The ornithologist admits the weather could have done it. So what does the argument need? Something that clears the weather. Pointing at the felled trees again won't do it; we already know the trees are gone. We need evidence that separates the two causes. If harsh winters were killing the birds, the share of birds that live through each winter should have dropped. If it didn't, the weather is off the hook. Most students pick (B) because nuthatches nest in cavities too, so it looks like the nest-site story. It fails because nuthatches are small birds that harsh winters also kill; the winters predict the same parallel decline.

choices.note: Restates the premise that marsh tits nest only in old-tree cavities. Confirming it doesn't help decide between nest sites and weather.
Tempting. Another cavity nester fell by half too. But nuthatches are small birds that harsh winters also kill. Both causes predict this pattern, so it doesn't favor nest-site loss.
Already implied: marsh tits nest only in old-tree cavities and most old trees were felled. Yes, cavities were lost. That doesn't show the loss, rather than the weather, caused the decline.
CORRECT. If harsh winters were killing more birds, winter survival would have dropped. It didn't. That clears the weather and leaves the lost nesting sites as the likely cause.
About the future. What the forestry service will do says nothing about what caused the decline so far.

questions.stimulus: Transit planner: The 8:00 a.m. express from Ashlow to the city is so crowded that many riders must stand for the whole trip, and most of them take it only because it is currently the sole morning express. So adding a second express that leaves Ashlow at 7:40 a.m. will substantially relieve crowding on the 8:00 train, since many of its riders will switch to the earlier one.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the transit planner's argument?
choices: Riders on the 8:00 a.m. express frequently complain to the transit authority that the train is too crowded for them to find a seat.
Some riders take the 8:00 a.m. express because it is the only train on the line with a quiet car in which phone calls are forbidden.
Within a few months of its introduction, the new 7:40 a.m. express is expected to be nearly as crowded as the 8:00 train is now.
Many Ashlow commuters who now drive say they would take the train if they could count on a seat on the 8:00 a.m. express.
Running the new 7:40 a.m. express will require the transit authority to hire two additional train crews at considerable expense.
questions.explanation: The planner reasons that if many riders move to the 7:40, the 8:00 will be less crowded. (D) shows why that need not happen: many drivers are staying off the train only because the 8:00 is too crowded, so seats freed by riders who switch will be filled by new riders, and the crowding will persist. (C) is the dominant trap: a crowded 7:40 sounds like a failure, but it means many riders did switch, which is what the plan predicts. (B) is the other near miss, but 'some' riders is compatible with 'most' taking the 8:00 only because it is the sole express. (A) restates the crowding, and (E) is about cost.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Adding a 7:40 express will substantially relieve crowding on the 8:00 train.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The 8:00 is packed; most riders take it only because it's the sole express; many will switch to the 7:40.

breakdown.analysis: The planner thinks about who will leave the 8:00. But crowding depends on who gets on, too. What if there are people waiting for room to open up? Then every seat that frees up gets taken. It's like widening a jammed highway: new lanes draw new drivers, and traffic is as bad as before. We need an answer that shows the space freed on the 8:00 won't stay free. Most students pick (C) because a packed new train sounds like the plan failing. It fails because a crowded 7:40 means lots of people switched, which is exactly what the planner is counting on.

choices.note: Restates the crowding the planner already describes. Confirming a premise doesn't weaken anything.

Tempting. It looks like a reason riders won't leave the 8:00. But it's only "some" riders, and the planner says "most" take it only because it's the sole express. Those claims fit together, so the plan's logic survives.

Tempting, because it sounds like the new train will be a mess. But why would the 7:40 be crowded? Because many riders took it. That's the switch the plan needs. The question is about crowding on the 8:00.
CORRECT. Drivers are waiting for a seat on the 8:00. As riders move to the 7:40, these drivers fill the freed seats, so the 8:00 stays about as crowded as before.
Wrong dimension. Expense might make the plan unwise, but it doesn't show the plan won't relieve crowding.

passages.title: Piranesi’s Imaginary Prisons
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Giovanni Battista Piranesi, who trained in Venice as an architect before settling in Rome in the 1740s, saw only one significant building of his own design completed: the remodeled church of Santa Maria del Priorato on the Aventine Hill. His reputation rests instead on etchings. His many views of Roman ruins and monuments, sold in great numbers to visitors, did as much as any images of the century to fix how Europeans pictured the ancient city. Yet the work that has most engaged later artists is a set of plates depicting no actual place: the Carceri d’invenzione, or Imaginary Prisons.

The series was first issued around 1750 as fourteen plates showing vast vaulted interiors, drawn with a quick, open line that leaves much of the copper bare. The scenes read as capricci, architectural fantasies of a kind familiar in eighteenth-century Italy, and their oddities are those of the rapid sketch: spaces that trail off into loosely indicated vaults. In the edition of 1761, about a decade later, Piranesi added two new plates and reworked the original fourteen so heavily that some are scarcely recognizable. Shadows are deepened with dense cross-hatching; new staircases, bridges, and galleries are threaded through the spaces; ropes and chains hang from beams that had been bare.

It is tempting to treat these additions as a change of mood, the airy fantasy of the first state turned into the oppressive dungeon of the second, and the darkening is real. But the more consequential change concerns how the space is constructed. In several of the reworked plates, a staircase that rises in the foreground arrives at a landing that, judging by the arches around it, must lie behind a wall seen earlier, and a gallery viewed from below at one edge of a plate seems to be viewed from above at the other. These effects are produced by the standard devices of architectural drawing—converging lines, human figures diminished to establish scale, the receding sequence of arches—on which an architect relies to make a projected building legible. Piranesi employs them with full competence, and the result is a space that each local passage makes convincing and that cannot be assembled into a whole. The viewer’s disorientation therefore comes not from vagueness, as in a hastily sketched fantasy, but from an excess of individually persuasive detail.

This helps explain the curious history of the plates’ reception. Thomas De Quincey, recalling in 1821 a description given him by Coleridge, called them records of the artist’s own fevered dreams, and for many viewers they have remained images of a troubled mind. The reading is understandable, but it inverts their source: the Carceri are disturbing because their maker understood the conventions of rational space well enough to set them against one another.

passages.title: Rising and falling IQ scores
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Because IQ tests are periodically restandardized so that the average score of a representative sample is set at 100, a score expresses only a person’s standing relative to contemporaries. For decades this convention concealed a remarkable fact. Comparing how successive cohorts had performed on the same tests, the political scientist James Flynn found in the 1980s that raw performance had risen steadily through the twentieth century in every industrialized country he examined: by roughly three IQ points per decade in the United States, and considerably faster elsewhere. Dutch conscripts tested in 1982 outscored those tested in 1952 by some twenty points on a test of abstract reasoning.

Gains so large over so short a period cannot be genetic in origin, and explanations have therefore centered on the environment. Some researchers have credited improved nutrition, which over the same decades added several centimeters to average adult height. Others have pointed to the expansion of schooling, or to familiarity with the tests. Each of these factors probably contributed something, but the pattern of the gains fits some explanations better than others. The increases were largest on tests such as Raven’s Progressive Matrices, which ask the test-taker to infer the rule governing a series of abstract figures, and smallest on subtests of vocabulary, arithmetic, and general information—precisely the material that schools most directly teach. A cause that worked chiefly through classroom instruction would be expected to produce something like the opposite profile. Flynn himself proposed that modern life had trained people to sort objects into abstract categories and to reason seriously about hypothetical situations, habits that matter little on a vocabulary test but a great deal on the Matrices.

A later development has complicated every account. Among people born after the mid-1970s, the gains slowed and then reversed in Norway, Denmark, and a few other countries. One explanation attributed the decline to changes in the population’s composition, such as differences in fertility between groups with higher and lower scores. Norway, however, tests most of its young men at conscription, and a 2018 analysis compared brothers born in different years. Younger brothers tended to score lower than their older brothers had, and since brothers share their parents, a shift in which families were having children could not explain the decline.

The finding does not identify what has changed. It does show that whatever drives these scores acts within families and within a few years, the timescale of environmental influences rather than of shifts in a population’s makeup, and so lends indirect support to the environmental accounts of the rise. But it also sets those accounts a harder test: a factor credited with raising scores for most of a century must now be shown to have stalled or reversed within a generation, and only in certain countries.

passages.title: The rule of Rylands v. Fletcher
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
In the 1860s some mill owners in northern England had contractors build a reservoir on their land. The contractors found disused mine shafts beneath the site but failed to seal them, and when the reservoir filled, water burst through and flooded a neighbor’s coal mine. The owners had not been careless, yet they were held liable. The rule, stated by Justice Blackburn in 1866 and affirmed by the House of Lords in Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), was that one who brings onto land something likely to do harm if it escapes keeps it at his peril and answers for the damage its escape causes, however careful he was. The Lords added a qualification: the rule applied only to a non-natural use of the land.

In England the rule has been narrowed at nearly every opportunity. Courts read “non-natural” to exclude most ordinary activities, and in 1947 the Lords held that a munitions inspector injured by an explosion inside a factory could not invoke the rule, since nothing had escaped from the defendant’s premises. In 1994 the Lords required that the type of damage be foreseeable, and in 2003, declining an invitation to abolish the rule altogether, they confined it to uses that are extraordinary and unusual for their time and place, holding that a water pipe serving a block of flats did not qualify.

Elsewhere the rule fared differently. The High Court of Australia concluded in 1994 that the rule had been so hedged about that it no longer did independent work, and absorbed it into the law of negligence. Several nineteenth-century American courts rejected it outright, yet American law eventually moved the other way: the Restatement of Torts, an influential summary of the law, came to state a rule of strict liability for abnormally dangerous activities, which courts have applied to blasting, the storage of explosives, and similar operations without requiring that anything escape from the defendant’s land.

The legal historian Anne Calloway offers an explanation for this divergence that seems to me correct. The judges in Rylands, she observes, framed the rule in the vocabulary of property: its elements are the defendant’s land, the thing accumulated there, and its escape onto a neighbor’s land. A rule so framed is a rule about relations between neighboring landholders, and courts that retained that framing tended—reasonably enough, in her view—to treat it as a variety of nuisance, the tort concerned with interference between neighbors, and to trim whatever did not fit. It was this framing, not hostility to strict liability as such, that set the limits of the English rule. American law, by attaching the rule to the activity rather than to land, asked what makes an undertaking dangerous rather than where the danger was kept, and so left the rule room to grow.

passages.title: Peto’s paradox
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Cancer begins when a cell accumulates mutations that free it from the controls on cell division, and since mutations arise largely as errors in copying DNA, every division is a small opportunity for the disease. It follows that an animal with more cells, or one that lives longer and so undergoes more divisions, should face a greater risk of cancer, and within a species the expectation is roughly borne out: taller people, for example, have a modestly higher incidence of several cancers. Across species, however, it fails. An elephant has roughly a hundred times as many cells as a human but is no more likely to die of cancer, while short-lived mice frequently develop it. The epidemiologist Richard Peto noted this discrepancy in the 1970s; it is now known as Peto’s paradox.

The paradox dissolves once one asks how large, long-lived animals could have evolved at all. A lineage that grew larger without improving its defenses against cancer would have suffered more cancer during the reproductive years, and selection would have opposed the increase. Large bodies and long lives should therefore have evolved only alongside improved suppression of tumors, so that the risk per cell falls as the number of cells rises.

Evidence for this view has emerged from comparative genomics. Most mammals carry a single copy of TP53, a gene whose product halts the division of a cell with damaged DNA and, if the damage is severe, causes the cell to die. Elephants carry some twenty copies, and elephant cells exposed to radiation that damages DNA are markedly more likely than human cells to die rather than attempt repair. Estimates from zoo populations put the elephant’s lifetime cancer mortality below five percent, against roughly eleven to twenty-five percent in humans. The bowhead whale, which can live for two centuries, shows distinctive changes in genes involved in DNA repair, and the naked mole rat, a rodent roughly the size of a mouse that can live for more than thirty years, resists cancer by yet another route: its tissues produce an unusually large form of hyaluronan, which appears to stop crowded cells from dividing.

That these defenses differ is itself telling. A rival explanation holds that large animals escape cancer because their cells, which burn energy more slowly, suffer less of the chemical damage that metabolism inflicts on DNA. If that were the main reason, the protection of large animals would follow from a single physiological cause shared by all of them and would scale smoothly with size. The evolutionary account predicts instead what the evidence shows: lineages that became large or long-lived independently arrived at protection by independent means, each improvising from the genes available to it. The metabolic factor may well contribute, but it cannot be the whole story.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Piranesi’s 1761 reworking of the Carceri turned a set of airy architectural fantasies into gloomy images of confinement, and that change of mood accounts for the series’ lasting hold on viewers.

The revised Carceri unsettle viewers chiefly because Piranesi, applying with full skill the methods by which architects make spaces legible, produced interiors that cannot be reconciled into a coherent whole.
Although Piranesi completed only one building, his etchings of Rome and of imaginary prisons show that he was a more accomplished architect than his few commissions would suggest.
The view of the Carceri as records of Piranesi’s dreams has obscured the fact that the plates belong to the familiar eighteenth-century genre of the architectural capriccio.
In reworking the Carceri, Piranesi replaced the vague, sketchy spaces of the first state with precisely rendered interiors in which every detail is architecturally consistent.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph carries the author's claim: the more consequential change in 1761 was how the space is built, using the ordinary devices of architectural drawing to make locally convincing spaces that 'cannot be assembled into a whole,' and the last paragraph applies that claim to the plates' reception. B says this in other words. A is the tempting trap: the author grants that 'the darkening is real' but calls the spatial change the more consequential one.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's central claim about what makes the reworked Carceri significant.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph (the 'more consequential change') and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Is the passage about the darker mood? The author mentions it only to set it aside: 'the darkening is real. But the more consequential change concerns how the space is constructed.' The rest builds on that: the standard drafting devices, used competently, yield spaces that are convincing piece by piece but impossible as a whole. We need an answer with both halves: skilled use of architectural conventions, and incoherence as the result.

choices.note: Tempting, since the darkening is real and the author says so. But the author calls the spatial change 'more consequential,' so mood is not what the passage says explains the plates' effect.

CORRECT. 'The methods by which architects make spaces legible' = the standard devices of architectural drawing; 'cannot be reconciled into a coherent whole' = 'cannot be assembled into a whole.' This is the author's thesis, which the last paragraph then applies to the reception.
The one building is mentioned only to say his fame rests elsewhere. The passage never argues that he was an underrated architect.

The capriccio label fits the first state ('read as capricci'), not the reworked plates the author is discussing. The author also doesn't say the dream reading hid their genre; it says the reading 'inverts their source.'
Half right and then reversed. Each part is convincing, but the whole is not consistent. 'Every detail is architecturally consistent' misses the contradictions that the passage describes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in preparing the 1761 edition of the Carceri, Piranesi
choices: reduced the number of plates so as to concentrate on the most elaborate interiors
replaced the vaulted interiors of the first state with views of actual Roman prisons
removed most of the human figures that had established scale in the original plates
both enlarged the series and substantially altered the plates it already contained
left the original fourteen plates unchanged and confined his additions to two new plates
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that in 1761 Piranesi 'added two new plates and reworked the original fourteen so heavily that some are scarcely recognizable.' D puts both facts into other words. E is the near-miss: it keeps the two new plates but contradicts the heavy reworking.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says Piranesi did for the 1761 edition.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The middle of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Two facts: he added two plates, and he reworked the original fourteen heavily. The right answer needs both.

choices.note: Reversed. He added plates, going from fourteen to sixteen.
The first paragraph says the Carceri depict 'no actual place,' and the vaulted interiors remain.
Nothing says he removed figures. Diminished human figures show up in the third paragraph as one of the devices he used.
CORRECT. 'Enlarged the series' = added two new plates; 'substantially altered' = reworked so heavily that some are scarcely recognizable.
Tempting, because the two new plates are right. But the original fourteen were reworked heavily, not left alone.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that the plates of the Carceri as first issued differed from the reworked plates in that the earlier plates
choices: depicted the same spatial arrangements as the reworked plates but with lighter shading
owed whatever strangeness they had more to loose execution than to contradictory spaces
were based on prisons that Piranesi had studied during his architectural training in Venice
made no use of the standard devices by which architectural drawings convey depth and scale
were conceived as preliminary studies for buildings that Piranesi hoped someday to construct
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the first-state plates read as capricci and that 'their oddities are those of the rapid sketch: spaces that trail off into loosely indicated vaults.' The third paragraph places the contradictory spaces in 'several of the reworked plates' and contrasts their effect with 'vagueness, as in a hastily sketched fantasy.' So the earlier plates' strangeness came from loose execution, not contradictory construction, which is B. A is the trap: the new staircases, bridges, and galleries changed the spaces, not only the shading.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer how the first-state plates differed from the 1761 versions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second sentence of the second paragraph (the first state's 'oddities') and the third paragraph (where the impossible spaces appear).

breakdown.analysis: Two pieces. The second paragraph tells you what was odd about the first state: 'the oddities ... of the rapid sketch,' spaces that 'trail off' into 'loosely indicated vaults.' The third paragraph tells you where the contradictory spaces show up: 'in several of the reworked plates,' a change the author calls 'more consequential.' Put together: first-state strangeness = sketchiness; reworked-state strangeness = contradictory construction. We need an answer that says that.

choices.note: Tempting if you remember only the darker shading. But new staircases, bridges, and galleries were 'threaded through the spaces,' so the spatial arrangements changed.

CORRECT. 'Loose execution' = 'the rapid sketch,' spaces that 'trail off' into 'loosely indicated vaults.' The contradictory spaces belong to the reworked plates. The hedge ('whatever strangeness they had') keeps it within what the passage says.
The passage says the Carceri depict 'no actual place.' Nothing ties them to prisons he studied.
Too strong. The passage never says the first state lacked perspective or scale figures; it says only that the later plates use such devices to contradictory effect.
Plausible for an architect, but the passage calls them capricci, or architectural fantasies, and says nothing about plans to build.

questions.stem: The author mentions Piranesi’s remodeling of the church of Santa Maria del Priorato (first paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: identify the kind of vaulted interior that the Carceri would later depict
show that Piranesi’s architectural ideas were realized in buildings as well as in prints
explain why Piranesi abandoned architecture in favor of etching views of Rome
suggest that the staircases added to the Carceri in 1761 were modeled on an actual building
establish that Piranesi’s renown rests on something other than the buildings he designed
questions.explanation: The church is offered as the only significant building of his own design completed, and the next sentence reads: 'His reputation rests instead on etchings.' The mention sets up that contrast, which is E. B reverses the point: the detail stresses how little he built.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author brings up the one church Piranesi remodeled.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first two sentences of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence that follows: 'His reputation rests instead on etchings.' The church is there to show how slight his built work was, so that his fame clearly comes from somewhere else.

choices.note: The church and the Carceri are never connected, and the Carceri depict 'no actual place.'
Tempting, because it is a real building. But the author's point is that it was the only one, a sign of how little he built, not proof that his ideas made it into stone.
The passage gives no reason why he turned to etching. It says only where his reputation lies.
Nothing links the 1761 staircases to any real building.
CORRECT. 'Only one significant building ... His reputation rests instead on etchings.' The church marks the limit of his architectural output, so his renown must come from elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the material presented in the passage?
choices: A body of work is introduced, a revision to part of it is described, that revision’s chief effect is identified, and an influential reading of the work is reassessed accordingly.
An artist’s career is surveyed, two interpretations of his best-known work are contrasted, and both are shown to be inconsistent with the historical record.
A series of works is described, a common view of its revision is qualified, and an influential early reading of the works is endorsed as having grasped what the revision accomplished.
An artist’s training is described, its influence on his early work is traced, and his later work is shown to have abandoned that training in favor of dreamlike fantasy.
A change in an artist’s work is described, two possible causes of that change are considered, and the more plausible cause is endorsed on the basis of the work’s reception.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 introduces Piranesi's etchings and the Carceri; paragraph 2 describes the 1761 reworking; paragraph 3 identifies the reworking's most consequential effect (the contradictory space); paragraph 4 uses that to reassess De Quincey's dream reading. A follows that sequence. C is the closest trap: its first two parts fit, but the author does not endorse the dream reading. The author says it 'inverts their source.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the sequence of the passage's four paragraphs.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The opening sentence of each paragraph, plus the verdict on De Quincey's reading in the last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: (1) the artist and the Carceri; (2) the 1761 revision; (3) what that revision chiefly did, which is impossible space built from standard devices; (4) the dream reading reconsidered in that light. Organization answers die on one wrong element, so check each clause.

choices.note: CORRECT. Each clause matches a paragraph in order, and 'reassessed accordingly' fits the last paragraph's verdict that the dream reading 'inverts' the plates' source.
The passage isn't a career survey, and it never claims either reading conflicts with the historical record. The author grants that the dream reading is 'understandable.'

Tempting: it starts right, and 'qualified' fits how the author treats the mood reading ('the darkening is real,' but the spatial change matters more). The last part fails. The author doesn't endorse De Quincey's reading as grasping the revision; it says the reading 'inverts their source.' Reassessed, yes; endorsed, no.
Reversed. The later work uses his architectural training to the full; the author rejects the idea that it is dream fantasy.
The passage offers no competing causes of the revision. It analyzes what the revision did, not why Piranesi made it.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The darkening of the plates in 1761 has had little effect on the way viewers have responded to the Carceri.
Piranesi reworked the Carceri in order to demonstrate that the conventions of architectural drawing are inherently unreliable.
The Carceri would have attracted greater admiration had Piranesi left the plates as he first issued them.
De Quincey’s reading of the plates, though mistaken about their source, answers to something genuinely unsettling in them.
Piranesi’s views of Rome, like the Carceri, depict spaces whose individual parts cannot be assembled into a coherent whole.
questions.explanation: In the last paragraph the author calls the dream reading 'understandable' but says it 'inverts their source,' because the Carceri 'are disturbing' for a different reason. So the author grants the effect and rejects the explanation, which is D. B is the strongest trap: the passage describes what the plates do, not what Piranesi intended, and never calls the conventions unreliable in general.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim the author's stated views support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last paragraph, with the third paragraph's account of how the effect is produced.

breakdown.analysis: The author's position on the dream reading has two parts: it is right that the plates disturb ('understandable'; 'the Carceri are disturbing'), and wrong about why ('inverts their source'). Look for an answer that keeps both parts. Be careful with answers that assign Piranesi a motive.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says 'the darkening is real' and only calls the spatial change more consequential. That doesn't mean the darkening had little effect on viewers.

Tempting, since the plates set the conventions against one another. But the passage describes an effect, not Piranesi's purpose, and it never says the conventions are unreliable in general. In ordinary use they make a building 'legible.'
The passage makes no such comparison. The reworked plates are the ones it treats as significant.
CORRECT. 'Understandable' plus 'the Carceri are disturbing' means the reading answers to a real quality; 'inverts their source' means it gets the cause wrong.
The views of Rome are mentioned only as images that shaped how Europeans pictured the city. Nothing suggests they contain impossible spaces.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The twentieth-century rise in IQ scores is best explained by the expansion of schooling, an explanation that the more recent decline in several countries has confirmed.
The recent decline in Norwegian IQ scores shows that changes in a population’s composition, rather than in its environment, drive changes in average test performance.
Although the cause of the twentieth-century gains in IQ scores remains undetermined, the evidence, including evidence about their later reversal, has narrowed the plausible explanations.
Because IQ tests are periodically restandardized, the gains Flynn reported reflect changes in scoring conventions rather than genuine changes in how people performed on the tests.
Flynn’s view that modern life cultivated habits of abstract reasoning accounts both for the twentieth-century gains and for their recent reversal in Norway and Denmark.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the gains, uses their pattern to favor some environmental explanations over others (second paragraph), and then uses the Norwegian brothers study to rule out a compositional account of the decline while noting that it 'does not identify what has changed' and sets the environmental accounts 'a harder test' (fourth paragraph). C captures both the open question and the narrowing. E is tempting because the author treats Flynn's proposal sympathetically, but the passage never says it explains the reversal.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the passage's overall conclusion about the gains and what explains them.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The end of the second paragraph and the whole fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What does the author actually settle? Not the cause: 'The finding does not identify what has changed,' and the last sentence sets every environmental account 'a harder test.' But the evidence does do work: the subtest pattern tells against a schooling-driven cause, and the within-family decline tells against compositional explanations. We need an answer that is unsettled but narrowed.

choices.note: The passage says schooling fits the pattern badly ('something like the opposite profile'), and the decline is never said to confirm it.
Reversed. The brothers study is what rules out the compositional explanation.

CORRECT. 'Still undetermined' = 'does not identify what has changed' plus the 'harder test' still to be passed; 'narrowed the range' = the subtest pattern and the within-family finding each eliminate or weaken candidates.
The passage says restandardization concealed the gains. Flynn found them by comparing raw performance on the same tests, so they are genuine.

Tempting, because Flynn's proposal fits the subtest pattern and the author seems sympathetic. But nothing connects his proposal to the reversal, and the last sentence poses the reversal as a test that any account of the rise has yet to pass.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the twentieth-century gains in performance on IQ tests
choices: were less pronounced on measures of school-taught knowledge than on measures of abstract inference
proceeded at about the same pace in each of the industrialized countries that Flynn examined
came to light when the tests were restandardized so that the average score was set at 100
were offset in part by declines in scores on subtests of vocabulary and arithmetic
were largest among people born after the mid-1970s in Norway and Denmark
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the increases were largest on Matrices-type tests of inferring abstract rules and smallest on vocabulary, arithmetic, and general information, 'precisely the material that schools most directly teach.' A says this in other words. C reverses the role of restandardization, which hid the gains.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the pattern of the gains.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The middle of the second paragraph, and the first paragraph for the distractors.

breakdown.analysis: Locate the sentence about where the gains were largest and smallest. Then watch for choices that reuse the passage's terms (restandardized, vocabulary, mid-1970s) in the wrong relation.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'School-taught knowledge' = vocabulary, arithmetic, general information; 'abstract inference' = inferring the rule behind abstract figures. Smallest gains on the first, largest on the second.
Contradicted: about three points per decade in the U.S., 'considerably faster elsewhere.'
Reversed. Restandardization 'concealed' the gains, and Flynn found them by comparing raw scores across cohorts.
The gains were smallest on those subtests, not negative. 'Smallest' isn't 'declined.'
Those cohorts are where the gains slowed and reversed.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that if the decline in Norwegian scores described in the third paragraph had resulted chiefly from changes in which families were having children, then
choices: younger brothers would have scored lower than their older brothers by an even wider margin than the analysis found
the decline would have shown up in Norway’s conscription records only after it had appeared in Denmark’s
scores on vocabulary subtests would have fallen faster than scores on tests like the Matrices
the gains of the earlier twentieth century would also have to be attributed to genetic causes
a younger brother would not generally have scored lower than his older brother
questions.explanation: The third paragraph reasons that since brothers share parents, a shift in which families had children cannot produce a gap between older and younger brothers. So if composition had been the cause, the within-family decline would not have appeared, which is E. A gets the logic backwards: a compositional cause predicts no within-family gap at all, not a bigger one.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the logic of the brothers study to the compositional hypothesis.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Why did comparing brothers rule out composition? Because composition changes which families exist, not what happens inside a family. Brothers share parents, so a compositional cause would leave younger and older brothers scoring about the same. The observed within-family drop is what killed it. We want the prediction that the compositional story makes.

choices.note: Backwards. A compositional cause predicts no within-family gap, not a wider one.
Nothing in the passage bears on the timing across countries.
The subtest pattern is discussed only for the earlier gains, and composition has no stated link to it.
Tempting, because composition and genetics sound related. But the passage says the earlier gains were too fast to be genetic, and the hypothesis here concerns only the decline.
CORRECT. Composition works across families. Brothers share parents, so it would leave scores within a family flat. The observed drop from older to younger brothers is what rules it out.

questions.stem: The author mentions the increase in average adult height (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that improved nutrition, unlike schooling, raised scores chiefly on tests of abstract reasoning
suggest that the gains in IQ scores may have had a partly genetic origin after all
support the claim that the gains were too large and too rapid to be genetic in origin
indicate that the gains Flynn found occurred only in countries where diets improved
lend plausibility to a proposed cause by noting a measurable effect it had in the same period
questions.explanation: The height gain is attached to 'improved nutrition, which over the same decades added several centimeters to average adult height.' It shows that the factor some researchers credit was having real, measurable effects in that period, which makes it a plausible candidate. That is E. C is tempting because the paragraph opens by saying the gains cannot be genetic, but the height detail serves the nutrition hypothesis, not that claim.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why height is brought up.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Height appears in a clause describing nutrition: researchers credit nutrition, which 'added several centimeters' to height. The detail is evidence that nutrition changed bodies in those decades, so it's credible that it changed test performance too. It's support for a candidate cause, not a verdict.

choices.note: Mixes up two parts of the paragraph. The abstract-reasoning pattern is discussed separately and is never tied to nutrition.
Opposite. The paragraph opens by saying the gains 'cannot be genetic.'
Tempting: same paragraph, and height also changed for non-genetic reasons. But the height detail is attached to the nutrition explanation, not offered as evidence against a genetic origin.
Too strong and unsupported. Nothing restricts the gains to countries with dietary change.
CORRECT. The height gain shows nutrition had measurable effects in the same decades, which is what makes it a credible cause of the score gains.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship of the fourth paragraph to the third paragraph?
choices: The fourth paragraph offers an explanation of the decline described in the third paragraph that the analysis described there did not consider.
The fourth paragraph concedes that the finding reported in the third paragraph fails to rule out the compositional explanation it was meant to test.
The fourth paragraph argues that the decline described in the third paragraph undermines Flynn’s account of the earlier gains.
The fourth paragraph limits what a finding reported in the third can establish, then draws from it a lesson for an earlier question.
The fourth paragraph extends the finding reported in the third paragraph to every country in which scores have declined.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph begins 'The finding does not identify what has changed' (a limit), then says it shows the cause works on an environmental timescale and so 'lends indirect support to the environmental accounts of the rise,' the question the second paragraph raised. D describes both moves. B is the trap: the limit concerns what the cause is, but the finding does rule out composition.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what the last paragraph does with the brothers finding.

setup.label: Where to look
