questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the glow is governed by an internal clock and ‘continues to rise and fall on a daily cycle under constant laboratory conditions,’ so its rhythm does not need day and night outside: C. B is a near-miss: the glow ‘intensifies at night,’ which does not mean it is absent by day. A describes exactly the evidence the fourth paragraph says is still needed, and D and E report findings the passage never mentions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a result of the 2015 study.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The study found two things: 1. the glow follows an internal clock, brighter at night and still cycling under constant conditions; 2. lit replicas caught more insects at night than unlit ones. ‘Constant laboratory conditions’ means no outside day-night change, so the cycle comes from inside the mushroom. Watch two traps: an answer that turns ‘intensifies at night’ into ‘only at night,’ and one that describes what the author says would still have to be shown.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the payoff of the insect experiment. But paragraph 4 says showing this ‘would require evidence’ the study didn’t provide. What’s still needed, not what was found.
Close, but too strong. The glow ‘intensifies at night’ and rises and falls; the passage never says it stops by day. Brighter is not only.

CORRECT. The glow kept rising and falling daily ‘under constant laboratory conditions,’ that is, with no outside day-night change to follow. So the variation didn’t depend on one: it’s run by an ‘internal circadian clock.’
The study compared lit and unlit replicas at night. No daytime comparison is reported.
The study concerned the mushroom’s glow. Nothing is said about its mycelium.

questions.stem: The author’s comparison involving “the heat of a running engine” (third sentence of the second paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: clarify the sense in which, on one view, the light would serve no function for the fungus
suggest that the reaction producing the light wastes energy the fungus could put to other uses
indicate that the light-producing reaction gives off heat in addition to giving off light
concede that the by-product view cannot explain why the light follows a daily rhythm
illustrate how the reaction that produces the light disposes of reactive forms of oxygen
questions.explanation: The comparison explains what ‘incidental’ means on the by-product view: the light is a side effect of a reaction that exists for another purpose, just as heat is a side effect of an engine: A. E is the trap: it reuses the paragraph’s wording about reactive oxygen, but the engine comparison is about the light, not about how the reaction neutralizes oxygen. B and C read the analogy too literally, and D draws on the fourth paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the engine comparison does in the paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: An engine exists to move a car; the heat is a side effect. On the by-product view, the reaction exists to neutralize damaging oxygen; the light is a side effect. So the comparison explains what ‘incidental’ means. Analogies in RC usually clarify the claim in the same sentence.

choices.note: CORRECT. The comparison shows how the light could be ‘incidental’: a side effect of a reaction that exists for another reason, like an engine’s heat.
Tempting if you think of wasted heat. But the passage says nothing about wasted energy here. The point is that the light isn’t the reaction’s purpose.
Too literal. Heat is the comparison, not a claim about the fungus.
The daily rhythm comes up in paragraphs 3–4. Paragraph 2 lays out the by-product view without conceding anything.
Tempting, because the sentence before is about reactive oxygen. But the comparison doesn’t explain how the reaction neutralizes oxygen; it explains why the light would be beside the point.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A puzzling phenomenon is described; two explanations of it are presented; an experiment that decides between them is reported; and the rejected explanation is used to account for a remaining anomaly.
A long-standing explanation of a phenomenon is criticized; the author proposes an alternative to it; and the evidence for that alternative is acknowledged to be incomplete.
A recent finding is reported; earlier attempts to explain the phenomenon it concerns are reviewed; and the researchers who made the finding are said to have misinterpreted it.
A phenomenon is introduced; a view denying it any function is set out along with its support; evidence favoring a rival view is described; and what that evidence leaves unsettled is considered.
A phenomenon is introduced; a view assigning it a function is set out; evidence against that view is reported; and the view is then revised so that it accommodates the evidence.
questions.explanation: The passage introduces fungal light (first paragraph), sets out the by-product view and the mycelium evidence for it (second), describes the 2015 findings that support the insect view (third), and weighs what they do and do not show (fourth): D. B is the trap: the rival view is reported as ‘a rival view’ held by others, not proposed by the author. A says the experiment decided the matter, C has the author accuse the researchers, and E gets the order of the views backward.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the order of the passage’s moves.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of each paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: P1 the phenomenon and the puzzle; P2 the ‘no purpose’ view plus its evidence (the buried mycelium); P3 the insect view plus the 2015 evidence; P4 what that evidence does and doesn’t show, and other suggestions. Now check every element of each choice against the map. A structure answer is wrong if a single element is wrong.

choices.note: ‘Decides between them’ is too strong: paragraph 4 says no account can yet be preferred.

Tempting, because the passage does criticize the old view and does call the evidence incomplete. But the author doesn’t propose the alternative. Paragraph 3 reports it as ‘a rival view,’ held by others.
The passage begins with the phenomenon, not the finding, and the author never says the researchers misread their own results.
CORRECT. Phenomenon (P1); ‘no purpose’ view with the mycelium as support (P2); evidence for the insect view (P3); what that evidence doesn’t settle (P4).
Backward. The first view described denies any function, and the passage never revises a view to fit evidence.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the glow of honey mushrooms of the genus Armillaria
choices: is probably not governed by an internal clock, since animals are unlikely to see light given off below the ground
establishes that the reaction producing fungal light first arose as a means of neutralizing reactive forms of oxygen
protects the fungus from animals that feed on it, since the light is confined to the parts such animals would eat
would be harder to explain as an aid to spreading spores than is the glow of the Brazilian mushroom studied in 2015
shows that the conclusions drawn from the 2015 study of Neonothopanus gardneri were mistaken
questions.explanation: Armillaria’s mushrooms do not glow, only its mycelium does (first paragraph); spores form on the mushroom’s gills (third paragraph); and the dispersal view leaves ‘unexplained the mycelium that glows unseen’ (fourth paragraph). So Armillaria’s glow fits the spore-dispersal view worse than a glowing mushroom does: D. B is the main trap: the passage says the buried mycelium is evidence the by-product view’s proponents cite, but ‘establishes’ is far stronger than that. A assumes a clock depends on being seen, C turns a speculation the passage mentions into a fact, and E is too strong.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer something about Armillaria by combining information from several paragraphs.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence (only the mycelium glows); paragraph 3, first sentence (spores form on the gills); paragraph 4 (the mycelium ‘glows unseen’).

breakdown.analysis: Why would anyone care that Armillaria’s mushrooms don’t glow? Chain it: 1. the insect view says light draws insects that carry off spores; 2. spores form on the mushroom’s gills; 3. in Armillaria only the buried mycelium glows, away from the spores and out of sight. So Armillaria is a bad fit for the insect view, and a worse fit than a mushroom whose own glow draws insects. We need a comparative answer. Most students who miss this take the answer that turns ‘evidence for’ the by-product view into proof of it.

choices.note: We don’t know this. Whether a glow is timed by a clock has nothing to do with whether it can be seen; the passage gives no information about Armillaria’s timing.

Tempting, because paragraph 2 says the by-product view’s supporters point to buried glowing mycelium. But the author treats this as support, and the last paragraph says no account can yet be preferred. ‘Establishes’ is far too strong.
The passage mentions that some researchers ‘propose that the glow deters animals,’ but it presents this as untested. Nothing says the light is confined to what animals would eat.

CORRECT. Spores form on gills; Armillaria’s mushrooms don’t glow; its glowing mycelium is buried and unseen. A light that draws insects to the spore-bearing mushroom (as in the 2015 study) fits the dispersal view; Armillaria’s doesn’t.
Too strong. Armillaria might be a poor fit for the dispersal view without making the 2015 findings about a different species wrong. The author treats those findings as real evidence.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with answering which one of the following questions?
choices: Why have the courts that allow recovery for a lost chance limited such recovery to cases of medical malpractice?
Is it justifiable to compensate a patient’s estate in proportion to the chance of survival that negligence destroyed?
Under what circumstances does the more-likely-than-not rule let a court decide what probably happened in a case?
Should a patient who survives despite negligent treatment be permitted to recover for a reduced chance of survival?
Does the traditional rule of causation give physicians too little reason to take care with patients whose prognoses are poor?
questions.explanation: Passage A argues against the lost-chance doctrine and passage B defends proportional recovery, so both address whether compensation proportional to the lost chance is justified: B. E is the main trap: it is the heart of passage B’s argument, but passage A never discusses the traditional rule’s effect on physicians’ care. A and D come only from passage A’s third paragraph, and C is a passing remark at the start of passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question both passages are mainly trying to answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph (‘achieves fairness only by redefining the injury’); passage B, second and third paragraphs (‘Proportional recovery corrects both errors’).

breakdown.analysis: A says the lost-chance doctrine is a bad idea. B says proportional recovery is a good one. Same doctrine, opposite verdicts. So the shared question is ‘should courts do this?’ For a ‘both passages’ question, check every choice against BOTH passages; the trap is usually one passage’s central concern.

choices.note: Only passage A raises this, and only in its last paragraph. Passage B never mentions the limits.
CORRECT. A says no (it redefines the injury and has no natural boundary); B says yes (it charges negligent physicians for the harm they actually cause).
Passage B mentions this in its first sentence on the way to its real point. Passage A doesn’t address it.
Only passage A raises the surviving patient, and only as a consequence of the doctrine’s logic. Passage B is silent.
Tempting, because it’s the core of passage B (‘a duty that cannot be enforced’). But passage A never discusses how the traditional rule affects physicians’ care. One passage’s concern, not both.

questions.stem: According to passage A, an estate that recovers damages under the lost-chance doctrine is compensated for
choices: the full value of the patient’s death, reduced by the cost of the treatment the patient actually received
an estimate, drawn from statistics, of how long the patient would have lived had the tumor been treated in time
a loss that the court has found the patient in fact suffered as a result of the physician’s negligence
the difference between the chance of survival the patient had and a chance of exactly one-half
a loss gauged by what tends to happen to similar patients, not by what befell this particular patient
questions.explanation: Passage A says ‘The estate is compensated for a statistic about patients like the decedent, and the court never determines whether this patient was among those who would have lived,’ so E is correct. C is a trap: it describes what courts do under the traditional rule, which passage A says the doctrine skips. B is a near-miss that borrows the word ‘statistic’ but attaches it to life expectancy, which passage A never mentions. D invents a formula (the passage says the fraction tracks the chance destroyed), and A is never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says the estate is actually paid for.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph, last sentence; first paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A’s complaint is that the doctrine pays for ‘a statistic about patients like the decedent’ and never asks whether this patient would have lived. So the answer should say the loss is measured by a group, not by this person.

choices.note: Passage A says recovery is a fraction ‘proportional to the chance of survival the negligence destroyed.’ Nothing about subtracting treatment costs.

Tempting, because passage A does say the estate is paid for ‘a statistic.’ But the statistic is about survival among ‘patients like the decedent,’ not about how many years this patient had left. Right word, wrong content.

Tempting, because that’s what a court normally finds in a negligence suit. But passage A’s whole objection is that ‘the court never determines whether this patient was among those who would have lived.’ This is the opposite.
An invented formula. The fraction is ‘proportional to the chance of survival the negligence destroyed,’ not measured against one-half.

CORRECT. ‘A statistic about patients like the decedent’ = what tends to happen to similar patients; ‘never determines whether this patient was among those who would have lived’ = not what befell this patient.

questions.stem: By saying that physicians owe some patients “a duty that cannot be enforced” (first sentence of the second paragraph of passage B), the author of passage B most probably means that
choices: under the traditional rule, careless treatment of certain patients carries no legal consequence for physicians
physicians have no legal obligation to treat those patients whose chance of survival is below one-half
courts usually lack the evidence they need to determine whether a physician’s treatment was careless
patients with poor prognoses seldom bring negligence suits against the physicians who treated them
the standard of care owed to patients with poor prognoses is too vague for courts to apply it consistently
questions.explanation: The phrase sums up the first paragraph of passage B: under the traditional rule every patient whose chance was below one-half ‘lost nothing, however careless the treatment,’ so negligence toward those patients brings no liability. A says this. C is the trap: passage B’s uncertainty concerns causation, whether the patient would have survived, not whether the treatment was careless, which its examples take as given (‘negligently reduces’). B denies that the duty exists, which the phrase presupposes, and D and E are never suggested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decide what passage B means by a duty that can’t be enforced.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph, last sentence, and second paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: A duty that ‘cannot be enforced’ still exists; the problem is that breaking it costs nothing. Why does it cost nothing? Paragraph 1 says: under the traditional rule, a patient below one-half ‘lost nothing, however careless the treatment.’ The 45-to-10 example makes it concrete: clearly negligent, no liability. So the phrase means ‘physicians can be careless with these patients and face no legal consequence.’ Note what is uncertain here: whether this patient would have lived, not whether the doctor was careless.

choices.note: CORRECT. Below one-half, the traditional rule says the patient ‘lost nothing, however careless the treatment,’ so breaching the duty carries no liability.
The phrase assumes the duty exists (physicians ‘owe’ it). The problem is enforcement, not the absence of an obligation.

Tempting, because passage B is all about uncertainty and evidence that ‘will never reveal’ something. But what can’t be revealed is whether the patient would have survived: causation. Its examples stipulate the negligence (‘negligently reduces’). Wrong kind of uncertainty.
Passage B says nothing about how often such patients sue. The point is that suing would get them nothing.
Passage B never says the standard of care is unclear. Its examples treat the negligence as clear; the obstacle is the causation rule.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A?
choices: a requirement that a plaintiff show that the defendant’s negligence more likely than not caused the harm that he or she complains of
a patient whose chance of survival was negligently reduced but who nonetheless went on to survive
a case in which negligence that only slightly reduced a patient’s chance of survival results in liability for an entire death
damages reduced in proportion to the chance of survival that a physician’s negligence destroyed
a defense of the doctrine of lost chance on grounds of fairness to patients and their estates
questions.explanation: Passage B’s physician who ‘reduces a 55 percent chance to 50 percent is liable for the full value of the death,’ and passage A has no such case, so C is correct. D is the main trap: passage B calls it ‘proportional recovery’ without spelling it out, but passage A describes it in its first paragraph, so it appears in both. A is also in both; B and E appear only in passage A (its third and second paragraphs).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find something passage B mentions that passage A does not.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph, second sentence. Check each choice against all of passage A.

breakdown.analysis: Go choice by choice and check both passages; don’t trust memory. The 55-to-50 physician is in B only: a five-point drop and full liability. Proportional damages look like B’s idea because B names ‘proportional recovery,’ but A describes the same thing in detail (‘a fraction of the damages … proportional to the chance … destroyed’). Fairness looks like B’s theme, but the word appears only in A. ‘B but not A’ questions punish answers that are in both, or only in the other one.

choices.note: This is in both. Passage A opens with it, and passage B’s ‘more-likely-than-not rule’ is the same requirement.
Only passage A mentions this, in its third paragraph, as a consequence of the doctrine’s logic.
CORRECT. Passage B’s 55-to-50 physician: a small drop in the chance of survival, full liability for the death. Passage A gives only the 40 percent example, where the estate recovers nothing.

Tempting, because ‘proportional recovery’ is passage B’s phrase. But passage A describes exactly this in its first paragraph: ‘a fraction of the damages for the death, proportional to the chance of survival the negligence destroyed.’ It’s in both.
Passage A says the doctrine ‘is usually defended as a matter of fairness.’ Passage B’s defense rests on making physicians pay for the harm they cause, and it never uses the word. Only in A.

questions.stem: The attitude of the author of passage A toward the limits that courts adopting the lost-chance doctrine have placed on it (third paragraph of passage A) is most accurately described as
choices: approval, on the grounds that the limits follow directly from the doctrine’s own conception of the injury it compensates
disapproval, on the grounds that the limits deny recovery to plaintiffs whom the doctrine’s reasoning would entitle to it
indifference, since the author’s objection to the doctrine concerns only the way in which it defines the injury
suspicion, since the limits are taken to disguise the courts’ real reason for adopting the doctrine in the first place
denial that the doctrine supports them, combined with the view that they betray the courts’ unwillingness to accept its consequences
questions.explanation: Passage A says ‘nothing in its logic supports either limit’ and reads the limits as signs that the courts ‘sense where the doctrine leads and decline to follow it,’ which denies the limits any doctrinal footing and treats them as revealing the courts’ refusal to accept where the doctrine goes: E. B is the strongest trap: passage A does say the doctrine’s logic reaches survivors and risk-exposed people, but it presents that extension as a problem for the doctrine, not as a right the limits wrongly deny. A reverses ‘nothing in its logic supports,’ C ignores the third paragraph, and D invents a hidden motive.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decide how the author of passage A feels about the courts’ limits on the doctrine.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Two separate judgments are packed into the last two sentences. 1. ‘Nothing in its logic supports either limit’: the limits aren’t justified by the doctrine. 2. The limits are ‘signs that these courts sense where the doctrine leads and decline to follow it’: the courts see the doctrine’s consequences and won’t accept them. The author uses that as evidence against the doctrine. Most students who miss this read ‘nothing supports the limits’ as ‘the limits are bad’ and pick the disapproval answer.

choices.note: This reverses the paragraph: ‘nothing in its logic supports either limit.’

Tempting, because the author does say the doctrine’s reasoning would reach survivors and people merely exposed to risk. But the author offers that as a reason to doubt the doctrine, not as a complaint that those people are wrongly denied recovery.
Paragraph 3 is a second, separate objection about the doctrine’s lack of a natural boundary. The author is anything but indifferent to the limits.
The author reads the limits as an honest sign of unease, not as a cover for some hidden reason. Invented motive.

CORRECT. No support in the doctrine: ‘nothing in its logic supports either limit.’ Betray the courts’ unwillingness: the limits are ‘signs that these courts sense where the doctrine leads and decline to follow it.’

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the last paragraph of passage B and the argument made in the third paragraph of passage A?
choices: Passage B’s last paragraph concedes passage A’s argument but maintains that the traditional rule suffers from the same difficulty.
If passage B’s last paragraph is correct, it supplies a basis for one of the limits that passage A says the doctrine cannot justify.
Passage B’s last paragraph does not bear on passage A’s argument, since it concerns how an injury is defined rather than how far a doctrine extends.
Passage B’s last paragraph strengthens passage A’s argument, since a harm that is measured as a probability could be claimed by anyone exposed to a risk.
Passage B’s last paragraph rebuts passage A’s argument by pointing out that courts have in fact confined recovery to cases of medical malpractice.
questions.explanation: Passage A’s third paragraph says that if a diminished chance is itself the injury, survivors and anyone exposed to risk would have claims, so nothing in the doctrine supports limiting it to patients who suffered the harm. Passage B’s last paragraph says the injury is still death, measured as a probability; if so, a patient who survives has suffered no compensable injury, which grounds that limit: B. C is the trap: passage B never mentions survivors or limits, but passage A derives its boundary problem from the definition of the injury, so a different definition bears directly on it. A and E misdescribe passage B, and D reverses its effect.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out how passage B’s closing claim bears on passage A’s ‘no natural boundary’ objection.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph (‘If a diminished chance is itself a compensable injury…’); passage B, last paragraph (‘measuring an old one, death’).

breakdown.analysis: Passage B never mentions survivors or careless drivers, so it’s natural to think it ignores passage A’s boundary objection. But look at how passage A builds that objection: IF the injury is a lost chance, THEN survivors and risk-exposed people have claims too. Passage B denies the IF: the injury is death, measured by probability. Then a patient who lived has no injury, which is exactly the limit (‘patients who actually suffered the harm’) that passage A says the doctrine can’t justify. So B’s reframing, if right, answers part of A’s objection without saying so. Most students pick the ‘does not bear on’ answer because the two paragraphs use different words; the link is in the logic, not the vocabulary.

choices.note: Passage B concedes nothing to passage A. It denies that the doctrine invents a new injury, and it never says the traditional rule has a boundary problem.

CORRECT. On passage B’s view, the injury compensated is death, so someone who didn’t die has no claim. That supports the limit to ‘patients who actually suffered the harm,’ one of the two limits passage A says ‘nothing in its logic supports.’ ‘One of the limits’ is right: B’s view doesn’t obviously confine the doctrine to medicine.

Tempting, because passage B’s last paragraph never mentions limits, survivors, or other kinds of cases. But passage A’s boundary objection starts from ‘If a diminished chance is itself a compensable injury.’ A claim about what the injury is goes straight to the premise of that objection.
This reverses the effect. On passage B’s view the injury is death, so mere exposure to risk, without death, gives no claim. That narrows the doctrine rather than widening it.
Passage B never mentions how courts have confined the doctrine. That fact appears only in passage A, and passage A uses it against the doctrine.
